shbl:story-001:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees' No. 1 | Wuzhong District, Tianping Mountain | Chinese Sweetgum
shbl:story-001:body-1.text_en:
Tianping Mountain, southwest of the old city of Suzhou, is where the family roots of Fan Zhongyan, a celebrated worthy of Wuzhong in the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127 CE), lie. On the southern slope of Tianping Mountain are 121 ancient Ming-dynasty (1368–1644 CE) Chinese sweetgums over 420 years old, planted during the Wanli reign of the Ming by Fan Yunlin, a 17th-generation descendant of Fan Zhongyan; they are the same age as Tianping Mountain Villa, a representative late-Ming Jiangnan mountain garden. Since the 1980s, the Tianping Mountain Scenic Area has held a Red Maple Festival, and going to Tianping Mountain to admire the red sweetgum leaves has become a must-do autumn activity for many Suzhou residents. This is the largest group of ancient Chinese sweetgums in East China; when temperatures fall, the net chlorophyll content drops, and during the color-change period the sweetgum leaves pass through three stages: green, yellow, and red.
Since field surveys began in 2022, every year at the end of October volunteers have had to keep pace with actual conditions; to photograph the ancient sweetgums when the whole forest is dyed, they ask daily, 'Have the sweetgums on Tianping Mountain turned red yet?' On October 24, 2023, we received a report from a journalist with the column 'The King Sends Him to Patrol the Mountain' from the front: 'A few trees have turned red; overall they haven't, and although the trees aren't fully red, the surging crowds are already in place!' Everyone joked: 'Waiting for plants to change color is like waiting for bananas to ripen—there's always a process. When viewing color-changing trees, at first you look for the multicolored display; if they all turned red at once, it would actually take away some of the fun of autumn viewing.' What is beyond doubt is that, under the anticipation of countless Suzhou residents, the ancient sweetgums always meet us once a year, keeping their appointment on schedule.
shbl:story-001:body-1.hook_zh: 天平山南麓121株明代枫香，与范允临的天平山庄同龄。
shbl:story-001:body-1.hook_en: The 121 Ming-dynasty sweetgums on Tianping Mountain's southern slope are the same age as Fan Yunlin's Tianping Mountain Villa.

shbl:story-001:body-2.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees' No. 1 | Wuzhong District, Tianping Mountain | Buddhist Pine
shbl:story-001:body-2.text_en: At the foot of Tianping Mountain stands a nearly 500-year-old Ming-dynasty Buddhist pine, traditionally said to have been planted by Tang Yin; it is the 'CP tree' (paired counterpart) of the wisteria planted by Wen Zhengming's own hand. The stout, upright, straight pine is too thick to encircle with both arms; its wrinkled, rough bark has witnessed the vicissitudes of time, and after countless storms it still stands proudly.

shbl:story-001:body-3.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees' No. 1 | Wuzhong District, Tianping Mountain | Masson Pine (no longer extant)
shbl:story-001:body-3.text_en: In ancient Suzhou, Masson pines were commonly planted in courtyards and at temples and monasteries, but most were felled and used for other purposes. According to documentary records, the largest concentrations of ancient pines were in the Tianping Mountain and Zhixing Mountain area west of the city; Masson pine was once the main tree species in Suzhou's mountain forests, and the naturally growing Masson pines of the western hills continued until the 1950s, after which they failed to survive because of infestation by the pine bast scale insect.

shbl:story-002:body-1.context_header_en: "Steles for Trees": Tree Stories, Entry 2 | Wuzhong District, Dongwan Well Field, Aiguo Village, Jinting Town | Camphor Tree
shbl:story-002:body-1.text_en: Suzhou has many camphor trees, and Xishan has especially many, including many ancient camphor trees over a thousand years old. Dongwan Well Field in Aiguo Village has the largest group of ancient camphor trees in Suzhou: five ancient camphor trees stand side by side in a row. Finding these trees takes some effort. Following the location of Aiguo Village, the volunteers drove in along a small road that grew narrower and narrower; but once they reached the village entrance, they felt as if they had "discovered another world." The ancient camphor grove is tall and dense, with luxuriant branches and leaves, lush and green, each tree different in form. Their trunk diameters are all over 1 meter, and their crowns together reach 1,000 square meters, like a natural curtain, a canopy of green shade.

shbl:story-002:body-1.hook_en: Five ancient camphor trees stand in a row at Dongwan Well Field in Aiguo Village, each trunk over 1 meter across, their crowns together spanning about 1,000 square meters.

shbl:story-002:body-2.context_header_en: "Steles for Trees": Tree Stories, Entry 2 | Wuzhong District, Sanguan Hall, Jinting Town | Dragon Juniper
shbl:story-002:body-2.text_en:
The oldest Dragon Juniper in the area stands at Sanguan Hall in Jinting Town and is about 1,500 years old. Seeing 吴中009 for the first time was a wondrous tree-seeking experience. At first the volunteers walked down a small path and saw the ancient camphor grove at the entrance to Aiguo Village; afterward, following a signpost beside the ancient camphors, they went deeper along the road. It was a long, narrow road, too narrow even for a car to pass, so they could only go on foot. At that moment, two of the tree-seeking volunteers independently thought of Tao Yuanming's "Peach Blossom Spring": "At first it was extremely narrow, barely admitting a person; after going on another few dozen paces, it suddenly opened out: level land, neat houses, with fine fields, beautiful ponds, and mulberry and bamboo. Paths crisscrossed, and the crowing of cocks and barking of dogs could be heard from one to the other."
Sanguan Hall is still a Daoist temple that local residents worship at on the first and fifteenth days of every lunar month. Inside the hall are enshrined statues of the Three Officials of Heaven, Earth, and Water; it was first built during the Northern and Southern Dynasties period. Unfortunately, on this first visit, which came about by chance, they had not done their homework thoroughly: the Dragon Juniper grows in the courtyard of Sanguan Hall, and to walk into the courtyard and touch its trunk, one can only come back when Sanguan Hall opens on the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month.
A tiny village and a tiny Daoist building can nonetheless accommodate a rare ancient Dragon Juniper of the Jiangnan region—truly unexpected. Through the transformations of the world, the tree has kept its roots here, growing upward, growing until it reaches the sky, and becoming a guardian spirit in the hearts of local residents.
shbl:story-002:body-2.hook_zh: 金庭三官殿院内约1500年的龙柏，为本地树龄最长，仅初一十五开门时可近。
shbl:story-002:body-2.hook_en: The roughly 1,500-year-old Dragon Juniper in the courtyard of Sanguan Hall in Jinting Town is the area's oldest tree, approachable only when the hall opens on the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month.

shbl:story-003:body-1.context_header_en: 'Trees with Steles' Tree Stories, Entry 3 | Wuzhong District, Jinting Town, Yinshan Island | Camphor Tree
shbl:story-003:body-1.text_en:
Driving onto Yinshan Island, between water and sky, one suddenly sees an ancient camphor standing tall, giving one the feeling of a lone tree keeping watch. For a very long period in the past, Yinshan Island hung in the middle of the lake with a sparse population; the ancient camphor was the representative of the island's lush vitality and could well be called the little island's guardian spirit. Local villagers say this tree was planted in the Tianji 4th year of Sun Hao of the Wu state during the Three Kingdoms period, more than 1,800 years ago, but judging by the current tree-age survey results, this legend can clearly only serve as mealtime conversation.
The ancient camphor's trunk is extremely massive; every time the volunteers went to Yinshan for field surveys, they could see tourists joining hands in a ring around the tree, trying to find out how many people it takes to embrace this ancient camphor with a circumference of 5.83 meters. A thousand-year-old camphor needs more room to grow, and the island's original residents are also glad to create good living conditions for the ancient camphor, and hung an 'Ancient Camphor Discussion Point' sign on its trunk, representing that this ancient camphor has become a public space for the villagers.
shbl:story-003:body-1.hook_zh: 阴山岛古樟树围5.83米，村民传说植于孙皓天纪四年，树上挂着“古樟议事点”。
shbl:story-003:body-1.hook_en: The Yinshan Island camphor measures 5.83 m around; villagers say it was planted in Sun Hao's Tianji 4th year, and it bears a 'Camphor Discussion Point' sign.

shbl:story-004:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees' in Tree Steles and Biographies, Entry 4 | Wuzhong District, Ancient Camphor Garden, Jinting Town | Camphor Tree
shbl:story-004:body-1.text_en: Xishan is a paradise for ancient camphor trees, and there is even a scenic spot named after the camphor: the Ancient Camphor Garden, situated at the eastern foot of the Xishan hills. A Song cypress and a Yuan cypress stand there, the two trees forming a grove, lush and green. When time returns to the 1990s, the area around the Ancient Camphor Garden was still an unremarkable warehouse district. The villagers of Houbao Village could not bear to see such a place of outstanding natural beauty go to waste, so they raised funds to renovate the buildings in this area. A stele stands at the mountain gate of the Ancient Camphor Garden, erected after Houbao Village renovated the garden in 1995; it records that the site of the Ancient Camphor Garden 'enshrined Guanyin in the Song and worshipped the City God in the Qing.' Both camphor trees long coexisted with the Guanyin Temple, the City God Temple, and other temples; in ancient times, temples such as the Guanyin Temple were themselves public spaces, serving to entertain the masses and to provide moral instruction. Here the ancient camphors played a role in which the ancient temple and the ancient trees complemented each other; on the other hand, because of their great height and other factors, the camphors could only be planted in open places, and in this way the camphor trees could functionally serve the public. Many temples and Daoist monasteries in Suzhou held temple fairs, markets, and similar activities, and the camphor trees themselves thus became markers of public space.

shbl:story-005:body-1.context_header_en: Tree Stories, Entry 5 | Wuzhong District, Jinting Town, Mingyue Bay Ancient Village | Camphor Tree
shbl:story-005:body-1.text_en: For a long period, Mingyue Bay on West Hill drew the attention of the world. The Suzhou Prefecture Gazetteer records that this was "the place where the King of Wu enjoyed the moon," hence the name Mingyue Bay. But judging from the documents currently visible, Mingyue Bay probably began to win the favor of literati around the Tang dynasty (618–907 CE). Bai Juyi, Prefect of Suzhou, often went boating on Lake Tai, and in a letter to a friend he expressed his love for the scenery of the valleys around Mingyue Bay: "Lake and hills everywhere are good for lingering; I love best the East Bay and the head of the northern valley." About half a century later, torrential rains caused disaster in Suzhou. Pi Rixiu, then military judge of Suzhou, and his friend Lu Guimeng went to Linwu Cave on West Hill to sacrifice to the water god, and took the opportunity to tour all the famous sites of West Hill, each leaving behind a poem on the same topic, "Mingyue Bay." Yet whether Bai Juyi or Lu and Pi, their fame at Mingyue Bay fell far short of another Tang poet, Liu Changqing—and all because of a tree. In his poem "Seeking He Jiu at Mingyue Bay but Not Finding Him," Liu Changqing records that he traveled to West Hill to visit a friend: "The old friend is absent, the bright moon is here; who has seen the lone boat come and go?" Legend has it that after failing to find his friend, Liu Changqing could not bear his melancholy and planted a camphor tree. This camphor tree has weathered more than a thousand years and has been preserved to this day. The story appears in no other document, and may be simply a beautiful legend.

shbl:story-005:interview-1.context_header_en: Tree Stories, Entry 5 | Wuzhong District, Jinting Town, Mingyue Bay Ancient Village | Camphor Tree | Interview: Mr. Huang
shbl:story-005:interview-1.text_en:
Mr. Huang: The name of Mingyue Bay Ancient Village comes from King Fuchai of Wu and Xi Shi coming here to enjoy the moon during the Spring and Autumn period. This ancient camphor is called by locals the Longevity Tree and the Immortal Tree. The tree was once burned. There are saw marks on its roots. Its 1,200-year history is like a museum. Its shape is like a grandfather carrying his grandson on his back. Its shade is especially cool.
Volunteer Luo Xinglin: I hear you always sit beside the ancient camphor, guarding this tree. Is there a story behind that?
Mr. Huang: In 1939, Japanese invaders went all over West Hill cutting trees. A local tyrant of West Hill brought people to Mingyue Bay to saw down the ancient camphor. The villagers could only pool money to avert disaster, and some elderly people even knelt and pleaded, only then did the men reluctantly agree to stop sawing. The saw marks left then are still there today. In 1940, a band of bandits rushed into Mingyue Bay and insisted on cutting the tree. The villagers rose up in opposition. Seeing they could not get their way for the moment, the bandits took advantage of people's inattention and kidnapped me, then only ten years old, from Mingyue Bay to Zhejiang. Only after 36 days did the villagers manage to collect 120 shi of rice and redeem me from the bandits. Later, I felt I had a responsibility to protect this tree. For decades, rain or shine, I have only felt at ease guarding beside this tree.
While being interviewed, Mr. Huang saw a passing tour group of elderly visitors. He warmly encouraged the elderly tourists to touch the sacred tree with both hands, mentioning several times that the Qianlong emperor (reigned 1735–1796) had also touched it, and wishing everyone peace and long life.

shbl:story-006:body-1.context_header_en: "Steles for Trees" Tree Stories, Entry 6 | Luohan Temple, Bingchang Village, Jinting Town, Wuzhong District | Camphor Tree
shbl:story-006:body-1.text_en:
Following the broad, level path through Luohan Hollow for some dozens of paces, one comes upon another stone-carved archway. Inscribed on its architrave in clerical script are the words "Ancient Luohan Temple," written by the Republic-era scholar Li Genyuan when he visited Xishan in 1929. On either side hangs a couplet composed by Shen Bingchun: "The wind makes melody of Buddhist chants; an ancient tree's path leads to quiet seclusion." Before seeing the tree, one already grasps its meaning. The wondrous sight of the wisteria and camphor intertwined stands before Luohan Temple. Two ancient camphor trees have flourished for six hundred years; their crowns rise above the surrounding grove, their branches and leaves lush, their deep shade blotting out the sun. Around the trunk of one of these camphor trees coils a three-hundred-year-old Chinese wisteria, its vines winding upward along the camphor's trunk as if rushing into the clouds.
On April 15, 2023, when volunteers came according to the wisteria's blooming season in the city, they could see only a few flower buds high up on the ancient wisteria deep in the mountain hollow. Everyone wondered: could it be that the wisteria has decided not to bloom this year? An uncle who volunteers at Luohan Temple told us that temperatures in the mountains are lower, the ancient tree's crown blocks the sun, and the ancient tree near the ground gets little sunlight, so every year its blooming season comes later than in the city; we might as well come back a week later.
To photograph the wisteria and camphor with the wisteria in full bloom as it entwined the camphor, on April 23, 2023, everyone drove again to Jinting Town. How to describe the tree-viewing experience that day? One volunteer recalled that this was the most spectacular ancient tree encountered since the field survey began: the wisteria seen from the drone's viewpoint clung to the tree and climbed, like a purple waterfall hanging down, like stars of the Milky Way studding the sky; sitting or lying beneath it, one could well forget the world.

shbl:story-007:body-1.context_header_en: "Stories of Trees" No. 7 | Chunxi Hall, Jinting Town, Wuzhong District | Lacebark Pine
shbl:story-007:body-1.text_en:
Chunxi Hall stands at Dongcai on West Hill in the Dongting area, a place of true retreat hidden within the town. In its garden grows a lacebark pine with snow-white branches and emerald leaves, tall and vigorous, aged 200 years. The lacebark pine, also called the toothpick pine or the guozi pine, was already widely planted in the private courtyards of Suzhou during the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE).
Chunxi Hall was first built during the Qianlong era (Qing emperor, reigned 1735–1796). The house's age is comparable to the tree's; its owners were Cai Chunxin and his son, who long did business away from home. According to local gazetteers, their building activity began in the Qianlong era and continued until the end of the Taiping Heavenly Kingdom movement. After that, no further construction at Chunxi Hall is recorded; by the late Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE), the Cai descendants even sold the ancestral residence to others. Leafing through dusty old papers, we found with difficulty that in March 1889 the Shenbao published a notice terminating the lease of Chunxi Hall, its lines filled with the family's poverty and destitution.
A painstakingly built family home changed hands because later generations managed it poorly. The lacebark pine, its roots and leaves having stood through several sixty-year cycles, was bound tightly to the fate of Chunxi Hall; as things changed and stars moved, this ancient tree also witnessed the line "The pavilion too stands empty; this tree, for whom does it wait?".

shbl:story-008:body-1.context_header_en: “Steles for Trees” Tree Stories, No. 8 | Wuzhong District, Dajue Temple Site, Chengdun Village, Luzhi Town | Ginkgo
shbl:story-008:body-1.text_en: In 1974, the former Chefang Commune of Wu County enclosed the lake to reclaim farmland on the western shore of Cheng Lake. After the lake water was pumped dry, a large number of ancient wells were discovered on the lakebed, and a great quantity of cultural relics was unearthed, among them the black-slipped pottery jar with incised symbols and tubular handles displayed in the “Archaeology Explores Wuzhong” exhibition hall. This site lies today in Chengdun Village and Dayao Village on the western side of Cheng Lake in Luzhi Town; it was originally “Yaocheng,” a fief of the Spring and Autumn period, and the natural village “Dongjieshang” in the southeastern corner of Chengdun Village was in ancient times the market street of Yaocheng. Not far away, Dajue Temple Bridge was first built in the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127 CE) and rebuilt in the 11th year of the Zhizheng reign era of the Yuan dynasty; its body bears rare and exquisite carvings, and 60 meters to its east stands a Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE) Xianghua Bridge. Dajue Temple no longer exists; only the two ancient ginkgo trees on the site remain, standing apart from the world, holding out against the vast torrent of time.

shbl:story-009:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees' No. 9 | Wuxiang Street, Wuxiang Village, Dongshan Town, Wuzhong District | Ginkgo
shbl:story-009:body-1.text_en: The site of the old Yilü Garden is on Wuxiang Street in Wuxiang Village, Dongshan Town. Two ginkgos surviving in the narrow lane grow next to each other, one male and one female; locals call them the husband-and-wife tree (though observation shows that both trees bear white nuts, which is puzzling). According to the Republican-era Wuxian County Gazetteer: "Yilü Garden is recorded at the foot of Mount Wu on East Dongting; it was built by the recluse Wu Shiya, and within it were such scenic spots as Nancun Thatched Hall, Shuixiang Yi, Feixia Pavilion, Xinjia Ge, and Ningxue Tower. It was first named Xiangqi Xiaozhu; Tao Zishi, a jinshi from Mount Yu, took a line from Du Shaoling's poetry and named it Yilü, and Xu Qianxue wrote a record of it." From this description, the garden once contained distinctive garden scenery, and the garden built at Wuxiang took its name from the meaning of Du Fu's line "a famous garden leans on green water." The ginkgos now on Wuxiang Street are two trees from the early Northern Song dynasty (960–1127 CE) preserved from the old garden; among them, tree "吴中084" is 48 meters tall and should be the ancient tree with the greatest vertical height in the entire greater Suzhou area.

shbl:story-010:body-1.context_header_en: 'Steles for Trees' Tree Stories, Entry 10 | Wuzhong District, Beiwang Lingxia Village, Dongshan Town | Ginkgo
shbl:story-010:body-1.text_en: Driving into Dongshan Town in autumn, you need not seek it out deliberately to take in the boundless scenery of this 'home of ginkgo': ginkgos are planted everywhere—in the fields, by the lakeshore, in front of and behind houses—glowing with color. In villages such as Huwan, Guangming, Yangwan, Shangwan, Chawan and Baisha there are ancient ginkgos more than 500 years old. The tree with the longest registered age in Suzhou is hidden in Beiwang Lingxia Village, Dongshan Town; if its 2,000-year age is accurate, then it was planted as far back as the Western Han. Villagers regard it as a 'sacred tree,' setting up an offering table beside it and building a small niche, where incense is kept burning year-round. The ancient tree's nameplate is wrapped around a slender new shoot; judging only from a photograph, one would mistake it for a young sapling. In fact, that is just one of the many suckering branches at the base of the trunk: after being struck by lightning, only a quarter of its trunk remained, yet dense new shoots sprouted from the roots. Long before humans appeared, the 'living fossil' ginkgo had already existed in the world for hundreds of millions of years. Its powerful capacity for self-healing and renewal is one of the secrets of this species' enduring survival.

shbl:story-011:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees Told by Steles' Story 11 | Beiwang Lingxia Village, Dongshan Town, Wuzhong District | Buddhist Pine and Chinese Chestnut
shbl:story-011:body-1.text_en:
During his residence in Suzhou from 1923 to 1937, Mr. Li Genyuan, a veteran of the Republican era, traveled throughout the western hills of Wu Commandery conducting antiquarian research and collecting and organizing a great deal of local historical material. He wrote such important documentary works as Records of Antiquarian Visits to the Western Hills of Wu and Epigraphic Record of Suzhou Studies, and took part in compiling the Gazetteer of Wu County. He once described the Buddhist pine at Lingyuan Temple thus: "Entering Lingyuan Temple, there is one Buddhist pine, so large that it takes several arm-spans to encircle. There is also a tree called qi, gnarled and knotted, coiled and spreading, shading the whole temple courtyard. Sitting a while in the Keyue Hall, boiling Ling Spring water and trying Biluochun tea, one finds a distinctive flavor. The beauty of Biluochun is renowned throughout the land—how could its fame be unearned! Ascending Biluo Peak, then going up to the Yanwu Mound, then up to the Tinggong Mound, and finally to the summit of Song Peak. Following the Baizhi Ridge down, I viewed the tomb of Ye Ting, a Song dynasty official with the rank of Zhongfeng Dafu. A great rain suddenly came on, and I returned to my lodging at Stone Bridge." Even today, Li Genyuan's cliff inscription can still be found on Biluo Peak.
Besides being extraordinarily old—traceable all the way back to the Northern and Southern Dynasties period 1,500 years ago—this Buddhist pine has also been endowed with spiritual power by the local people, who call it the "spirit tree," and so it is of extraordinary significance. When we spoke with Abbot Guohe of Lingyuan Temple, we learned that Lingyuan Temple was first built in the first year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty (502 CE) and was named for the temple's Ling Spring. Since its founding the temple has been destroyed several times; in the Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE) the Dongshan native Wang Jinzeng proposed its restoration, in the Republican era it was severely damaged and dismantled, and today it has been rebuilt anew.
The Buddhist pine, the same age as the temple, also miraculously underwent a "revival from death." According to Abbot Guohe of the ancient temple, this tree at one point had withered branches and trunk, and was once struck squarely by lightning, leaving a crack that ran all the way to the ground; yet now it has put out new shoots from the withered branches, with luxuriant foliage, vigorous and upright.
On the road from Lingyuan Temple toward Biluo Peak, one passes an ancient Chinese chestnut tree. Standing here and looking west, one can gaze far off to Lake Tai; this is also the best spot for photographing the Buddhist pine. As winter gives way to spring, each time the volunteers go to Dongshan for surveys, they make a point of visiting Lingyuan Temple to see the two ancient trees, finding them growing freely in the open country, like Lingyuan Temple itself, continuing the line of incense smoke and keeping watch over this land.

shbl:story-011:fieldnote-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees Told by Steles' Story 11 | Beiwang Lingxia Village, Dongshan Town, Wuzhong District | Buddhist Pine and Chinese Chestnut | Volunteer Visit Record
shbl:story-011:fieldnote-1.text_en:
Auntie Pingping photographed with the Chinese chestnut tree
The standard for defining an ancient or notable tree is 100 years of age or more, yet surveys of ancient and notable trees often overlook many trees growing in the countryside that are not easily noticed. Volunteers for 'Stories of Trees Told by Steles' met Auntie Pingping, who was gathering medicinal herbs near Lingyuan Temple. Hearing that we were surveying ancient trees, she mentioned the Chinese chestnut trees her maternal grandfather had planted. Auntie Pingping is now over sixty; her grandfather, during his lifetime, planted several dozen Chinese chestnut trees on Biluo Peak, and by reckoning of time these trees may already have passed the age threshold that defines an ancient tree.
She recalled that in those years her grandfather and granduncle planted several dozen trees on Biluo Peak; later, because of inadequate care, many had been cut down, leaving only some Chinese chestnuts, loquats, and orange trees mixed with tea on the hillside. After the interview ended, we suggested to her that we take a group photo of her with the chestnut trees her grandfather had planted. She smiled and lowered her head, one hand touching the tree and the other holding the tea leaves she had just picked, and said to us: "If you ever have the chance, please help speak up about the ancient trees too."

shbl:story-012:body-1.context_header_en: "Steles for Trees" Tree Stories, No. 12 | Wuzhong District, Dongshan Town, Mingshan Hall | Wintersweet
shbl:story-012:body-1.text_en: Wintersweet (Chimonanthus praecox) gets its name because its fragrance resembles that of plum and its color resembles wax. The ancients once confused wintersweet with plum blossom, until the Southern Song dynasty (1127–1279 CE), when Fan Chengda, who lived at Shihu in Suzhou, clearly pointed out in his Fan Village Plum Manual that wintersweet is not a plum: "Wintersweet is originally not of the plum kind; because it blooms at the same time as plum, its fragrance is also similar, and its color entirely resembles a honeycomb, it is so named." He also divided it into three categories according to flower form: "There are in all three kinds. Those grown from seed and never grafted have small flowers and faint fragrance and rank lowest; they are called Jiuying Mei, popularly corrupted to Gouying Mei. Those that have been grafted and whose flowers are half-open are called Jingkou Mei. Those deep yellow like red sandalwood and especially strongly fragrant are called Tanxiang Mei; this kind is the best." In recent decades, wintersweet has been cultivated in courtyards, gardens, and parks throughout Suzhou, flowering in early January each year.

shbl:story-012:body-2.context_header_en: "Steles for Trees" Tree Stories, No. 12 | Wuzhong District, Dongshan Town, Mingshan Hall | Chinese Boxwood
shbl:story-012:body-2.text_en: Inside Mingshan Hall in Dongshan there are three ancient trees. Besides the wintersweet and the camellia, the oldest is the Chinese boxwood (Buxus sinica) coded 吴中163, about 612 years old. Chinese boxwood is also called Wulong Mu ("dark-dragon wood") and Wannian Qing ("evergreen"). It tolerates shade but likes light, and paired with the rockery in a courtyard it is especially elegant. It grows slowly and is extremely difficult to care for; that this boxwood has survived the vicissitudes of time and still has luxuriant branches and a canopy of green shade is truly no small feat. Its trunk and branches are vigorous and thrust out beyond the courtyard's high wall toward the sky, much in the manner described in an old poem: "A boxwood a few feet tall, with a thousand layers of twisting branches; deep leaves like emerald in a garden, it sits ancient like a coiled dragon."

shbl:story-012:background-1.context_header_en: "Steles for Trees" Tree Stories, No. 12 | Wuzhong District, Dongshan Town, Mingshan Hall | Wintersweet and Chinese Boxwood | Background: Mingshan Hall
shbl:story-012:background-1.text_en:
Mingshan Hall
Mingshan Hall is located in the ancient village of Yangwan in Dongshan and is listed as a Major Historical and Cultural Site Protected at the National Level. It consists mainly of a brick-carved gatehouse, a main hall, a flower hall, and a Buddhist worship building. Its main hall is an early residential hall of the late Ming (1368–1644 CE) to early Qing (1644–1912 CE) period of exceptionally high artistic quality. The brick-carved gatehouse and the main hall are solemn and orderly in form, models of Suzhou residential architecture. The details of its three forms of carving and painted decoration incorporate the owner's aesthetic tastes: in the brick-carved gatehouse, for example, the spaces between the architraves are filled with inlaid floral geometric patterns, and the sumeru pedestals bear motifs such as peony scrolls and lotus with mandarin ducks; in the main hall, flowers and birds are carved in the mountain-mist and beam-embracing clouds, and the painted decoration is adorned with flowers such as lotus and baoxiang blossoms. These highly distinctive decorative features echo faintly the small garden in front of the flower hall. The flower hall stands to the front left of the main hall; its front courtyard contains a small garden planted with wintersweet and camellia, while its rear courtyard is planted with Chinese boxwood—in contrast to the solemn, orderly ritual order of the main axis, it appears more lively. Residential buildings in the Wuzhong area seem mostly to have treated the main hall as a stern place for receiving guests and socializing, while the flower hall to one side was the more relaxed study or place for enjoying the garden; for example, the lacebark pine of Chunxi Hall in this exhibition is likewise in the small garden in front of a flower hall. Times have changed, yet we can still imagine the owner's elegant life in Mingshan Hall's flower hall: admiring camellia in spring, leaning by the boxwood in summer, and picking wintersweet in winter. So where is autumn? Dongshan has been a land of ginkgo since ancient times; the cool autumn wind will of course invite sheet after sheet of yellow leaves onto the owner's desk.

shbl:story-013:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees Told by Steles' Story 13 | Wuzhong District, Yuwuxia Village, Dongshan Town | Qiu Catalpa
shbl:story-013:body-1.text_en:
A century-old qiu catalpa, numbered '吴中076', stands behind Mengjiang Hall in Yuwuxia Village, Group 5 of Biluo Village, Dongshan. The old tree is not easy to find, but Mengjiang Hall, which carries the faith of Dongshan's villagers, is known to everyone you ask. This small temple, three bays wide, is already a hundred years old, and its hall plaque reads 'Liu Fu Zhong Tian Wang' (Central Heavenly King of the Liu Estate). The catalpa is not inside the hall but in the courtyard of a Wang family household behind it. Curiously, two plaques for ancient and notable trees hang on the tree: one newly hung in 2018 identifies it as a qiu catalpa, while the one from 2004 reads 'zi catalpa' (Catalpa ovata). Nearby villagers, including 89-year-old Wang Quanxing, who lives in the small courtyard with the old tree, firmly believe it is a zi catalpa.
The Book of Han says: 'The catalpa—there are also those who mistakenly call it zi.' Being mistaken for a zi catalpa is almost the fate of every old qiu catalpa in Suzhou. Early records contain a note that 'there are eight zi catalpas in greater Suzhou', when in fact six of them are qiu catalpas. Besides Dongshan in Wuzhong, the two old qiu catalpas in front of Sanfeng Temple in Changshu also once bore plaques reading 'zi catalpa'; in 2015 He Wenyue, a member of the Changshu Peasants and Workers Party, submitted a 'Proposal on Reidentifying the Two Zicatalpas at Sanfeng Temple'. In 2018, Associate Professor Wang Jinhu of Suzhou University of Science and Technology went to the Suzhou Confucian Temple to admire the blossoms and judged from flower color and leaf shape that all three old trees bearing 'zi catalpa' plaques should be qiu catalpas.
qiu catalpa and zi catalpa are like a pair of similar twins. Both are trees of the genus Catalpa in the family Bignoniaceae, and both share the same virtues: fast growth, moderate hardness, light weight and wear resistance—fine timber. A folk saying runs, 'A thousand-year cypress, a ten-thousand-year fir, are no match for a single branch of catalpa.' In the Wuzhong Culture Museum's 'Archaeological Exploration of Wuzhong' gallery, the Warring States zither unearthed at Changqiao Village in Wuxian County was made of catalpa and maple wood; its body is hard in texture, and it is one of the earliest Spring and Autumn and Warring States zithers yet found in archaeological excavations.

shbl:story-013:body-1.hook_en: One old tree: a 2018 plaque says qiu catalpa, a 2004 plaque says zi catalpa, and its 89-year-old resident insists it is a zi catalpa.

shbl:story-014:body-1.context_header_en: 'Trees with Stele Biographies' Tree Stories, No. 14 | Wuzhong District, Dongshan Town, Xixiang, Qilong Hall | Dragon Juniper (now gone)
shbl:story-014:body-1.text_en:
This Dragon Juniper has now been removed from the official list of ancient and notable trees because it died. Its death is estimated to have occurred between 2017 and 2021. The 2017 edition of the Dongshan Town Gazetteer records that in 2013 most of the tree's branches suddenly died; after rescue efforts its growth recovered somewhat. Judging by the present outcome, those rescue efforts ultimately failed to save the ancient tree, which became an eternal regret.
The name Qilong Hall is connected to the locally circulated legend of Xu Qilong. According to the 2017 edition of the Dongshan Town Gazetteer, this building enshrines the fierce general bodhisattva, so it can also be understood as a fierce-general hall of the kind found in almost every village in Dongshan. The stone stele in front of the hall is the Ming Jiajing-era 'Wuxian 28th Du, 13th Tu Community' stele. According to the scholar Zhao Shiyu, it is powerful evidence that the Ming dynasty's community (lishe) system was implemented in Dongshan.
Today incense still burns continuously around the Dragon Juniper. It is said that villagers once invited an eminent monk to perform rites to help the withered tree recover, but parasitic plants around the ancient tree have long gone uncleared; vines cover it and young trees grow lushly, as if it had revived. Whether this is a withered tree coming back to life or a final flicker before death remains open to debate. In any case, perhaps this ancient tree can continue to shelter later generations after its death, achieving mutual fulfillment with this small temple submerged in the sea of history and with the ordinary yet devout villagers.

shbl:story-015:body-1.context_header_en: "Stories Told by Trees" Story No. 15 | Wuzhong District, Yushan Island | Chinese Zelkova
shbl:story-015:body-1.text_en:
The ancient and notable trees gazetteer includes a 1,000-year-old Chinese zelkova, so the most urgent task upon reaching Yushan Island was to find the tree. We set off by speedboat from the pier at Dongshan Town and reached the island in about five minutes; this is the last island in Suzhou to be connected to electricity. Islanders told the volunteers that not far from the pier stood a large tree—that was the thousand-year-old zelkova. Taking the tree as a starting point, one can circle the island either clockwise or counterclockwise. As everyone happily set out on the tree-finding journey, they soon came upon a tree with luxuriant branches and a dense, shady crown, growing in a chicken and duck farm. Because of the fencing, they could only see from a distance that it was a large tree, and everyone asked together: why has no ancient-tree plaque been hung on it? But looking around, no other towering tree could be seen, so they had no choice but to photograph and record it, intending to report the situation promptly.
During the circuit of the island it began to rain, and like survivors in the wilderness we hurriedly completed the journey. When we were finally about to reach the starting point, someone suddenly looked up and discovered a tree with a plaque. It turned out that we had gone the wrong way at the start and found the wrong tree. Homestays nearby were being renovated, and one side of the tree was covered with black cloth. Night was falling and the light was gradually dimming; we joked with a laugh: this zelkova probably never imagined that, despite being so highly recognizable in appearance, it could still be mistaken for another.

shbl:story-015:body-1.hook_en: Seeking a 1,000-year-old zelkova, volunteers circled Yushan Island and first mistook a poultry-farm tree; the real plaque stood beside black cloth.

shbl:story-016:body-1.context_header_en: "Tree Stele Biographies" Tree Stories, Entry 16 | Wuzhong District, Dongshan Carved Building | Hai'er Lian Camellia
shbl:story-016:body-1.text_en:
The Hai'er Lian camellia is distributed in southwestern China. Its flowers are small, delicate and exquisite, rosy like a child's cheeks and translucent when backlit, hence the name. Jin Youli's Qing-dynasty (1644–1912 CE) Taihu Beikao (Notes on Lake Tai) records: "There was formerly no such species in Wu. During the Shunzhi reign of the Qing, Weng Hanjin of Dongshan served as magistrate of Hexi County in Yunnan and brought it back, after which it came into the possession of the Xi family, who treasured it as a rarity. The flower does not set seed, and the root sends up no shoots, so it could not be propagated. Those keen on it divided it by the layering method, and there are now ten or twenty plants, while the original tree brought from Yunnan has also withered. This flower exists only in Dongshan and nowhere else." In the early Qing, Weng Hanjin (courtesy name Tianzhang), a descendant of the Weng family who had gone out from Dongshan in Suzhou, noticed these Hai'er Lian camellias blooming in the Yunnan mountains. Just when the southwestern frontier was unsettled, he submitted a petition saying that the Jixian Garden in Dongshan, built by his father, lacked this rare flower and that a plant needed to be transplanted to the garden to fulfill his filial duty. Having obtained permission from the court, Weng Tianzhang carried a Hai'er Lian camellia that had not yet flowered back to Dongshan, and on the pretext of caring for his parents at home he did not return to Yunnan to resume his post, thereby escaping the disaster of Wu Sangui's rebellion and death in its defeat.
In his later years Weng Tianzhang lived in poverty and, having no alternative, sold the Jixian Garden to the Xi family, who relocated and rebuilt it as the Dongyuan (East Garden) in Weng Lane, and the Hai'er Lian camellia likewise "came into the possession of the Xi family." Later, for various reasons (no longer ascertainable), the Hai'er Lian camellia planted in the East Garden was bought by the Weng family's descendants. It is said that in 1922, when the cotton-yarn merchant Jin Xizhi built the Carved Building by the Shi Lane riverside, the Jin and Weng families being related by marriage, a Weng cousin gave the Hai'er Lian camellia to the Jin family to congratulate them on their move. Jin Zhizhi, Jin Xizhi's younger brother, who supervised the construction of the Carved Building, saw that the Hai'er Lian camellia was already over 300 years old and had it planted in the garden in front of the Buddhist Hall. This is the Hai'er Lian camellia that can be seen today at the Dongshan Carved Building.

shbl:story-016:body-2.context_header_en: "Tree Stele Biographies" Tree Stories, Entry 16 | Wuzhong District, Dongshan Carved Building | Banana Shrub
shbl:story-016:body-2.text_en: Suzhou has a long history of cultivating the banana shrub. Wang Shizhen of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE) recorded in his Yanshan Yuan Ji (Record of Yanshan Garden): "Crape myrtle, winter jasmine, banana shrub and the like, ever mingling with the boat poles—this is called the Scattered Flowers Gorge." The banana shrub is an evergreen shrub, whose Chinese name, hanxiao ("holding a smile"), refers to flowers that remain partly closed as they bloom. According to the 2015 survey of ancient and notable trees, Suzhou retains a total of 3 ancient banana shrubs: 1 in Changshu City and 2 in Wuzhong District, all Grade III ancient trees. The oldest is in Qiyuan Garden in Huwan Village, Dongshan Town, Wuzhong District, aged 200 years; the next is in the Dongshan Carved Building, Wuzhong District, aged 150 years and growing vigorously.

shbl:story-016:background-2.context_header_en: "Tree Stele Biographies" Tree Stories, Entry 16 | Wuzhong District, Dongshan Carved Building | Hai'er Lian Camellia and Banana Shrub | Background: Dongshan Carved Building
shbl:story-016:background-2.text_en:
About the Dongshan Carved Building: the Dongshan Carved Building is an important residence-garden in the Wuzhong area, divisible into the Ming-dynasty (1368–1644 CE) hall Qinde Tang and the Republican-era storeyed hall Chunzai Lou, the latter added by expanding northward from the former. What we know today as the Dongshan Carved Building usually refers to Chunzai Lou, but Qinde Tang, as a relatively well-preserved Ming hall with a comparatively early recorded date in Suzhou, is also an indispensable component; some ancient and notable trees, such as Buddhist pine, purple nanmu and wintersweet, are also distributed around Qinde Tang.
Chunzai Lou faces east and takes its name from the phrase "a sunny household enjoys spring forever." It consists of four parts: the brick-carved gatehouse, the front building, the rear building and the garden. The whole building makes extensive use of traditional auspicious patterns and opera-story carvings, while also employing Western architectural elements such as Corinthian columns, cast-iron railings and stained glass. Interestingly, the Ming Changwu Zhi (Treatise on Superfluous Things) holds that "three-storey high pavilions are the most vulgar," and storeyed halls in the Wuzhong area are mostly of two storeys, yet the rear building of Chunzai Lou chose a double-eaved three-storey form. Beyond the family's outstanding economic strength, this also reflects an open-minded attitude willing to break through dogma, and these architectural features in turn influenced the layout of the garden.
The Chunzai Lou garden lies in the narrow, elongated space north of the storeyed hall, running laterally across the brick-carved gatehouse, front building and rear building, serving a connecting role similar to a service passage. Because it is enclosed east and west by tall buildings and walls and is extremely narrow north to south, the choice of garden vegetation is quite bold: tall trees are densely planted—Chinese juniper, crape myrtle, Hai'er Lian camellia, banana shrub and others—while low plantings of wintersweet, nandina and the like provide accents. To enrich the layers of scenery and enhance three-dimensional depth in the cramped garden, galleries were built on the upper floors and pavilions topped with upper storeys, so that high buildings lean on tall trees and one can pluck the stars by hand; below, long pools are bridged to extend the water and rockeries rise against the walls, so that low scenery faces low trees and the foot can tread the cosmos. Together these ultimately form the garden with the highest density of ancient and notable trees in Wuzhong District.

shbl:story-017:body-1.context_header_en: Tree Stories, Entry 17 | Wuzhong District, in front of Dunyu Hall, Dongshan Town | Chinese Wisteria
shbl:story-017:body-1.text_en:
On the stone-slab path on the southeast side in front of the gate hall of Dunyu Hall stands a thousand-year-old Chinese wisteria. Zheng Yanshao's Qing-dynasty (1644–1912 CE) Continued Notes on Taihu records: "In the street before the hall there is one wisteria, stretching across several hundred paces; a trellis of timber supports it, great stones prop it, and iron ropes run through it. In flowering season the blossoms hang down like tassels, scattering fragrance over the ground; this place has become a market, and no one knows how many years it has been so. When this plant was set here, it surely was not in the marketplace; its lifespan, like that of the legendary dachun tree, can hardly be reckoned. I once asked the elders, who said: 'From childhood to old age we have never seen it grow larger. Now several decades more have passed, and the trunk remains as before.' All things that neither wither nor flourish excessively attain long life; one may grasp this principle from it."
In April 2023, in the season when the wisteria blooms, volunteers from the Tree Stele and Biography project went to Dongshan Old Street to record this wisteria. They happened upon an 81-year-old neighborhood uncle, especially talkative, who recalled that about 30 years ago this wisteria had been rescued: when the borer holes in the main trunk grew large, they were sealed with material. Earlier, when utility lines were buried, in order not to harm the wisteria's roots, the pavement near the wisteria was not dug up; instead the original drainage pipe was borrowed, but that year the flowers bloomed less well than in previous years.
Mr. Ye, who lives next door to Dunyu Hall, warmly invited the volunteers up to his rooftop to view the wisteria and incidentally look down into the interior of Dunyu Hall. He explained that Dunyu Hall originally belonged to the Xi family of Dongshan and was about 150 meters deep; after Liberation most of it was divided up. The part now visible had once been a tea factory; after the tea factory moved away it stood empty, and after restoration it served for a time as a celebrity museum; after the museum moved a few years ago it has again stood empty to this day. The courtyard is overgrown with weeds, dead vines fill the spaces between the tiles, and Boston ivy trails from the load-bearing columns all the way to the door lintel. The old man sighed that a house easily deteriorates once no one lives in it, and that the old buildings of Dunyu Hall were a pity. As we left, Mr. Ye could not help seeing us off, escorting us all the way to beneath the wisteria blossoms.

shbl:story-017:fieldnote-1.context_header_en: Tree Stories, Entry 17 | Wuzhong District, in front of Dunyu Hall, Dongshan Town | Chinese Wisteria | Volunteer Visit Record
shbl:story-017:fieldnote-1.text_en:
At the gate of Dunyu Hall the volunteers found old neighbors sitting under the ancient wisteria, sunning themselves and chatting. Volunteer Chen Ping, a Suzhou native and a talkative man, soon joined their conversation in the local dialect and asked about the ancient tree.
The 81-year-old uncle sunning himself said he was a retiree of the town traffic-management office and lived nearby. About 30 years ago this wisteria had been rescued: the borer hole in the main trunk had originally been rather small, and when it later grew large it was sealed with material. Earlier, when utility lines were buried, in order not to harm the wisteria's roots, the pavement near the wisteria was not dug up; instead the original drainage pipe was borrowed. The flowers in the previous two years had clearly been better than this year's.
Then a 90-year-old Mr. Ye nearby added: "Dunyu Hall originally belonged to the Xi family and was about 150 meters deep; after Liberation most of it was divided up. The remaining part now here was once a tea factory; after the tea factory moved away it stood empty, and after restoration it served for a time as a celebrity museum; after the museum moved a few years ago it has again stood empty to this day."
When he heard the volunteers say they wanted to find a better angle from which to observe the wisteria, Mr. Ye voluntarily opened his home's balcony and showed us how to photograph the wisteria at its best.

shbl:story-018:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees' Entry 18 | Wuzhong District, Situ Temple in Guangfu | Chinese Juniper
shbl:story-018:body-1.text_en:
The cypress and juniper family is a common group of ancient trees in Suzhou, including Chinese juniper, needle juniper, and dragon juniper. During the Tang (618–907 CE) and Song (960–1279 CE) dynasties, many Suzhou temples and shrines planted cypresses and junipers; because they stay green through all four seasons, they always presented a dense, luxuriant scene with mist and clouds veiling them. The "Bai Gong Gui" (gui being another name for cypress) recorded in Fan Chengda's Wu Jun Zhi (Gazetteer of Wu Commandery) of the Song dynasty is the earliest Suzhou example of cypresses planted in a domestic garden. It is said that during the Tang dynasty, while Bai Juyi served as Prefect of Suzhou, he planted cypresses in front of the Guangting Pavilion by the rear pond of the prefectural residence; later, during the Zhenghe reign era of the Northern Song (960–1127 CE), they were presented by Zhu Chong to the imperial court in Bianjing and died on the way.
The ancient cypresses in the best condition, of the greatest age, and most famous in Suzhou are the four Han cypresses at Situ Temple in Guangfu, known as "Qing, Qi, Gu, Guai" (Clear, Peculiar, Ancient, and Quaint), each 1,900 years old. Legend says Situ Temple is the ancestral shrine of Deng Yu (2–58 CE), a general of the Eastern Han dynasty (25–220 CE). As early as the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE), there is a record of the literatus Li Liufang visiting Situ Temple at night: the shrine was already overgrown, yet the cypresses "stood tall and dark green for a thousand years." In the Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE), when Emperor Qianlong (reigned 1735–1796) toured south to this place, he was struck with admiration at the vigorous ancient cypresses and bestowed on them the names "Qing, Qi, Gu, Guai." Not long afterward, Shen Fu's Six Records of a Floating Life gave a more detailed record of the names and appearances: "To the left of the mountain are four ancient cypress trees, named Qing, Qi, Gu, and Guai. The Qing one is a single upright trunk, luxuriant like a green canopy; the Qi one lies on the ground in three bends, shaped like the character zhi; the Gu one has a bald, broad, flat top, half-rotted like a palm; the Guai one has a body like a spiral shell, its branches and trunk all so, said by tradition to be a thing from before the Han." This is basically consistent with the forms we see today. Looking through the literature, claims such as "planted by Deng Yu's own hand" and "named by Qianlong" have no clear basis, but as the painter Wu Guanzhong said, "I don't care who planted them by hand or who named them; I only wish that, braving wind, frost, and lightning strikes, they may live on forever with tenacity."

shbl:story-019:body-1.context_header_en: "Steles for Trees" Tree Stories, Entry 19 | Wuzhong District, Tongguanyin Temple, Guangfu | Camphor Tree
shbl:story-019:body-1.text_en: The camphor tree is a common street tree in Suzhou, able to absorb smoke and hold dust and to repel mosquitoes and insects. Unlike ordinary camphor trees, the camphor tree of more than 600 years before the Mahavira Hall of Tongguanyin Temple has an especially spreading crown, broad with dense shade and a majestic bearing, full of presence, like a tolerant old man creating a patch of quiet, easy shade in the courtyard. A Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE) camphor tree still does not count as very old in this ancient temple, first built in the second year of the Tianjian era of the Liang (503 CE). Tongguanyin Temple was originally named Guangfu Jiang Temple; because its incense offerings were extremely abundant, the whole small town took the name "Guangfu," and in the Song dynasty (960–1279 CE) a Tang dynasty (618–907 CE) bronze Guanyin statue was found beside the temple, so the temple changed its name. The temple leans against Gui Mountain; on the summit, the seven-story Guangfu Pagoda is a Song imitation of a Tang brick-and-wood pagoda, its wooden eaves restored in imitation of the Songjiang Square Pagoda. The temple bridge, built spanning the river, has fine carvings; its two side edges are of Wukang stone, old material from the Song dynasty, and when struck it gives a sound, ringing and clanging, so it is also called "Pipa Bridge." Today Tongguanyin Temple cannot be called famous; it seems to welcome guests from all directions only when the late-spring cherry blossoms bloom, quietly telling people of its hidden past.

shbl:story-020:body-1.context_header_en: "Stories of Trees" Entry 20 | Wuzhong District, Sheng'en Temple, Xuanmu Mountain, Guangfu | Chinese Juniper
shbl:story-020:body-1.text_en:
Sheng'en Temple stands at the foot of Xuanmu Mountain on the shore of Lake Tai. The Gusu Zhi, compiled by Wang Ao of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE), records: "Xuanmu Mountain—legend has it that Yu Taixuan was buried here, hence the name. It lies southwest of Dengwei and is also called Wanfeng Mountain." Geographically, Xuanmu Mountain connects with Dengwei Mountain to the north, faces Lake Tai to the south, leans against Midui Mountain to the east, and neighbors Changqi Mountain to the west; the three mountains wind along and link together, overlooking Lake Tai. Thus Xuanmu long ago earned the reputation of a "famous mountain," and in Suzhou famous mountains often have famous monasteries; Sheng'en Temple is truly an ancient and renowned monastery.
Sheng'en Temple was first built during the Tianbao era of the Tang dynasty (618–907 CE), and it once enjoyed an extremely glorious period. A glimpse of the bustling crowds of pilgrims in those days can be had from the appraisal by the Ming dynasty eminent monk Hanshan Deqing (1546–1623): "It is truly beyond comparison with ancient monasteries on other mountains; it should be the foremost Buddhist site in Wuzhong." Master Kuanchen of Shibi Yonghui Chan Temple mentioned: compared with before, Sheng'en Temple is now much smaller in scale; fortunately, the temple still preserves two stone inscriptions each from the Ming and Qing (1644–1912 CE) dynasties, as well as some ancient buildings including the "Sutra Library."
Two towering Jin-dynasty junipers stand on either side of the Mahavira Hall; their tall, steep forms are like two soldiers stationed before the hall, guarding it tirelessly for more than 1,000 years. Just as a hunched old man needs a cane, these two aged ancient junipers likewise need something to lean on. Ancient-tree protection experts made concrete columns imitating the texture of the trunks, letting the two ancient trees lean against them at an angle to share the weight of the trunks. This ingenuity not only deceived our eyes but also deceived the eyes of vines and other epiphytic plants; before anyone noticed, many new lives had already climbed onto these two concrete columns.

shbl:story-021:body-1.context_header_en: 'Trees with Steles and Biographies' Tree Stories, Entry 21 | Wuzhong District, Yonghui Chan Temple at Shibi, Guangfu Town | Chinese Photinia
shbl:story-021:body-1.text_en:
The Chinese photinia is evergreen, with a rounded crown, white flowers and red fruits, and its young and old leaves are a vivid red. According to a botanical science writer, apart from the brief flowering season when it gives off an unpleasant smell, the Chinese photinia is all merits: easy to plant, easy to keep alive, able to purify the air, inexpensive and fast-growing, and it has now become one of the best street trees in the Jiangsu–Zhejiang–Shanghai region.
Zhu Changwen of the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127 CE) records in the Wujun Tujing Xuji (Continued Records of the Illustrated Gazetteer of Wu Commandery) that among the 'ten topics in the school' was the Chinese photinia. The Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE) Qingjialu says that at the year's end Suzhou people had the custom of 'picking branches of pine and cypress, paired with Chinese photinia and holly; villagers tie them into small bundles in the waning year and peddle them from door to door, for residents to put in the New Year rice'.
An ancient Chinese photinia hidden away against the rear wall of the temple twists and coils, having taken root and sprouted among the rock crevices 800 years ago and grown up in coils. A plaque stands on the rock face, indicating that this tree emerged from the rocky cliff during the Yuan dynasty (1271–1368 CE), and it is also called the 'Sleeping Dragon'. Looking closely, the roots twist and coil, half thrust into the crevices of the steep cliff and half exposed on the cliff face; the branches climb to the top of the cliff and then spread out, so that one must look up to take in the whole leafy crown. The ancient Chinese photinia resembles a grey dragon lying in wait, and on its right are carved the vigorous large characters 'Crouching Dragon on the Wall', together with a poem by the lay Buddhist Guangzhao: 'The Buddha of the sacred mountain sent a divine dragon, soaring on clouds straight to the east of Dongting. The vast cliff stands erect for a thousand years; bell and chant awaken the pine wind.'

shbl:story-021:body-1.hook_en: In a cliff crevice behind Yonghui Chan Temple, a Chinese photinia coils like a crouching dragon beside the inscription 'Crouching Dragon on the Wall'.

shbl:story-021:interview-1.context_header_en: 'Trees with Steles and Biographies' Tree Stories, Entry 21 | Wuzhong District, Yonghui Chan Temple at Shibi, Guangfu Town | Chinese Photinia | Interview: Master Kuanchen
shbl:story-021:interview-1.text_en:
Wang Mingyu, Wuzhong Museum staff member: Could you briefly introduce Yonghui Chan Temple to us?
Master Kuanchen: Our temple dates from the Longqing reign of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE), when Master Hanshan (Hanshan Deqing, 1546–1623) traveled here, built a thatched hut on this spot and practiced, and later it gradually became a temple. Master Hanshan later went to Guangdong, and it was there too that he passed away. Originally this place was called 'Shibi Jingshe' (the Stone Wall Retreat), and only later was it renamed Yonghui Chan Temple.
Wang Mingyu: We are volunteers from the Wuzhong Museum, currently working on a survey project on ancient and notable trees; we came here once before when we went to Shangzhen Temple to see the yulan magnolia. This time we happen to have come when the Chinese photinia is in flower—so besides the Chinese photinia, what other ancient trees are here?
Master Kuanchen: At the gate there is also Chinese boxwood, and there are Chinese hackberry, Chinese zelkova and Chinese boxwood; it is said there used to be golden-thread bamboo too.
Volunteer Zhou Yuan: Why are there so many stone inscriptions by famous people here?
Master Kuanchen: It is relatively quiet here, backed by hills and facing water, looking out toward Lake Tai; many literati and refined gentlemen liked to come here to visit.
Volunteer Zhou Yuan: Do you know what the earliest cliff inscription here is? What we see now is mostly from the Republic of China period.
Master Kuanchen: The oldest should be that piece to the north; a fairly representative one is Master Xuyun's 'Ying wu suo zhu' (Dwell nowhere).
Wang Mingyu: The second is Master Hongyi's stone inscription—is the seal below it 'Hongyi'? It looks very simple, not quite like it.
Master Kuanchen: No, that seal is 'Yanyin', which is Hongyi, that is, Li Shutong.

shbl:story-021:interview-2.text_en:
Volunteer Zhou Yuan: Since the temple was founded, has its layout changed?
Master Kuanchen: At first the mountain gate of Yonghui Chan Temple stood between two ancient ginkgo trees; to the right of the 'Sheng Da Huanxi' (Great Joy Arises) Hall there was originally a kitchen, which was later converted into the Thousand-Hand Guanyin Hall.
Wang Mingyu: Does Yonghui Chan Temple usually have dealings with other large temples in Suzhou, such as Sheng'en Temple, which is fairly close, or Hanshan Temple and Xiyuan Temple in the city?
Master Kuanchen: Our temple was originally a 'sub-temple' (xiayuan) of Shilin Temple. When Buddhist assemblies require it, such as meetings of the Buddhist Association, we go over to meet with them.
Wang Mingyu: May I ask how to understand 'sub-temple'?
Master Kuanchen: It is like a branch campus of Nanjing University in Suzhou.
Wang Mingyu: About how many people practice here at Yonghui Chan Temple now?
Master Kuanchen: Including me, we are five now; we take care of the daily running of the place ourselves.

shbl:story-022:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees' No. 22 | Wuzhong District, Shangzhen Temple on Qionglong Mountain | Yulan Magnolia
shbl:story-022:body-1.text_en:
Suzhou has a long history of cultivating yulan magnolias. Yuan Xuelan of the Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE) records in Wujun Suihua Jili (Annual Splendors of Wu Commandery): "Behind Tiger Hill in Wu there was a tree of the Yulan House; it was purchased in Fujian by Zhu Mian of the Song dynasty (960–1279 CE) and, before it could be presented to the throne, was transplanted here. During the Tianqi era of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE), it was destroyed by a great wind, and afterwards it grew again." In the Qing dynasty, Suzhou people had the custom of going to Tiger Hill to "view the flowers at the Yulan House."
When the white yulan magnolia blooms, it is like bits of broken jade hung on the branches, flawless white and green, radiant in the wind—it is hard not to love. Li Yu, a literatus of the late Ming and early Qing, once exclaimed: "The world has no jade tree; let this flower serve as one. There are many white flowers, but all are confused by the color of their leaves; this one blooms without leaves, sharing the spirit of plum. Thousands upon thousands of buds all open at once—truly a grand occasion." When the yulan was "about to bloom," Wen Zhengming could not restrain his eagerness to enjoy the flowers and playfully painted a 'Picture of White Yulan Magnolia,' taking only a single branch from a tree full of blossoms; many of the flowers were still shyly waiting to open, yet full of vitality and delightfully fragrant.
A yulan magnolia blooms only after growing for a certain number of years; every flowering tree is the result of time's brewing. The ancient white yulan magnolia in Shangzhen Temple on Qionglong Mountain in Suzhou is already more than two hundred years old and is said to have been planted by Qianlong, Qing emperor (reigned 1735–1796), with his own hand during his journeys south of the Yangtze. However, searching through all the poems and prose Qianlong wrote during his visits to Shangzhen Temple, none mention planting a tree; and Suzhou has several trees said to have been planted by Qianlong, which makes these planting stories confusing and hard to tell true from false.

shbl:story-023:body-1.context_header_en: "Stories of Trees" Entry 23 | Wuzhong District, Yan Family Garden in Mudu Ancient Town | Southern Magnolia
shbl:story-023:body-1.text_en:
Compared with the gardens inside the old city, the Yan Family Garden in Mudu Ancient Town west of the city may seem lesser known, yet it is very popular with visitors. Volunteers who visited several times all noticed a two-hundred-year-old southern magnolia. In early summer, white flowers bloom in profusion; in autumn, it bears very strange fruit. The first time a volunteer saw the southern magnolia's fruit, they were so excited it was as if they had discovered a new continent: it is an aggregate fruit, the red seeds have already fallen away, leaving a shell similar to a pinecone, scattered all over the ground.
In the quarter of an hour spent squatting on the ground "picking up litter," visitors to the Yan Family Garden came in one group after another. Guides enthusiastically recounted an anecdote about "Qianlong planting the southern magnolia by hand": the garden was originally the residence of the Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE) Suzhou literatus Shen Deqian, and the Qianlong Emperor (reigned 1735–1796) had always admired his poetic talent. When visiting Mudu Ancient Town, the emperor once stopped here. It is said that he accidentally knocked over a potted southern magnolia on a flower stand; Shen Deqian defused the awkwardness by saying that "the southern magnolia wishes to kneel and pay respects to the Son of Heaven," whereupon Qianlong personally planted the southern magnolia in the garden. The lake rock beneath the tree is inscribed with the two characters "惜缘" (cherish this bond), precisely to commemorate this connection. The guides' versions of the story vary widely, and some even mistakenly call the southern magnolia "white yulan magnolia." In fact, the southern magnolia is an introduced species, native to eastern North America, and was only introduced and planted in the mid-Qing. Because its flowers are larger than those of the white yulan magnolia, it was called "large yulan" at the time. The Republican-era "Wuxian County Gazetteer," in its products section, records: "Large yulan, a shrub, commonly called 'foreign yulan.' Flowers white as jade, leaves large as lotus; blooms in the fifth month, yellow-dark green, and smooth, also larger than the yulan; each plant grows very fast, the tall ones ordinarily do not shed leaves in winter, vigorous and long-lived, unafraid of frost and snow; those who cultivate flowers graft it using the rootstock of the wooden-pen magnolia."
Calculating the tree's age, the story of Qianlong planting the tree is not very reliable, but the widespread planting of southern magnolias in Mudu Ancient Town today may be an echo of this legend.

shbl:story-023:body-2.context_header_en: "Stories of Trees" Entry 23 | Wuzhong District, Gusong Garden in Mudu Ancient Town | Buddhist Pine
shbl:story-023:body-2.text_en: Gusong Garden is the former residence of Cai Shaoyu, a wealthy man of Mudu in the late Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE), with the residence in front and the garden behind. Because it contains a Buddhist pine over 500 years old, it has in recent years been named "Gusong Garden" (Ancient Pine Garden). The garden has built a two-story covered corridor centered on the Buddhist pine; climbing the steps and strolling along the corridor, one gains a rare high vantage point to look down on the garden scenery and gaze into the distance at Lingyan. The Buddhist pine takes "pine" in its name, but it is not a pine tree. In summer the Buddhist pine bears fruit; the green seeds and red seed receptacles are joined together, like a little monk with a round head wearing a red monk's robe.

shbl:story-024:body-1.context_header_en: "Steles for Trees" Tree Stories, Entry 24 | Wuzhong District, Shuidongbang, Yaosheng Harbor, Yaosheng Village | Ginkgo
shbl:story-024:body-1.text_en:
Before searching the map for this tree's coordinates, the volunteers knew nothing of the place name "Shuidongbang." One autumn, they drove there on the off chance, and sure enough, behind a house they saw a blaze of gold: a 600-year-old ginkgo. Although the surroundings are mostly orchards and farmland, beneath the tree are large characters reading "Dongbang," along with fitness equipment and chairs, making it veritably a new community center.
The other tree is much more slender and stands across the paddy fields. On the way over, they unexpectedly discovered that the single-span stone slab bridge connecting the two trees is an old bridge: the abutments on both sides are original Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE) fabric, while the bridge slabs are Republican-era remains, and the side of a slab is carved with "Rebuilt Xinglong Bridge."
Bridge, temple, tree—this is the standard Jiangnan ancient-ginkgo configuration. According to the Chefang Town Gazetteer, these two ancient ginkgos correspond respectively to the Jade Emperor Temple and the City God Temple; both face south toward "Huangnidou," a small lake inlet on the western side of Cheng Lake, which is why this place is also called Shuangmiao Harbor ("Twin Temples Harbor"). The Jade Emperor Temple was once grand in scale and thronged with worshippers; today boats come and go, and the villagers still make their living by fishing.

shbl:story-025:body-1.context_header_en: "Steles for Trees" Story 25 | Wuzhong District, Baosheng Temple, Luzhi | Ginkgo
shbl:story-025:body-1.text_en: "After the turmoil, none knew the monks had gone; a few heaps of yellow leaves lay by the open temple gate." When the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE) poet Gao Qi came to Baosheng Temple, the monastery that had once burned incense so abundantly already looked dilapidated; only the ginkgos stood silent, saying nothing. Nearly 600 years passed. When Gu Jiegang and other writers of the Republican era were struck by the arhat sculptures here, the Mahavira Hall of Baosheng Temple was already tottering. In the end, half the hall collapsed, and only half the set of arhats remained. Baosheng Temple has long been famed for its Tang dynasty (618–907 CE) wall sculptures; for over a thousand years, standing shoulder to shoulder with the Tang material remains have been the ancient ginkgo trees. Around Baosheng Temple there are four ginkgos with plaques giving ages of over 1,000 years: a wolfberry grows inside the trunk of one, an elm inside another; some grow unhurriedly in the scenic area's west courtyard, while others are left behind on an abandoned primary-school playground. They probably all stirred the "clear breeze over the duck pond" of the Tang poet Lu Guimeng when he lived in seclusion at Luzhi, and all have listened to the sound of reading aloud when the educator Ye Shengtao taught at the Fifth Higher Primary School. When volunteers interviewed them, staff who had grown up in the town still remembered climbing the ginkgo on the playground as children; the trees are part of daily life.

shbl:story-025:background-1.context_header_en: "Steles for Trees" Story 25 | Wuzhong District, Baosheng Temple, Luzhi | Ginkgo | Background: Baosheng Temple
shbl:story-025:background-1.text_en:
About Baosheng Temple: Luzhi has been prosperous since ancient times and has long enjoyed the reputation of "the hall of the five lakes," and old gazetteers often sum up the rise of Luzhi with the phrase "the market grew up around the temple." Legend has it that Baosheng Temple, which set the whole ancient town on its course of growth, at its height covered half of Luzhi—ample evidence of the temple's outstanding status. Today's Baosheng Temple is divided into east and west courtyards. The western part is open and spacious; in the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127 CE) the Bailian Temple was built here, and now only column bases remain, with three ancient ginkgos standing on the spot. Another ancient ginkgo stands on the grounds of the former primary school north of Baosheng Temple, ample evidence of the temple's former grand scale.
The eastern part is the central axis of the existing temple buildings. Entering the mountain gate, one first crosses a dry bridge, seemingly a simulation of Luzhi's dense water network—a water landscape made on dry land—and then, coming straight into view, three solitary lake-rock peaks rise before one, seemingly representing the three immortal mountains of the sea, each with a wolfberry twining at its base; the wolfberry in the very center is a century-old tree, seemingly taking the meaning of the Queen Mother of the West's staff. Next comes the Hall of Heavenly Kings, a Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE) hall; Li Min's research holds that the hall partially preserves Song dynasty (960–1279 CE) components. Behind the Hall of Heavenly Kings is a Tang dynasty (618–907 CE) stone sutra pillar, which, together with the Tang sutra pillar at Xingfu Temple in Changshu, is the earliest non-archaeological ground structure in the greater Suzhou area.
Finally, what meets the eye is the Baosheng Temple Antiquities Hall, a Republican-era building reconstructed on the original site of the collapsed Northern Song hall to protect the half-set of Song arhat sculptures rescued from the ruins. Baosheng Temple's arhats have long enjoyed the reputation of "only two and a half sets of arhats under heaven," and although they are said to be the work of the Tang "sage of sculpture" Yang Huizhi, after appraisal by authorities such as Ōmura Seigai and Gu Jiegang, the academic world has generally classified them as Northern Song works. Apart from the world-famous half-set of arhats, the original hall was once an important hall in the Jiangnan region second in age only to the Mahavira Hall of Baoguo Temple in Ningbo; fortunately, Ōmura Seigai left rich and clear photographic records of it, so that today we can still glimpse fragments of this great hall.

shbl:story-026:body-1.context_header_en: Tree Stories, No. 26 | Husha Temple, Yangwan Village, Dongshan Town, Wuzhong District | Chinese Zelkova
shbl:story-026:body-1.text_en:
Yangwan Village lies in the southwestern part of Dongshan Town. The natural villages along the lakeshore include Shangwan, Tunwan, Chengwan, Husha, Wanli and others; their names alone reveal the water-ringed topography here. Husha Temple is built on a hillside. The plaque above the temple gate reads "Hujie Tang Chaowang," and there are also the characters "Taihu Xinglong She"; a flag reading "Taihu Xinglong She" hangs there as well.
The name "Xinglong She" has appeared in Wujiang. Xia Yihong, one of the authors of *Chuihong Wensu: Modern and Contemporary Jiangnan Society and Culture in the Field*, did a case study of the Xinglong She at the Xu Family Gongmen Temple in Miaogang, Wujiang. Zhao Shiyu, author of *The General Returns Home: A New Jiangnan History of Dongting Dongshan*, believes they belong to the same system. The person in charge of Husha Temple is also surnamed Xu and indeed moved here from Wujiang. He also thinks the meaning of "Chaowang" may be related to Taihu fishermen's "Four Courts, North and South"—that is, Husha Tang may be a branch temple of one of the shrines in the "Four Courts." Some scholars have investigated the "Four Courts, North and South" of Wujiang fishermen as "the Southern Court: Liu Mengjiang at Liansidang, Jiaxing; the Northern Court: the Great Mother at Shangfang Mountain, Suzhou; the Eastern Court: Lord Yang at Jinze Town, Qingpu; the Western Court: San Taijun at Shicong, Huzhou." Different parts of the Taihu region have different versions, but in any case these are spatial markers of the water world in fishermen's consciousness, similar to the Five Sacred Mountains and the Four Seas.
The ancient tree in front of the temple is a Chinese zelkova over 200 years old. In spring it puts forth captivating new green, guarding the village's peace together with the little temple. It has been observed that the tree has a very large hollow. The ancient-tree conservation worker Zhang Ji mentions that such a tree scar formed when disease or pests were not treated in time, and because rainwater flows back in, the hollow has grown larger and larger. Yet we can always trust the tree's capacity for self-healing: even a scar close to the diameter of the trunk at breast height can gradually be wrapped up by newly grown bark. Gazing at the twisted trunk, we seem able to imagine its struggles and perseverance over these hundred years.

shbl:story-026:interview-1.context_header_en: Tree Stories, No. 26 | Husha Temple, Yangwan Village, Dongshan Town, Wuzhong District | Chinese Zelkova | Interview: ancient-tree conservation worker Zhang Ji
shbl:story-026:interview-1.text_en:
From 2023 to 2024, volunteers visited several ancient Chinese zelkovas on Yushan Island in Dongshan and at Husha Temple and other places. Their colorful swaying in late autumn and their new green sprouting in late spring are both captivating, but what left the deepest impression on the volunteers were the huge hollows and scars on the trunks—wounds left by the years, yet all the more highlighting the ancient trees' powerful vitality.
Around "tree scars," the volunteers specially interviewed the ancient-tree conservation worker Zhang Ji.
Wang Mingyu, staff member at the Wu Museum: Teacher Zhang, we found that these Chinese zelkovas all have some tree scars. How are they caused?
Zhang Ji: Scars on a tree are like scars on a human body. After breakage, tearing, mechanical damage and the like, the surviving part, in order to heal the wound, rapidly divides cells in the cambium at the damaged area and grows new tissue to protect itself, preventing harm from rain, pests and disease. Tree scars form different shapes depending on the wound. Because they are newly grown, they differ greatly in color and shape from the old bark, showing obvious scars on the tree body.
Volunteer Zhou Yuan: The two ancient trees on Yushan Island and at Husha Temple both healed through tenacious self-healing after being injured. What kind of mechanism is this?
Zhang Ji: Ancient trees are living organisms. When they suffer external damage, they show the ability to protect themselves and resist invasion from outside. The tree body relies on its bark to protect itself and to contact the outside world; this is a defensive barrier. Once the barrier is destroyed and cannot heal, the interior of the tree easily dies and forms a hollow. The variously shaped healed wounds we see on ancient trees are in fact expressions of their self-repair, and the wounds on ancient trees are often quite large, so it is a long process.
