shbl:story-026:interview-2.context_header_en: Tree Stories, No. 26 | Husha Temple, Yangwan Village, Dongshan Town, Wuzhong District | Chinese Zelkova | Interview: ancient-tree conservation worker Zhang Ji
shbl:story-026:interview-2.text_en:
Volunteer Zhou Yuan: What artificial methods can we use to protect injured ancient trees?
Zhang Ji: Ancient trees have different kinds of wounds.
1. Some have large areas of bark damaged or missing. We can scrape the damaged edges clean with a sharp blade, clean and preserve the wood that lacks bark protection, and artificially provide a temporary protective barrier until the surrounding bark slowly grows and wraps around, healing the wound.
2. Some have large hollows or broken branches, especially wounds from torn branches. In such cases, we first clean the opening of the hollow or the break; dead wood must not protrude from the opening or extend beyond the living bark, because dead wood will hinder the wrapping and healing.
Wang Mingyu, staff member at the Wu Museum: In the process of ancient-tree protection, are there any unforgettable stories you can share?
Zhang Ji: Actually, I think the process of ancient-tree protection is a kind of archaeology, especially when working on the underground part. The surface appearance of ancient trees today has been greatly changed by human activity, and many ancient-tree problems need to be solved underground. Unless you dig open the soil around the roots, you will never know the secrets buried below. And as ancient trees grow they send out signals; we must discover the signals in time and promptly investigate and resolve the problems, so that the ancient trees can extend their lives in the lives of our generation.
For example:
1. An ancient tree may for a long time have sparse branches and leaves, small leaves, an unhealthy color, and lack of vigor; sometimes one side of a tree is vigorous while the other side looks listless. If we dig open the soil on the listless side, we may find too many stones underground or the ruins of earlier buildings, which obstruct root growth and cause malnutrition.
2. The leaves may be half withered and yellow, half green, with gray-black between the yellow and green, and a large amount of fallen leaves may be seen under the tree. If we dig deep into the soil, we may see that the deep soil is very wet, the roots black or even foul-smelling, and sometimes we can find drainage ditches built by people in earlier years that, through long neglect or abandonment amid urban and rural construction, no longer drain the standing water, so the ancient tree lives uncomfortably here—and so it sends people signals.
3. Some ancient trees in the countryside have peculiar wounds on certain parts. According to oral accounts of nearby elders, in some cases many years ago, when this was a natural village, this was the place where cattle were tethered and raised; in others, near a river, it was where small boats moored and tied their cables.
4. Some ancient trees have roots that have wrapped around stone steles, Buddha statues, millstones and the like; some lean in front of old houses, giving the doorway a natural great umbrella; some stand quietly at the village entrance, letting you hang bells and paste wedding notices on them, quietly watching over each generation of the village as they come and go and finally return. Looking at the people at the village entrance who entrust their nostalgia to the ancient tree, I think this expresses a kind of harmony and inclusiveness between humans and nature.

shbl:story-026:fieldnote-1.text_en: Field note: Before becoming a volunteer for Tree Stories, I had seen Teacher Zhang Ji interviewed by newspapers and television, and everyone called him "Plant Doctor." I was very lucky that after joining this project I had many exchanges with Teacher Zhang Ji, and only then discovered that his WeChat nickname is indeed "Plant Doctor." I believe he sincerely loves this work. This interview about "tree scars" began as a very casual question, yet I never expected Teacher Zhang to give such detailed and professional answers—for example, his account of "underground soil" is a part rarely touched on in our fieldwork, and it must be a special feeling that only an ancient-tree conservation worker who has devoted himself with care and feeling for decades could have. Trees quietly guard generation after generation, and at the same time people like Teacher Zhang silently care for the trees. This mutual understanding and support builds a deeper connection between us and the ancient trees.

shbl:story-027:body-1.context_header_en: 'Trees with Steles' Tree Stories, Entry 27 | Wuzhong District, in front of Husha Cemetery (Liu Gong Tang) | Ginkgo
shbl:story-027:body-1.text_en:
The first field visit to this tree was in spring, and the volunteers present all marveled: a ginkgo in spring could actually be this beautiful. Most of the old streets and houses in Husha have been rebuilt in recent years; Liu Gong Tang, built in the Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE), is one of the few surviving historic buildings, with two successive courtyards, and its gatehouse is three bays wide, built in the Qing dynasty. It once served as the office of the Overseas Chinese Cemetery; after repairs, a ceiling was installed and walls were built, and it is now abandoned.
The ginkgo in front of the gate is 500 years old. In 1956, the master of Chinese painting Li Keran sketched in Dongshan and left behind the work 'Suzhou's Thousand-Year Ginkgo,' which is probably this tree. While we were gathered around the tree discussing it, an Aunt Chen from the village passed by, said the ancient ginkgo belonged to her family, and warmly invited the volunteers to sit at her home; the ginkgo's canopy can be seen from her courtyard. In her parents' generation, several families raised and protected this ginkgo together. There is a government subsidy of two thousand yuan each year; generally fertilizer is applied once in autumn, and pests and diseases are promptly dealt with and reported, so its overall health is good, and caring for it has become part of several families' lives. Aunt Chen married into the Shi family of Husha from Duqiao decades ago and has of course benefited from the ginkgo; the fruit is also divided among three Shi households, 200 jin for the large household and 100 jin for the small ones. This grafted female ginkgo can yield more than five hundred jin of ginkgo nuts a year; the nuts are small, the flesh round, green when shelled, and sweet in taste.

shbl:story-027:interview-1.text_en:
Interviewee: Ms. Chen Aidi; Interviewer: Luo Xinglin; Time: April 8, 2023
Location: met by chance near the zelkova in Husha Village, Yangwan; lives next to the ginkgo at Liu Gong Tang.
Aunt Chen said she was born in 1976 in Duqiao Village, Dongshan, and married into the Shi family of Husha Village, Yangwan, in 1996. The current house was rebuilt on the original site, and the ginkgo canopy can be seen from the courtyard. In her parents' generation the ginkgo was allotted in part to her family; this grafted female ginkgo can yield more than five hundred jin of ginkgo nuts a year. The nuts are small, the flesh round, green when shelled, and sweet in taste. The tree's fruit is divided among three households surnamed Shi in the village; the large household gets about 200 jin and the small ones about 100 jin. Each year the tree receives a government subsidy of two thousand yuan, divided among the three families; generally fertilizer is applied once in autumn, and at other times no special care is needed. Because the ancient tree grows at their doorsteps, the families also routinely watch for pests and diseases, dealing with and reporting them promptly, so the tree's overall health is good.

shbl:story-028:body-1.context_header_en: 'Trees with Steles and Biographies' Tree Stories, Entry 28 | Wuzhong District, Dongshan Town, Zijin Nunnery | Sweet Osmanthus
shbl:story-028:body-1.text_en:
Suzhou has a long history of cultivating sweet osmanthus. In the Tang dynasty (618–907 CE) it was called "small osmanthus," and the matching poems "Ode to the Small Osmanthus of the Public Study" by Pi Rixiu and Lu Guimeng have been handed down; in "Taihu Poems" they also recorded osmanthus planting in the Dongting Mountain area at that time. By the Song dynasty (960–1279 CE), osmanthus cultivation in Suzhou had become even more widespread; poems by Fan Zhongyan and Fan Chengda have been handed down, and Fan Chengda recorded the two names "rock osmanthus" and "muxi" (osmanthus).
Private residences and nunnery and temple grounds liked to plant osmanthus, and places featuring osmanthus as a landscape were common. In the Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE), every eighth lunar month there was an "osmanthus market" at Shantang in Tiger Hill (Huqiu Mountain); the poet Cai Yun wrote in "Wu Yu": "Seven li of Shantang, seven li of boats, in the fragrance of muxi song and strings seethe." Suzhou's cultivated osmanthus is broadly divided by flower color and flowering period into golden osmanthus, silver osmanthus, red osmanthus, and four-season osmanthus. There are 190 ancient osmanthus trees extant, and the oldest and stoutest first-class ancient osmanthus trees are all inside Zijin Nunnery. The two golden osmanthus trees in front of the hall lean toward the Arhat Hall; this was once interpreted as "piously worshiping the Buddha." Today the osmanthus trees, tied with red prayer ribbons, spread a great umbrella above the tea room, adding a further touch of worldliness.

shbl:story-028:body-2.context_header_en: 'Trees with Steles and Biographies' Tree Stories, Entry 28 | Wuzhong District, Dongshan Town, Zijin Nunnery | Chinese Boxwood
shbl:story-028:body-2.text_en:
Boxwood is said to "grow one cun a year," commonly called "the boxwood that does not grow big in a thousand years," and among the people it has another name that is practically a "personal attack": "the thousand-year dwarf." The Northern Song (960–1127 CE) poet Su Shi wrote, "Countless grasses and trees in the garden spring in spring, only the boxwood suffers in leap years"; Li Yu put it even more bluntly: "Boxwood grows one cun each year, not a hair more; in leap years it instead shrinks one cun—this is a fate limited by Heaven."
Against this background of knowledge, when the volunteers saw Zijin Nunnery's two 1,500-year-old boxwoods, they were still shocked by how "thin and slender" they were. The two trees are 9.4 meters tall but only 30 centimeters in diameter—"a thousand-year boxwood only as thick as a bowl's mouth." According to horticultural experts, boxwood does not necessarily fail to grow tall, but it certainly does not grow thick; even in forty or fifty years it can only reach 5 centimeters. The two trees are staggered front and back, occupying only a very small corner of the courtyard. Yet squatting in a corner of the courtyard and looking up at the sky, one can still faintly feel the vicissitudes of history; the canopy completely covers the courtyard, with luxuriant branches and leaves and abundant greenery.
Once you know boxwood, you will notice it is common in gardens, but because it is evergreen and small in form, it is not conspicuous. Its slow growth seems to be storing energy—so sluggish, yet so steady. Perhaps it is precisely this tenacious quality, unperturbed by favor or disgrace, that gives boxwood its long lifespan and wide adaptability and makes it much loved; there is even a saying, "Keep boxwood at home, and generations will be pillars of the state," in stark contrast to its understated appearance. Zijin Nunnery's two boxwood trees are said to have been planted when the nunnery was founded during the Northern and Southern Dynasties period, and may be the oldest surviving historical witness in the temple.

shbl:story-028:background-1.context_header_en: 'Trees with Steles and Biographies' Tree Stories, Entry 28 | Wuzhong District, Dongshan Town, Zijin Nunnery | Sweet Osmanthus and Chinese Boxwood | Background: Zijin Nunnery, Dongshan Town
shbl:story-028:background-1.text_en:
Driving up the winding mountain road along the shore of Lake Tai through Ximao Valley in Biluo Village, an unassuming yet great hall comes into view. Folk tradition has it that "of the world's Arhat halls, there are two and a half; Wuzhong alone holds one and a half," and one of these halls refers to the Arhat statues of Zijin Nunnery. Legend says the sixteen Arhats seated on the sumeru platforms on the left and right walls of the main hall are the work of Lei Chao and his wife, famous Southern Song (1127–1279 CE) folk sculptors; later generations added the Buddhas of the Three Ages, the Four Heavenly Kings, the Twenty Devas, and others, making it a veritable pantheon of the East. People today often say the hall contains three treasures: the dragon subdued by the Dragon-Subduing Arhat coiled around the hall's pillars, the central main Buddha whose eyes forever look toward the beholder, and the canopy on the sculpted wall of mountains, seas, and clouds behind the hall, which drifts like real cloth.
Outside the hall it is equally splendid, seemingly embraced by ancient and famous trees. In front of the hall, ginkgo leaves pave the ground and osmanthus fragrance drifts; behind the hall, yulan magnolias vie in spring and boxwoods increase. The ancient trees lean toward the main hall, which people call worshiping the Buddha; crossing the hall is like passing through spring and autumn, baptized by the gods seated within. This brilliant pearl of Lake Tai has since ancient times been protected by the gods and Buddhas filling the hall and by the ancient and famous trees outside it.

shbl:story-029:body-1.context_header_en: 'Trees Carved in Stone' Tree Stories, No. 29 | Wuzhong District, Haiyun Temple | Intertwined Camellia (no longer extant)
shbl:story-029:body-1.text_en:
(No longer extant)
Camellias were cultivated in Suzhou early on and have long been a principal planting in gardens. By the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE) several varieties were already recorded. Those produced in Sichuan and Yunnan were prized, and among them the Baozhu camellia was especially esteemed. The Humble Administrator's Garden once preserved a Baozhu camellia, and the products section of the Wuxian County Gazetteer, from the early Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE) and the Republican period, also records more than ten camellia varieties—a profusion of types that leaves one marveling.
In the fourteenth year of the Chenghua reign era, Wu Kuan and his good friend Shi Minggu set out on a journey to the mountainous country west of Suzhou. This trip was at the invitation of Xu Yongzhuang of Guangfu. The two traveled by boat south along the Xu River, passing Mudu Town and Cangshu Town to reach Guangfu Town, and Wu Kuan wrote Record of a Journey to the Western Hills. When Ming-dynasty literati traveled, they already listed rare ancient trees and wondrous sights as scenic attractions. In succession the handscroll mentions the ancient sleeping pine at Xuanmu and Haiyun Temple's intertwined camellia, said to have been planted by Han Shizhong.

shbl:story-029:body-1.hook_en: In 1478 Wu Kuan sailed west and recorded the intertwined camellia attributed to Han Shizhong.

shbl:story-030:body-1.context_header_en: 'Trees with Steles and Biographies' Tree Stories, No. 30 | Gusu District, Humble Administrator's Garden | Banks' Rose
shbl:story-030:body-1.text_en:
Banks' rose is often cultivated in gardens, climbing over trellises or walls and hedges, and is a common flower in Suzhou. Wen Zhenheng of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE) records in Changwu Zhi (Treatise on Superfluous Things): "I have often seen that in the gardens of households, bamboo is invariably used to make a screen, with five-colored roses drawn over it, and timber framed into a pavilion, called a Banks' rose trellis. When the flowers bloom, people of all kinds sit together beneath it—how is this different from a tavern? Yet these two kinds cannot be planted without a screen or trellis; perhaps moving them to the women's quarters, for the ladies to pick, would be somewhat acceptable. There is another kind called yellow rose, the most prized, whose flowers are also profuse and pleasing to the eye."
A Banks' rose trellis is a fence-like frame built of bamboo and timber, over which shrubs and clustering flowers such as roses and Banks' roses are trained to grow, forming a flowering hedge. In the Ming (1368–1644 CE) and Qing (1644–1912 CE) periods this flowering hedge was also called a flower screen, and such garden scenery is also very common in Ming dynasty Wumen painting and calligraphy.
Suzhou currently has three ancient Banks' rose trees; it is truly not easy for shrubby, clustering flowers to survive to this day, and the one yellow Banks' rose and one white Banks' rose in the Humble Administrator's Garden are especially important. The layout of the yellow Banks' rose is almost identical to "framing timber into a pavilion," while the white Banks' rose is even more distinctive: its overall layout is a round disk, that is, a great round disk holds up the hundred-twined, thousand-layered Banks' rose flowers, and at the four corners in the middle of the disk there are still beams to support it. Beneath the Banks' rose flowers, ring-shaped stone benches are thoughtfully provided, and many slender Banks' rose branches hang down and sway in the wind. Seen from afar, it is like a naturally formed pavilion of unique elegance; visitors resting their feet can also enjoy the nimble, touching beauty of the Banks' rose flowers, which shows the craftsmanship of the designers of that time.

shbl:story-030:body-1.hook_en: The white Banks' rose in the Humble Administrator's Garden is lifted by a round-disk trellis, its hanging branches like a natural pavilion.

shbl:story-030:body-2.context_header_en: 'Trees with Steles and Biographies' Tree Stories, No. 30 | Gusu District, Humble Administrator's Garden | Chinese Wisteria
shbl:story-030:body-2.text_en: The most famous Chinese wisteria in Suzhou's gardens is surely the one Wen Zhengming planted by hand in the Humble Administrator's Garden. Legend has it that in the twelfth year of the Jiajing reign of the Ming dynasty (1533), when Wen Zhengming painted the Album of Thirty-One Views of the Humble Administrator's Garden for Wang Xianchen, he took the opportunity to plant a Chinese wisteria in the garden by hand. The Republican-era Wuxian County Gazetteer describes this ancient vine as having "twisted branches and stems, shade covering one mu, and exceedingly profuse blooms." Over more than 400 years the garden changed owners several times; today, in the small courtyard of Woqiu Hall in the Zhongwang Mansion of the Suzhou Museum, separated from the Humble Administrator's Garden by a single wall, the wisteria, twisting like a horned dragon, "forms a grove of itself on a lush trellis," and beneath the trellis a stone tablet bears the eight characters "Vines Planted by Mr. Wen Hengshan," inscribed by Duanfang, Jiangsu provincial governor in the Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE). "Because it is Wen Zhengming's wisteria, it surpasses all the wisteria in the world." In late spring in April, the blossoms hang down like jeweled pendants in a profusion of purple, and the garden gatherings of Ming dynasty Jiangnan literati overlap with today's "stealing half a day of leisure from a busy life"; the cultural thread of Gusu, like the Wen vine, endures without end.

shbl:story-031:body-1.context_header_en: "Stories of Trees" No. 31 | Gusu District, Lion Grove Garden | Chinese Wisteria
shbl:story-031:body-1.text_en: Lion Grove Garden has two ancient wisterias, numbered 狮012 and 狮013, both 130 years old, located respectively southeast and northeast of Jiejia Bridge. Judging from old photographs of Lion Grove Garden, the history of the wisteria corridor can be traced back to the Bei family's remodeling of Lion Grove Garden during the Republican era. What the Bei family initially built was in fact an iron wisteria trellis, a style popular in the Republican period, and the ages of the two ancient wisterias are also fairly consistent with the era of the Bei family's construction. The wisteria corridor was later reinforced and rebuilt several times, finally taking on the present form of a stone corridor with a wooden roof. At the corner of the corridor there originally stood a small pavilion with a pyramidal roof, originally the "Imperial Stele Pavilion." In early old photographs from before the Bei family took over Lion Grove Garden, one can seemingly still see a surviving image of this sealed and reinforced Imperial Stele Pavilion. In old paintings and early photographs, plant trellises are shown set up at Jiejia Bridge, very likely planted with wisteria. In other words, whether it was the planting of wisteria beside Jiejia Bridge or the setting up of the small pavilion at the corner of the corridor, neither was actually a passing whim of the Bei family, but rather important historical and cultural information retained through historical inertia when Lion Grove Garden was remodeled. It may therefore be inferred that the history of wisteria cultivation at Lion Grove Garden is far longer than 130 years.

shbl:story-032:body-1.context_header_en: "Stories of Trees" in Shubei Lizhuan, Entry 32 | Gusu District, Shilinli Residential Compound | Ginkgo
shbl:story-032:body-1.text_en:
Every year in late autumn, looking west from Lion Grove Garden, there is an ancient ginkgo inside Shilinli Residential Compound just beyond the wall; its golden crown towers into the sky and draws the eye. As is well known, Shilinsi Lane at the entrance of Lion Grove Garden is named because Shilin Temple once stood there in the Yuan dynasty (1271–1368 CE). According to the earliest temple record of Lion Grove Garden, the "Record of the Orthodox Bodhi Temple of Lion Grove," Shilin Temple was first built in the second year of the Zhizheng reign of the Yuan (1342 CE). Through the Ming (1368–1644 CE) and Qing (1644–1912 CE) dynasties, judged against historical images, the temple was grand in scale, and on the west side of the main hall stood several ancient trees, among them ginkgos.
By matching present-day aerial photographs with Qing dynasty prints, it is not hard to infer that the ginkgo standing in Shilinli Residential Compound is right near the main hall of the former Shilin Temple. If the ancient ginkgo's age of 640 years is accurate, this ginkgo was planted just when Lion Grove Garden was first established, and it may be the only physical relic left by Shilin Temple from the Yuan dynasty to the present; it has witnessed almost the entire history from Shilin Temple to Lion Grove Garden.
Unlike those ancient ginkgos whose living space has been squeezed by urban development and that huddle in corners, the residential compound has set aside a whole plot of open ground for it to rest and grow, its falling leaves as profuse as they were several hundred years ago. At first, Lion Grove Garden was a temple garden; later the temple halls and the temple garden were separated, the temple was occupied during the Republican period, a factory was established there after the founding of the People's Republic, and then a residential compound was built. As the buildings vanished into the long sweep of history, the ginkgo remained, silently witnessing the stories that once unfolded here.

shbl:story-033:body-1.context_header_en: “Steles for Trees” Tree Stories, Entry 33 | Gusu District, Lingering Garden | Ginkgo
shbl:story-033:body-1.text_en: Walking through the Lingering Garden, one of China's "Four Great Famous Gardens," you may unexpectedly encounter century-old trees. The Chinese elm beside Wenmuxixiang Pavilion (the Pavilion for Enjoying Osmanthus Fragrance), the black pine outside the Daiyun Nunnery, the southern magnolia at the entrance to Youyi Village, and the persimmon tree on the south side of the earthen hill in the western part lead us into winding paths and meditation rooms. Most striking of all, however, are the tall, upright ginkgos on the central rockery: one about 500 years old and another about 220 years old, making this the largest number and the highest grade of ancient ginkgos among Suzhou's gardens. Gusts of cool wind wrinkle the water's surface and spread out a carpet for the banquet; ginkgo leaves glitter in the warm yellow sunset like thousands of butterflies dusted with gold powder, fluttering their wings and offering their first and final dance above the shimmering lake light.

shbl:story-034:body-1.context_header_en: Tree Biographies, Story 34 | Gusu District, Lingering Garden | Chinese Wingnut (no longer extant)
shbl:story-034:body-1.text_en:
Without comparing old photographs, we could not imagine that there was once a highly recognizable ancient Chinese wingnut in front of Quxi Tower in the Lingering Garden. Garden enthusiasts spotted it in old photos and, using Quxi Tower and the octagonal window on its outermost bay, accurately reconstructed the position of this ancient tree. In 1926, the American Florence Powell came to Suzhou to photograph gardens. Beneath this photograph she wrote: "Te corner as whole: the window in the covered corridor as the appear from the outside, the old camphor tree casting shadows on the white walls, the two-story tea house, a small stone bridge, a rocky pathway, and a stone lantern shrine to the god of evil, a warning of danger." Clearly, she believed it was a camphor tree. Later, the photographer Dorothy Graham also photographed the same spot. From the lotus leaves in the image it is not hard to judge that it was summer, but the time of photography is missing; one can only work backward from the publication date of 1938, before which the ancient Chinese wingnut was still alive. (It is no longer extant.)
In the early 1950s, Liu Dunzhen began surveying Suzhou's gardens, measuring and recording them one by one. In Suzhou Gardens, published in 1957, we can still discover to our delight that the Chinese wingnut was still there. It was not until 1960, when Liu Dunzhen completed the first draft of Suzhou Classical Gardens, that the measured plan in the text marked this place as Chinese wingnut (dead). Although such a record is disappointing, the ancient-architecture scholar's meticulous surveying and recording also confirmed the species of the ancient tree for later generations who could not see it on site.
An old photograph of a tree, over the course of several decades, is like a relay race, telling us roughly which period the ancient tree survived into, what once existed here, and what has vanished. Today, Quxi Tower is here, the octagonal window is here, the corridor is here, the stone bridge is here, and the stone sutra pillar is here too—only on the old site where the ancient Chinese wingnut once grew, another tree has been planted.

shbl:story-035:body-1.context_header_en: 'Steles for Trees' Tree Stories, Entry 35 | Gusu District, Master of the Nets Garden | Chinese Juniper
shbl:story-035:body-1.text_en:
Walking into the Master of the Nets Garden, visitors can easily spot a "bare tree" on the far side of Caixia Pond. This unassuming-looking Chinese juniper is more than 900 years old and is said to have been planted by hand by Shi Zhengzhi, a vice minister of the Southern Song dynasty (1127–1279 CE) and the garden's first owner. The ancient juniper is about 10 meters tall, the "high point" around Caixia Pond, and the oldest tree in Gusu District. More than 130 years ago, the garden's owner planted a lacebark pine beside it; today the pine and juniper stand shoulder to shoulder. "Pines and junipers are naturally solitary and upright, ill-suited to the faces of peach and plum"; compared with brief splendor, they have chosen enduring resilience.
People who observe trees over the long term pay attention not only to the changes of the four seasons but are drawn even more to distinctive tree forms. The volunteers of the Tree Stele project jokingly consider 网003 a tree with personality: its lower trunk is tall and straight, and the juniper foliage at the top grows sparser with age, yet its branches and trunk are like a person dancing for joy, retaining vigorous vitality. Searching through Wu-school painting and calligraphy, we find that Wen Zhengming's 'Cunju Tu' (Painting of Preserved Chrysanthemums) also depicts a tree with personality. Comparing the forms of the branches, we cannot help wondering: might the literati of the Wu school of painting also have noticed this ancient juniper?

shbl:story-035:body-2.context_header_en: 'Steles for Trees' Tree Stories, Entry 35 | Gusu District, Master of the Nets Garden | Chinese Wisteria
shbl:story-035:body-2.text_en:
Chinese wisteria is a climbing vine that is good at clinging. Several famous wisterias stand in Suzhou's gardens: the Wen wisteria at Woqiu Hall in the Loyal King's Residence, the wisteria at the Thirty-Six Mandarin Ducks Hall in the Humble Administrator's Garden, the wisteria at Xiaopenglai in the Lingering Garden, the wisteria at the Jiejia Bridge in the Lion Grove Garden, and the wisteria by Caixia Pond in the Master of the Nets Garden. The first four combine the plant's own characteristics with artificial ingenuity, whereas the ancient wisteria at the rockery east of Zixia Pond in the Master of the Nets Garden borrows the garden's landscaping and climbs according to the terrain.
Every April the wisteria comes into flower. Its rugged, vigorous branches sprawl over the yellow stone beside Caixia Pond. In addition, outside the window of Dianchun Yi there is another wisteria, unadorned and growing naturally; when the doors and windows are opened, purple vapor comes from the east, like a spring breeze on the face.

shbl:story-036:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees Told by Steles' No. 36 | Gusu District, Garden of Harmony | Crape Myrtle
shbl:story-036:body-1.text_en:
The crape myrtle has a long history of cultivation in Suzhou. It is also called wei hua ("wei flower") and is named after the Ziwei star. Little known is that "Ziwei lang" ("Gentleman of the Ziwei Star") was another name for a Secretariat Drafter; the playful self-mockery in the line "Ashamed all day long to face you, for I am no Ziwei lang" captures the fondness for the crape myrtle among the great and powerful of successive dynasties.
Wen Zhenheng of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE) records in Changwu Zhi (Treatise on Superfluous Things): "There are four kinds of wei flower: besides the purple, the white is called white wei, the red is called red wei, and the purple with a touch of blue is called emerald wei." The crape myrtle has a long flowering period and is an important summer flowering plant. Changwu Zhi also says: "This flower opens in the fourth month and fades in the ninth; commonly called 'Hundred-Day Red.' Planted in a mountain garden, it may be called a 'friend that endures.'" The one in the Garden of Harmony is a rare "Silver Crape Myrtle": not a vivid purplish red but a plain, clean white, adding further refinement.
Suzhou's gardens are not short of ancient crape myrtles either, though unfortunately each has more or less a flaw: the 640-year-old crape myrtle in the Garden of Harmony is said to have been planted by the top scholar Wu Kuan; its main trunk has now died, leaving only one side branch cautiously continuing the literary line—the trunk withered, the flowers blooming as before, and even reaching out beyond the wall, presenting different views inside and outside the moon gate. The Garden of Harmony was built on the site of the old residence of Wu Kuan, a Ming-dynasty top scholar of Suzhou, and tradition says the ancient tree was planted by Wu Kuan himself, earning it the name "Top Scholar's Crape Myrtle." Counting back the years and consulting the literature, this claim is not accurate; however, Wu Kuan was quite interested in plants, and after going to the capital to serve as an official he often missed the common plants of Jiangnan, writing a long essay as a record of them.

shbl:story-036:body-2.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees Told by Steles' No. 36 | Gusu District, Garden of Harmony | Camellia
shbl:story-036:body-2.text_en: Camellias are a common sight in gardens; what is rare is an ancient one, and rarest of all is an ancient camellia leaning against lake rock. This solitary peak south of the Jinsu Pavilion in the Garden of Harmony is indeed a superior piece: though its form is fixed, it has a sense of dynamic ascent—no wonder the ancients always likened "rock to the root of clouds." This little scene is like a cloud within sight and reach, captured for the beauty of the human world, willingly giving up the boundless sky to become a stubborn rock locked deep within white walls, leaning close to a red camellia for a hundred years without regret—thought of this way, it is extraordinarily romantic.

shbl:story-037:body-1.context_header_en: “Stories of Trees” No. 37 | Gusu District, Canglang Pavilion | Chinese Wingnut
shbl:story-037:body-1.text_en:
The Chinese Wingnut is extremely tolerant of water and damp. Its fruits have wings on both sides and are shaped like ingots; they hang in strings from the tips of the branches and are quite handsome. It is often planted in low-lying damp places such as stream banks and river flats. Precisely for this reason, in recent years some scholars have boldly imagined that in “Mooring by Maple Bridge at Night”—“The moon sets, crows caw, frost fills the sky; river maples, fishing fires, face sorrow as one sleeps”—the “river maples” (jiangfeng) refer to Chinese Wingnuts by the river.

The two Chinese Wingnuts at Canglang Pavilion grow on the west side of Yangzhi Pavilion. Their trunks are hollow, and at the base of the roots of one of them there is a huge opening. Because the garden commonly has farm cats and other animals, every time one sees this ancient Chinese Wingnut, one cannot help imagining: is this the rabbit hole from Alice's Adventures in Wonderland? Might one enter another fantastical place?

shbl:story-038:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees Told by Steles' Entry 38 | Gusu District, Couple's Retreat Garden | Single Red Camellia
shbl:story-038:body-1.text_en:
On the yellow-stone rockery in front of Chengqu Thatched Hall in the East Garden of Couple's Retreat Garden, two camellias spread out in elegant ease, their branches covered with fully opened pink petals that look especially bright and lovely in winter. These two camellias are 'Meiren Cha' (Beauty Camellia), a horticultural cultivar of the sasanqua camellia; it blooms very early, flowering as early as December. Meiren Cha is also called 'Yangfei Cha' (Yang Guifei Camellia). The poem 'Yangfei Cha' says: 'Once her peerless beauty was compared to a famous flower, / and another soft red blush suffused her face like rosy clouds.' One of the two is a century-old ancient tree; judging by its age, it may have been planted when the Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE) literatus Shen Bingcheng and his wife Yan Yonghua were living in the garden, and it has witnessed their romance, expressed through poetry and wine.
Meiren Cha also once appeared in the scene of Daiyu burying flowers in the 1987 television adaptation of Dream of the Red Chamber. Mr. Deng Yunxiang, the production's folklore consultant, wrote in his essay 'Falling Flowers at Couple's Retreat Garden': 'Because its colors are delicate and tender, it is very suitable for display on screen, so Daiyu picking up fallen flowers was chosen to be filmed here. What she picks up and holds in her palm to admire is a small, tender red camellia blossom.'

shbl:story-039:body-1.context_header_en: 'Steles for Trees' Tree Stories, Entry 39 | Gusu District, Dongyuan | Chinese Wisteria and Ginkgo
shbl:story-039:body-1.text_en: Old Suzhou natives all know that Dongyuan (East Garden), on the east side of the ancient city and adjacent to the Couple's Retreat Garden, was once Suzhou's zoo. Its predecessor was the Changshan Bureau, a charitable institution founded during the Daoguang reign of the Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE), which once took on burial functions. The Wu Men Yuan Shu Wenxian (Documents on Gardens and Villas of Wumen), compiled in the Republic of China era by Fan Guangxian of Wu County, records: "The zoo east of the city, at Er Men Kou, was originally the mortuary halls of the Changshan Bureau; it has long had flowers, trees, water and rocks, and its layout is full of quiet charm." The ancient ginkgo, the ancient cypress and a trellis of white-flowered Chinese wisteria that we see in Dongyuan today all have a history of more than 200 years; they are relics of the Changshan Bureau.
shbl:story-039:body-1.hook_zh: 东园曾是苏州动物园，园中200多年的古银杏、古柏和一架白花紫藤，都是清代昌善局的遗物。

shbl:story-040:body-1.context_header_en: "Stories of Trees" No. 40 | Gusu District, Xinsuili, Donghai Island | Ginkgo
shbl:story-040:body-1.text_en:
In today's old city of Suzhou there are still many small lanes that electronic maps have never explored. Following the vague wording "Xinsuili, Donghai Island" in the gazetteers, we wandered round and round the narrow alleys until at last, through a gap between clothes-drying poles and electric wires, we glimpsed a tree in all its splendor. Legend says the ancient tree was "planted by Zhang Shicheng at the end of the Yuan dynasty," but 540 years ago was the Chenghua era of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE), so this claim is easy to disprove. Yet the legend of its being "planted by Zhang Shicheng" is not without reason: not far from the ancient ginkgo is a lane called "Chengtian Temple Front." When Zhang Shicheng held Suzhou, he first occupied Chengtian Temple and built the eastern and western temporary palaces; because these two palaces were woven with waterways and seemed impregnable as metal walls and boiling moats, the place names "Donghai Island" and "Xihai Island" have been passed down to this day, and only then did this ancient ginkgo—younger than Zhang Shicheng—become his friend across the generations.
Today all kinds of mops hang from its thick trunk; residents loll about in twos and threes on bamboo chairs beneath the tree, chatting; now and then an auntie draws water from the well; little children run about cheering for the falling ginkgo leaves, as if this tree had become an inseparable member of the big family. It is so tall, yet hides its greatness in the city; it is so ancient, yet fits so naturally into the life of ordinary lanes.

shbl:story-041:body-1.context_header_en: Tree Stories, Entry 41 | Gusu District, Xibei Street | Camphor Tree
shbl:story-041:body-1.text_en:
On the route from Beisita Metro Station to the Humble Administrator's Garden, if you look from Xibei Street toward Tingyuan Road, you can see that this road has made a small roundabout for a tree. A camphor tree stands at a slant in the center, its branches and leaves lush, huge as an umbrella.
An ancient tree occupying a good location has witnessed the vicissitudes of several hundred years. Its site was originally the residence of the Zhang family of the Song dynasty (960–1279 CE), who later donated the house to become a temple. During the Jiajing reign of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE), Fujian merchants, following the example of the Tianfei Palace in Taicang, also built a Tianhou Palace in Suzhou dedicated to Mazu, and chose this site. The Wu Men Biao Yin records: "On the stone archway at the gate of the Tianhou Palace, to the left and right are carved sixteen characters: 'The gods are near; each should be reverent; officials, scholars, and common people, dismount here.' Made by imperial order in the Ming Jiajing era." Over the past century or so, the Tianhou Palace has successively been used by Beijie Central Primary School, the Municipal No. 38 Middle School, a vocational middle school, and the No. 3 Middle School branch campus; today it has been developed into a villa area. The ancient camphor tree is precisely the survivor of the two camphor trees that once stood before the main hall of the Tianhou Palace. When the road was built at the beginning of this century, between building a straight road and making a detour to protect the tree, the people of Suzhou chose the latter. A city willing to yield the road to a tree—that is some foresight, and no little deep feeling.

shbl:story-042:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees Told by Stele' Entry 42 | Gusu District, Suzhou City God Temple | Ginkgo
shbl:story-042:body-1.text_en: The Wenmiao (Confucian Temple), where the 'Shouxing' (Longevity Ginkgo) lives, treasures the Southern Song dynasty (1127–1279 CE) map 'Pingjiang Lu'; the City God Temple, which preserves the Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE) 'Stele of the Three Horizontal and Four Vertical [Waterways] Map,' likewise has a 530-year-old ginkgo for company. Trees and steles seem equally solid, becoming witnesses to the city's growth. 'Chenghuang' originally referred to the 'moat'; later it gradually evolved into 'the city's local guardian deity.' The City God Temple has enjoyed extremely abundant incense since ancient times and was once on a very large scale; what survives today is only a small complex of buildings centered on the Gongzi Hall (I-shaped Hall) of the Hongwu era. For this reason, both inside and outside the City God Temple there are many ancient ginkgos over a century old—some surrounded by high-rises, others hidden away in deep lanes; in the past they were all presumably under the protection of the City God.

shbl:story-043:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees Told by Steles' Story of a Tree, Entry 43 | Gusu District, Quyuan Garden | Crape Myrtle
shbl:story-043:body-1.text_en: Quyuan Garden, in Mayike Lane, is hardly among the famous gardens of Suzhou, yet it has its own delights. More than 100 years ago, the master of Chinese classical studies Yu Yue lived here. Amid the turmoil of worldly affairs, he chose to hide away in his small building, teaching and writing books—like the crape myrtle in the garden, which blooms in summer and “does not claim the finest spring in the garden.” The garden's two halls are named “Spring Remains” and “Joyful Knowledge,” taking the meanings “though flowers fall, spring remains” and “rejoice in heaven and know one's fate.” We can imagine that when Yu Yue, disappointed in officialdom, resolved to retire to Suzhou, he had already found a refuge for his spirit.

shbl:story-044:body-1.context_header_en: “Stories of Trees Told by Steles” Story 44 | Gusu District, No. 23 Mayike Lane shared courtyard compound | Ginkgo
shbl:story-044:body-1.text_en:
Turning from Renmin Road into Mayike Lane, after just a few steps you can glimpse “No. 23” on a small blue plaque on the left; walking along the internal main path, you soon find them. These two ginkgo trees are each enclosed within the courtyards of two households. According to a ninety-year-old resident grandmother, the 180-year-old one was originally in a public area; later a resident, moved by the tree, enclosed it within a courtyard while rebuilding the house—a fine tale brought about by a tree lover.
This place was originally the ancestral hall of Shen Shixing. Because the age of the trees does not match the “Wanli era” when the hall was first built, it can be determined that the ancient trees were planted at a different time from the hall’s construction. According to early research on the Shen ancestral hall and old photographs, the Ming-dynasty (1368–1644 CE) painted decoration in the hall was extremely lavish, consistent with the historical background of Shen Shixing’s long tenure presiding over the Grand Secretariat and his later retirement to his hometown. The ancestral hall disappeared in 1967; it is not hard to imagine that these two ancient ginkgos once stood here together with the original old buildings and the wooden-and-stone archway, guarding the family glory of the Shen clan.

shbl:story-045:body-1.context_header_en: “Steles for Trees” Tree Stories, Entry 45 | Gusu District, Daru Central Primary School | Ginkgo
shbl:story-045:body-1.text_en:
Daru Central Primary School is not on Daru Lane but on Nanshizi Street. An ancient ginkgo on the school grounds has survived thanks to the intact historical character inherited along Pingjiang Road; it may be the tallest elder on the whole street beneath the signal tower.
Although this ginkgo was originally a relic of the “Xu Family Chunhui Charity Estate,” ginkgo and schools seem always to have been a match made in heaven. In ancient times, government-run education maintained the tacit arrangement of “temple on the left, school on the right,” and neither the stern Confucian temple nor the solemn school palace could do without ginkgoes as a foil.

shbl:story-046:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees Told by Steles' Story 46 | Gusu District, Wangxima Lane | Ginkgo
shbl:story-046:body-1.text_en: Setting out from the Art Garden for the Mountain Villa of Secluded Beauty, passersby on Wangxima Lane can always catch an inadvertent glimpse of the two towering ginkgos in front of the Lord Chunshen Temple, and from them recall that distant story. Suzhou at that time was not the earthly paradise later so lavishly praised; what Huang Xie, one of the Four Lords of the Warring States and chancellor of Chu, faced was by no means the great city of Helü built by Wu Zixu—the Wu region had already been incorporated into Chu's territory. He took on the perilous mission of securing the river defenses in the west and eradicating the floods of Lake Tai and the Xu River. Today the Lord Chunshen Temple is so deserted that sparrows could be caught at its gate; those past stories seem to have fallen away together with the two century-old ginkgos at its entrance—but the leaves will always sprout anew.

shbl:story-047:body-1.context_header_en: "Steles for Trees" Story No. 47 | Gusu District, opposite the Changmen Community Veterans Service Station | Ginkgo
shbl:story-047:body-1.text_en: Though the Yuanning Guild Hall (元宁公所) is honored as one of Suzhou's first batch of controlled protection sites, material that can be found about it online is exceedingly scarce—only one old photograph, reposted so often it has acquired a digital patina. "Yuanning" is taken from the two counties of Shangyuan and Jiangning in Nanjing; the guild hall was jointly built by fur merchants in the late Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE), but was soon destroyed at the hands of the Taiping rebels ("the Long Hairs"). Although it was rebuilt during the Tongzhi reign, it subsequently became a primary school building and then a factory building, until in recent years it was completely abandoned. In this bleak season, when even Jiangnan grows desolate, a disappearing ancient building is healed by a single ginkgo tree: its leaves fall rustling down, as if covering the cluttered courtyard with a dignified and splendid coffin; ginkgo leaves drift along the broken roof frame into the long-uninhabited inner rooms—who knows whether to guide the fur merchants who have not returned for so long, or to bid farewell to the workshop workers who left not long ago. As if single-handedly, it has paved a golden avenue outside the door; surrounded by construction waste, wrapped in gold, it is like a martyr, taking leave of the past as it keeps watch.

shbl:story-048:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees' No. 48 | Gusu District, Suzhou Confucian Temple | Ginkgo and Qiu Catalpa
shbl:story-048:body-1.text_en:
The Suzhou Prefectural School Confucian Temple was first built in the second year of the Jingyou reign of the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127 CE), in 1035 CE. Today, many ancient trees can still be found in the Confucian Temple. Six weather-beaten ginkgos stand guard on the south side of the Dacheng Hall. The one on the west, numbered '沧501,' was planted in the Southern Song dynasty (1127–1279 CE) and is more than 800 years old; it is called the 'Longevity Ginkgo' (Shouxing). Because it was once struck by lightning, only half its trunk remains, leaning slightly. The 600-year-old 'Intertwined Ginkgo' (Lianli Xing) was also struck by lightning, and remarkably, a Chinese hackberry and a qiu catalpa grew out of its hollow interior, embracing as one body—hence its name. The 'Three Firsts Ginkgo' (Sanyuan Xing) was completely destroyed by lightning in the Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE); when Qian Qi, a student at the Suzhou Prefectural School, successively placed first in the provincial, metropolitan, and palace examinations, new shoots grew from the old root in three forks, and the world called it the 'Three Firsts Ginkgo.'
Four hundred years ago, the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE) Wumen painter Qian Gong depicted a scene in the south of Suzhou, including the Lingxing Gate and Dacheng Hall of today's Confucian Temple; the architectural form and layout are little different from today, with ancient trees standing in groves before the Dacheng Hall, among them three ginkgos that have grown to the present day.
Photography first arrived in China in the nineteenth century. The Dacheng Hall of the Suzhou Confucian Temple, with its rich heritage and grand architectural form, attracted many Chinese and foreign photographers to stop and photograph. Looking through old black-and-white photographs, the earliest images of these ancient trees date back to 1889: the Dacheng Hall photographed by the Norwegian explorer Carl Bock, probably a winter scene, with the Longevity Ginkgo and the Intertwined Ginkgo in the front courtyard both bare-branched; the setting sun stretched the Longevity Ginkgo's shadow very long. What is moving is that this moment of sparse vegetation is only one several-hundredth of its long years; in the following year, the cycle repeats, and the ginkgos before the hall will continue to sprout until the vegetation is lush.
The Confucian Temple continues Suzhou's thousand-year cultural lineage. As one of the main ancient buildings in the central urban area, politicians, scholars, and tourists visiting Suzhou come in droves, and in the old images they took, we see the ancient trees guarding the Dacheng Hall face to face, year after year, just the same.

shbl:story-049:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories Told by Trees' No. 49 | Gusu District, Suzhou No. 100 Hospital | Lacebark Pine
shbl:story-049:body-1.text_en:
Inside Suzhou No. 100 Hospital stands a seven-span granite beam bridge called the Jiecao Nunnery Stone Bridge. This site was originally Dayun Nunnery, founded in the Yuan dynasty (1271–1368 CE) and also known as Jiecao Nunnery; it was rebuilt several times in the Ming (1368–1644 CE) and Qing (1644–1912 CE) dynasties. Today its halls and stone pagoda are all destroyed, yet the square life-release pond has been preserved, and the form of this stone bridge is likewise a unique example within the old city of Suzhou.
Standing here together with the stone bridge is an ancient lacebark pine roughly 220 years old. This place may have been a paradise for ancient lacebark pines. In the tenth year of the Hongzhi reign of the Ming (1497), Shen Zhou spent the night at Dayun Nunnery and later painted the 'Record of a Visit to the Thatched Nunnery' (Caoan Jiyou Tu). Through the 'Poems Recording a Visit to the Thatched Nunnery' (Caoan Jiyou Shi) and the painting and calligraphy, the layout of Dayun Nunnery can still be reconstructed: 'In the quarters of the abbot, Master Mao, situated in the east side, there is a Buddha hall; behind it stretches an earthen ridge some forty zhang long and over three zhang high, on which stands an ancient kuo pine, towering ten xun, its branches crooked and deeply green—a thing of several hundred years.' 'Kuo' here means the lacebark pine. In the upper-left corner of the painting we can clearly see that the simply outlined trunk bears mottled, scaly bark, a typical feature of the lacebark pine. Although the age of this ancient lacebark pine, 沧529, does not match the Ming dynasty of more than four hundred years ago, just like Canglang Pavilion next door to No. 100 Hospital—'Today at Canglang, ask not who is master; a hundred years of rise and fall are but the same waves'—the ancient tree and the ancient architectural remains pass the baton onward, wave after wave, intermittently yet completely bearing witness to the succession of the years.

shbl:story-050:body-1.context_header_en: Tree Steles and Biographies, Tree Stories, Entry 50 | Gusu District, Former Site of the Jiangsu Provincial Surveillance Commission | Yulan Magnolia
shbl:story-050:body-1.text_en:
As the only ancient magnolia in the old city, "沧553" has stood at the Former Site of the Jiangsu Provincial Surveillance Commission for more than three hundred years. As early as the early Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE), this place was the provincial water conservancy sub-office; in the fourteenth year of the Hongzhi reign, it was changed to a surveillance sub-office, and later it handled military preparedness affairs exclusively and was called the "Military Preparedness Circuit"—which is how the road name "Daoqian Street" came about. In the eighth year of the Yongzheng reign of the Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE), the Jiangsu Provincial Surveillance Commissioner moved from Jiangning to Suzhou, and the Military Preparedness Circuit office was changed into the Provincial Surveillance Commissioner's yamen, which was in charge of judicial and penal affairs in the province. In the sixth year of the Tongzhi reign of the Qing dynasty, Governor Guo Boyin rebuilt this place; during the Republican period it was changed into the Jiangsu High Court. For more than three hundred years, this ancient tree has witnessed changes in the administrative functions of the ancient buildings.
Observing and recording ancient and notable trees has never been work that can be completed in a single year; for two consecutive years, the volunteers of Tree Steles and Biographies visited this place. In March 2023, because the ancient buildings at the Former Site of the Jiangsu Provincial Surveillance Commission, a provincial-level protected site, were being restored, scaffolding was put up in the courtyard; in this, one of her more than three hundred bloomings, she kept company with the scaffolding and the construction workers. In March 2024, the restoration of the ancient buildings was completed and the former site reopened to the public; the ancient tree still bloomed in spring with vigorous vitality.
In ancient times the purple magnolia was called Xinyi or Mubi; the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE) painter Shen Zhou painted the handscroll Xinyi and Ink Cabbage. This tree is recorded in the register as "Purple Magnolia," but judging from its characteristics, it is more likely an Erqiao Magnolia. The purple magnolia and the Erqiao Magnolia have similar flower shapes and close flower colors, and sometimes the two are hard to distinguish. The Erqiao Magnolia is a hybrid of the yulan magnolia and the purple magnolia; it inherits the flower color of the purple magnolia and the tree habit of the yulan magnolia, and its tree form is slightly smaller than that of the yulan magnolia—it is a small tree that flowers before leafing out and has nine petals. The purple magnolia has a late flowering period; it is a low shrub that flowers and leafs out at the same time, its outermost whorl of tepals is reduced to narrow sepal-like structures, and its inner whorl has six tepals.

shbl:story-051:body-1.context_header_en: 'Trees with Stele Biographies': Tree Stories, Entry 51 | Gusu District, Suzhou No. 1 Middle School | Chinese Wisteria
shbl:story-051:body-1.text_en: Everyone who graduated from No. 1 Middle School surely has, in their memories, the faint fragrance of a wisteria trellis. This ancient wisteria, with a history of more than 500 years, is the school's "treasure that anchors the school," located in the old architectural courtyard in the northwest corner, named "Wisteria Court." In fact, this place was once the site of the Yuanhe County Yamen of the Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE); it has witnessed the vicissitudes of this place's transformation from a government office into an academy, and embodies the meaning of "it takes ten years to grow a tree, but a hundred years to cultivate a person." The Wisteria Gathering held in late spring each year has already become a tradition; its profound cultural heritage, like spring wind and rain, benefits later generations.

shbl:story-052:body-1.context_header_en: 'Steles for Trees' Tree Stories, Entry 52 | Gusu District, No. 13 Yingfengqiao Lane | Chinese Red-bean Tree
shbl:story-052:body-1.text_en:
At the 'Office for Educational Equipment and Work-Study Management' at No. 13 Yingfengqiao Lane, through the fence at the entrance, we can see an unremarkable Chinese red-bean tree. It is not beautiful; in spring and autumn it is bare, and only in early summer does it put out new branches. Yet across the whole of southern Jiangsu only about ten ancient red-bean trees survive, and this 360-year-old Ming-dynasty red-bean tree is the oldest one inside the old city—extremely rare. 'No. 13 Yingfengqiao Lane' is not an area open to the public, but the red-bean tree is famous far and wide, and when asked about it, the elderly people nearby and the guard at the gate will recite the line 'May you gather more of them; this thing best stirs longing.'
The red-bean tree originally belonged to No. 37 Wuyachang, in the former residence of Wu Zhijia, a Ming-dynasty Suzhou native and Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Justice. The street name 'Wuyachang' comes precisely from him. In the history books there are only a few brief lines about Wu Zhijia: he was caught up in the protracted 'Contest over the Heir Apparent' during the Wanli reign, Wu Yuanjia of Changzhou, Ye Chuchun of Wuxian, and Zhang Dong of Kunshan were all censured and sent home, known at the time as the 'Three Remonstrators of Wu.' In one lifetime he left behind an alley, a red-bean tree, and a line in the history books—enough, one might say, to have 'not failed the world of men.'

shbl:story-053:body-1.context_header_en: "Stories of Trees" No. 53 | Gusu District, Soochow University | Ginkgo
shbl:story-053:body-1.text_en: A university's greatness lies in its grand buildings, its great scholars, and also in the great trees that carry a deep cultural accumulation. Across Soochow University's Tiancizhuang campus are nearly 70 ancient trees, including camphor trees, Chinese zelkova, sweet osmanthus, Chinese juniper and dragon juniper, as well as the city's only century-old climbing fig, lush and green, covering a brick wall. The 320-year-old ginkgo outside the north gate, like the Wenxing Pavilion on campus, is a relic of the old Changzhou County School, and it echoes across the other side of Ganjiang Road with the Dacheng Hall of the Changzhou County School, likewise a gathering place of ancient ginkgos. In modern times, when the imperial examinations were abolished, Soochow University took over the mantle of the county school and continued to nourish its students; a brand-new Western-style clock tower rose up, and together with the old Wenxing Pavilion it formed a cultural landscape in which Chinese and Western stand side by side and past and present reflect each other.

shbl:story-054:body-1.context_header_en: "Stories of Trees" No. 54 | Gusu District, Dinghui Temple | Ginkgo
shbl:story-054:body-1.text_en:
The Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE) Wumen painter Qian Gu once painted the "Picture of the Dinghui Temple Chan Monastery." From the inscription on the right side of the scroll, which states it was made on a spring day in the xinyou year (1561), we know that this realistic long handscroll records the actual scene of the Dinghui Temple monastery more than 500 years ago: in front of the mountain gate were farm fields, and the temple's structures were, in order, the mountain gate, the Heavenly King Hall, the Mahavira Hall and the meditation quarters, with the Twin Pagodas, first built in the Song dynasty (960–1279 CE), beside them. Comparing ancient and modern building structures, it is not hard to see that the temple's ancient buildings were later rebuilt: the Heavenly King Hall was changed from a double-eaved hip-and-gable roof to a single eave, and the Mahavira Hall was changed from three bays wide to the present five bays wide.
Today, pilgrims entering Dinghui Chan Temple are sure to be drawn to two ancient ginkgo trees. In autumn, the dense golden leaves weighing down the branches have also become a reason for visitors to come and pay their respects. The two ancient trees are more than two hundred years old and stand symmetrically on either side of the Mahavira Hall. According to the recollection of Teacher Zhang Ji, an ancient-tree conservation worker, the ancient ginkgos in front of the Dinghui Temple hall once grew so vigorously that they lifted the floor tiles inside the hall. In the ancient-tree conservation plan, both the ancient trees and the ancient building had to be protected; in the end, the tree doctors reduced the roots so that both could be preserved. This reminds people that the tenacious vitality of ancient trees, rooting downward, far exceeds imagination.

shbl:story-055:body-1.context_header_en: “Steles for Trees” Tree Stories, Entry 55 | Gusu District, Former Site of the Suzhou Independent Branch of the Communist Party of China | Deodar Cedar
shbl:story-055:body-1.text_en:
In 1924, the educator Zhang Jiyou planted a deodar cedar at Huangfeiji in the old city of Suzhou. Surrounding the cedar was the newly founded Leyi Girls' School; “Leyi” means “optimistic and enterprising, beneficial to society.” In early September 1925, the young teachers Hou Shaoqiu, Zhang Wentian and Ye Tiandi, whom Zhang Jiyou had invited from Shanghai, secretly founded the Suzhou Independent Branch of the Communist Party of China together at Leyi Girls' School; from then on, Suzhou opened a new chapter. In the previous survey, the deodar cedar had not yet been entered in the register of ancient trees; this year happens to be its “hundredth birthday.”
Zhang Jiyou's daughters are the famous Four Zhang Sisters. Zhang Yunhe once wrote in a memoir, “Teacher Zhang Wentian taught me Chinese for only half a year, yet he gave me a lifelong influence on how to conduct myself. This was true ideological education. What I especially cannot forget is his earnest exhortation: in life, be a person beneficial to humanity; in work, do things beneficial to the world; a true person is one who keeps the whole world in view.” The young girls of that time may not necessarily have understood the great principles of saving the nation and the people, but the influence of a good teacher lasts a lifetime, just like the deodar cedar: taking root, sprouting, and growing into a towering tree.

shbl:story-056:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees' in Tree Steles and Biographies, Entry 56 | Wujiang District, Sanjiaojing Ginkgo Square, Songling Town | Ginkgo
shbl:story-056:body-1.text_en:
Sanjiaojing Ginkgo Square stands at the junction of two main roads, Liuhong Road and Zhongshan Road. It is the site of Shengshou Chan Temple and was once the city center of Wujiang; today only a single ginkgo remains, which happens to stand behind a bus stop, and because of this the stop is praised by locals as the 'Ginkgo Station.' Legend has it that Sanjiaojing was built by Wu Shan, a man of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE). In his post at the Ministry of Justice he carefully examined the records of prisoners' crimes and overturned more than a hundred doubtful cases; Sanjiaojing is therefore also tangible evidence of Wu Shan's treating others with virtue.
As the urban area of Wujiang expanded, Shengshou Chan Temple long ago disappeared, and naturally no one inquired after Sanjiaojing either; and with the outward relocation of modern commerce, the square no longer performs its original function, yet it remains an important landmark in people's hearts. Sanjiaojing, the ginkgo and the square have, since their birth, benefited from this city's prosperity and development; after the passing of white clouds and the transformations of seas and mulberry fields, the surroundings may be vastly different, and so they step forward once more to bear witness to that distant yet still vivid era. They are time, they are the years, they are history, and still more they are witness, spirit and eternity.

shbl:story-057:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees' No. 57 | Yuantong Temple, Songling Town, Wujiang District | Ginkgo
shbl:story-057:body-1.text_en:
According to the Wujiang Archives, Yuantong Temple was formerly Yuantong Nunnery. The earliest record of Yuantong Nunnery appears in the Continued Gazetteer of Wujiang County from the Kangxi reign: "Yuantong Nunnery is at Hupu; it was built by the monk Songyin in the first year of the Tianqi reign of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE)." By modern times, only two old ginkgo trees and a few dilapidated buildings remained of Yuantong Nunnery. Because more than ten other kinds of plants grow as epiphytes on one of the ginkgos, it has the alternative name "Ten Scenes."
Temples were sometimes called "conglin" (monastery groves), and ginkgo was customarily used in place of the bodhi tree. The ginkgo also happens to be a long-lived species, so in Jiangnan settlements the companion of an old ginkgo is very likely an old temple; this seems almost a fixed pattern. Nearly every settlement crossed by a river once had such a scene: on the first and fifteenth of each lunar month, barefoot children would clutch candles and go flitting unsteadily across a ramshackle yet solid old bridge; as soon as they reached the ginkgo, the sound of sutra chanting from the old temple would swirl around their ears. Half understanding, they would hand their candles to a grandmother in a flowered headscarf, her face flickering in and out of view in the light filtered through the ginkgo leaves, as devout and sacred as the incense burning in the censer.

shbl:story-058:body-1.context_header_en: "Steles for Trees" Tree Stories, Entry 58 | Wujiang District, Gengle Hall, Tongli | Lacebark Pine
shbl:story-058:body-1.text_en:
Mr. Chen Congzhou held that the lacebark pine "stands alone in Chinese gardens." With its twisting, dragon-like form and its ethereal white color, it is indeed a landscape tree of exceptional ornamental value. Compared with the stout, burly ancient lacebark pines of Beihai's Round City and Jietai Temple in Beijing, the lacebark pines in Suzhou gardens often appear crooked. Suzhou people call this "mentou" (cutting back the main branch): while the tree is still small, the main branch is cut off, and the branches may then spread at a slant. I believe the main reason for this north-south difference is the difference in architectural purpose. Whether it is the "White-Robed General" or the "Nine-Dragon Pine," both create a sense of stern order, whereas most Suzhou lacebark pines appear in private gardens, accompanied by lake rocks, winding bridges, and flowing water, presenting a literati painterly mood.
Guo Xi, a painting theorist of the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127 CE), held that "water should seem distant; if it is fully shown, it is not distant; if it is screened and its flow interrupted, then it is distant." In the literati landscape paintings of the Wu region, ancient pines can often, from particular angles, use visual overlap to obscure stretches of water, creating a sense of endlessness and setting off the depth and distance of the flowing water. But these ancient pines are usually straight and tower into the clouds; this feature, common in old paintings, is in fact relatively rare on the ground in Suzhou gardens.
Joseph Needham held that "generally speaking, distance in Chinese painting is expressed by height; usually objects placed behind are painted higher than those in front, but not necessarily smaller, which gives many Chinese paintings the character of a bird's-eye view, all objects seeming to be seen from a certain height." When we stand in a particular garden ourselves, we lose this "bird's-eye view" perspective, and those straight, towering trees naturally lose the visual effect of partly concealing the water. By contrast, a crooked tree like the lacebark pine at Gengle Hall can, at a height closer to our own line of sight, create a stronger sense of depth. Before the Kan Song Du Hua Pavilion ("Viewing Pines, Reading Paintings") in the Master of the Nets Garden there is likewise a lacebark pine with a similar function. In the content of "viewing pines, reading paintings," is there not also the method of ancient pines partly concealing the water?

shbl:story-059:body-1.context_header_en: "Stories of Trees" No. 59 | Wujiang District, Wumengtang Site, Yejia Dai, Lili Town | Wintersweet
shbl:story-059:body-1.text_en:
This ancient wintersweet stands within the Wumengtang site at Yejia Dai in Beishe, yet the Wumengtang exhibition hall connected with it is on the second floor of the community library at the northeast bank of Xihe Bridge in the old town area of Beishe. That building is the Liu residence known as Shuxuan Tang, which originally had no connection with Wumengtang; one must contact the administrator to find the key before entering. Only by visiting both places can one fully grasp the story of this ancient wintersweet.
When wintersweet is mentioned, Chao Buzhi contributed its most famous literary anecdote: "Its fragrance is faint and its bearing plain, / I recall Su'er, just like this plum"—using his friend's maidservant Su'er as a metaphor for wintersweet to create a celebrated line. From then on, Su'er became another name for wintersweet.
Yejia Dai in Beishe, Wujiang, has the oldest wintersweet in the whole Suzhou municipality. Wintersweets are inherently hard-pressed to live long, and this one also marks a brilliant literary coordinate—Wumengtang. The Ye family of Wumengtang was a famous literary clan in Wujiang's history: Ye Shaoyuan and his wife Shen Yixiu, together with their seven sons and four daughters, who were steeped in their parents' influence, were all rich in literary thought and talent, producing a great quantity of poetry and prose, collected in the Collected Works of Wumengtang (Wumengtang Ji).
Among them the best known member is surely Ye Xiaoluan. Folk legend says that although Ye Xiaoluan was born into the Ye family, where literary culture flourished, in her childhood she was for some reason raised by her maternal uncle's wife, who fortunately was likewise a beauty of both talent and learning and devoted herself to teaching Ye Xiaoluan. Later Ye Xiaoluan returned to the Ye family and planted a wintersweet in front of Shuying Tower to commemorate her aunt's nurturing kindness; thereafter she produced a great many works and enjoyed some renown in the literary world of the time. Yet heaven envied her talent: Ye Xiaoluan, deeply cherished by her parents, sadly died of illness before her marriage. As if struck by this blow, and with the times in turmoil, the Ye family gradually declined thereafter. Folk tradition therefore once widely held that Ye Xiaoluan was the prototype for Lin Daiyu in Dream of the Red Chamber.
This legend has circulated for a long time, but many details remain hard to verify. It has no dramatic twists and turns; everyone is full of truth, goodness, and beauty, as in an ideal realm, yet it ends with a cruel twist of fate, as if witnessing the collapse of an ivory tower. I believe the legend of Wumengtang is so widely told not only because of the scholarly standing of the Collected Works of Wumengtang, but also because it embodies the general public's admiration for the Ye family's atmosphere, their regret over the talented beauty Ye Xiaoluan's ill fate, and their grief over a literary heaven crumbling overnight. The family environment Ye Shaoyuan created had a modernity that transcended its era: elders and young in harmony, no distinction between sons and daughters, masters and servants close to one another. Judging from the episode in the legend of planting the plum in commemoration, Ye Xiaoluan's talent most likely grew up under the family's careful nurture—and in olden times, how many people's talents were buried in the snow of history, becoming one after another "Su'er," vases left high on a shelf?
There is only one Wumengtang, and the wintersweet is ultimately aloof and solitary; the myriad flowers do not enter its discerning eyes, the many trees cannot set off its purity and ease. It can only dance alone with its shadow, its hidden fragrance drifting by on its own through this deep winter.

shbl:story-060:body-1.context_header_en: “Stories of Trees” No. 60 | Wujiang District, Zhenze Town, Xiajiadou Village, Cishan Temple | Ginkgo
shbl:story-060:body-1.text_en:
The “Cishan Temple” in Xiajiadou Village gives one a subtle sense of something half-familiar. In Jiangnan, Cishan worship usually refers to the Great Emperor of Cishan—the hero Zhang Bo, who was elevated to godhood for his achievements in taming floods; this may also be a regional cult of the water deity.
This faith is not especially common in Suzhou, but it is widely distributed in Huzhou, and Zhenze Town already borders Nanxun District of Huzhou, which may reflect the frequent cultural exchange between the two places.
In Wuyue Village, Qidu Town, also in Wujiang District, there is a protected “Cishan Temple Bridge,” and beside that bridge stands another Cishan Temple; on its gable wall is boldly written “Namo Amitabha”—because in more recent history Buddhism gradually gained the upper hand, and the Great Emperor of Cishan was transformed into the Bodhisattva of Cishan and incorporated into the Buddhist system. Perhaps the local people do not care whether it is Buddhist or Daoist; they believe only in the deity “Cishan,” just as, in the broad context of feudal society, no matter how emperors changed dynasties, the most grassroots social history was still written by local gentry and prominent clans.
Turning from the main road onto the village road, the way to the Cishan Temple in Xiajiadou Village passes three old bridges. Among them, Wanfu Bridge uses sturdier piers rather than the row-pillar construction prevalent in the beam bridges of the Suzhou area, showing that the river channel was once swift; no wonder the nearby area enshrines the Great Emperor of Cishan, famed for taming floods.
Concrete slabs have been laid over the steps of all three old bridges, perhaps in the old days to make passage easier for two-wheeled vehicles. Beside each old bridge, moreover, a brand-new highway bridge runs across, taking over the baton of responsibility for “connecting what was impassable,” yet the locals did not “cross the river and tear down the bridge”; instead they carefully sealed off the old, decayed, inefficient bridges to one side, the two rainbows side by side, the new and the old echoing each other. Just so, the ancient temples scattered across the land of Wujiang and modern science coexist in harmony; grassroots community deities are not merely feudal superstition—they also commemorate heroes and great figures, and still more they transmit history and culture.

shbl:story-061:body-1.context_header_en: "Stories of Trees" No. 61 | Wujiang District, Dabei Nunnery, Shijiabang, Zhenze Town | Ginkgo
shbl:story-061:body-1.text_en:
"Dabei Nunnery" is another fairly common name for a community temple. If we could get into the halls to observe, many things would be readily resolved—yet once again we were met with a closed door.
Fortunately, this is a place where temple-and-bridge culture is strikingly at work. The Yangjia Bridge beside it is also called Huiyuan Bridge; "Huiyuan" ("confluence of sources") can sometimes also be understood as a kind of water-deity worship—where river sources meet, the currents surge and race, so naturally the waters again need to be subdued. Judging by the geographical setting, the rivers on both the east and west sides of Yangjia Bridge become broad, making bridge-building inconvenient; this kind of hydrological feature is popularly called a "gourd pocket" (huludou). Thus Yangjia Bridge, which grips the neck of the gourd pocket, became a transport hub. Because temples need believers, they often choose sites where people are dense, and they also like to plant ginkgos—so many ancient ginkgos in Wujiang stand at bridgeheads. Often, finding a tree means finding a temple, finding a bridge, finding a narrow place in the river; not every link in the chain necessarily survives, but tracing back layer by layer never hurts. The origins of temple-and-bridge culture are simple and blunt.
In Haining, Zhejiang, there is a Huiyuan Nunnery dedicated to Lord Guan (Guandi). The legend of Guan Yu flooding the seven armies with water is famous far and wide, so it is hardly strange that he could become a god who governs water. The Dabei Nunnery beside Yangjia Bridge here in Shijiabang may also be connected with this. If so, the great-compassionate martial god really does take on a touch of black humor—a kind of salvation by force.
On the western side of Yangjia Bridge, a Wukang stone bridge-center slab / dragon-gate stone is built into the steps; some sources say it may be a relic of Dabei Nunnery. The main body of Yangjia Bridge is mostly Jinshan stone, but judging by the bluestone masonry on the bridge abutments at both ends, it must have a long history and have been rebuilt many times; this carved Wukang stone slab may well be an original component of Yangjia Bridge. This ginkgo is called a "thousand-year ginkgo" in some sources; taking the Suzhou Gazetteer of Ancient and Notable Trees as authoritative, it is 125 years old—yet it is indeed more splendid than many ginkgos that have been listed as 500 years old.
