shbl:story-062:body-1.context_header_en: Tree Stories, Entry 62 | Wujiang District, Sidu Village, Hengshan Town | Ginkgo
shbl:story-062:body-1.text_en:
Usually, when we discuss a particular ginkgo, we have to trace it back to its roots. The records of Chongwu Temple in the old gazetteers are much the same, mostly recounting a history of several rises and several declines. But a turning point came with the 2004 edition of the Hengshan Town Gazetteer, which recorded the following story in written form:
"In Zhangjiagang Village there was a Granny Wu who had worked as a servant in Yuan Shikai's household. Once she followed her master to Mount Wutai to burn incense, and there met a monk who told her: this monk's patriarch, in order to fulfill the dying wish of a Yuan-dynasty Princess Baihua, had made a special trip to Wujiang and planted one ginkgo each at Pingwang's Shusheng Temple, Shuangyang's Yongle Temple, and Sidu's Chongwu Temple."
The key phrase is plainly 'Princess Baihua,' and Princess Baihua is likewise a frequent figure in folk legend; from the very name we can glimpse the feelings of truth, goodness, and beauty that people have invested in her.
For example, in Changfeng County, Hefei, Anhui, there is a Tomb of Princess Baihua. Legend says that to guard the tomb and protect the mausoleum she built a temple beside the tomb of the King of Wu, and that out of loyalty to her ruler and love for her father she later left a dying wish to be buried there herself. But this Princess Baihua was the youngest daughter of Yang Xingmi, King of Wu during the Yang Wu period, which clearly does not match the Yuan-dynasty setting of the Wujiang legend.
And in Kunqu opera, four acts of Baihua Ji (Record of the Hundred Flowers) happen to survive. Its plot is said to be adapted from Ming-dynasty popular literature and roughly tells how during the Xuanhe reign of the Song, in the Fang La uprising, Fang La's sister, Princess Baihua, was a female general who led the rebel army bravely against the Song forces but was undone by the traitor Jiang Liuyun, and took her own life after defeat—a tragic and heroic tale. Although this again conflicts with the background of the ginkgo legend, Baihua Ji already contains many Suzhou traces, such as the siege of Dongting Mountain, and even an episode involving a mustering platform, which can echo the old gazetteers of Wujiang.
In the article 'The Ginkgo Trees of Wujiang,' published in the Jiangnan Times, the author holds that Princess Baihua was the daughter of a general who fought against the Jin; she formed a women's army and joined the fight against the Jin, and was named for the crown of a hundred flowers she wore. Unfortunately, no source for this version of the legend could be found, and this story undoubtedly still has its deviations.
In fact, among the old gazetteers of Suzhou itself, one can find only the record in the Daoguang Pingwang Zhi: 'The mustering platform is at Dayu Weir; legend says it is the place where the Yuan Princess Baihua mustered her troops; it is now ruined.' This background at last satisfies the account in the 2004 Hengshan Town Gazetteer, and incidentally matches the episode of the female general reviewing her troops in Baihua Ji.
Since the legend in the 2004 Hengshan Town Gazetteer was itself formed relatively recently (as an oral account by Yuan Shikai's servant), may we not consider that this legend of tree-planting to fulfill Princess Baihua's dying wish was itself compounded from several legends: roughly inheriting the episode of the female general mustering troops from the Kunqu play Baihua Ji, and grafting on an ending like that of the legend in Changfeng County, Hefei, Anhui, of a dying wish to be buried alongside. And the three temples in the legend—Pingwang's Shusheng Temple, Shuangyang's Yongle Temple, and Sidu's Chongwu Temple—are precisely three rather famous ancient-ginkgo viewing spots that survived in Wujiang into modern times. Although the ginkgo at Pingwang's Shusheng Temple was destroyed in 1972, the Dashun Sauce Garden on its former site still produces 'Ginkgo Brand' chili oil and chili sauce.
In fact, we need not insist on the truth of the legend itself. In the great majority of cases, legends do not arise without cause; whether intentionally or not, the phenomenon itself directly or indirectly reflects the conceptions and subconscious of its subject, regardless of whether the phenomenon itself is right or wrong. Discussing and studying the process and causes of its formation is of benefit to the exploration of social history as a whole.

shbl:story-063:body-1.context_header_en: “Stories of Trees Told by Steles,” Story 63 | Wujiang District, Tongji Nunnery, Lujiawan, Hengshan Town | Ginkgo
shbl:story-063:body-1.text_en:
Lujiawan has a community shrine called Tongji Nunnery—“the benefit of boats and oars, by which one crosses what is impassable.” Although I was not fortunate enough to see the interior, since it is the deity of “Tongji” (universal passage), this is undoubtedly another ancient temple with a water-deity cult. The water-laced terrain of the southern shore of Lake Tai determined the prosperity of fishing and commerce here, and deities with “Tongji” functions displayed their powers; in nearby Pingwang Town there is also a community shrine with a similar name. And judging from the “wan” (bend) in Lujia, this may be somewhat similar to the situations of Daxian “gang” (harbor) and Tingzi “gang.”
To my delight, an old stele is set into the wall of the rebuilt hall. Steles beside community shrines are generally donation steles, sometimes also recording the shrine’s history. After reading it, however, I found this stele had nothing to do with the shrine: it records a village-boundary dispute, in which two villages came to blows over ownership of a stretch of water, later filed a lawsuit at the county yamen, and this stele amounts to the government’s ruling.
A saying circulates among the villagers: at first the old stele stood by the boundary waters to mark the line. But the struggle did not stop; each side moved the stele to manipulate the boundary in its own favor, until finally a wise man of Lujiawan moved the stele overnight to the front of the shrine, and only then did both sides tacitly accept the existence of the village boundary, and the dispute ended. In the special period the shrine was demolished, but the stele alone was preserved through the villagers’ joint efforts; only when the shrine was rebuilt in recent years did the stele see the light of day again.
The secular county yamen’s judgment rose to become a contract under the gaze of the deities; both sides lived by the water and naturally had to respect the authority of the “Tongji” deity. Whether the water deity actually protected travelers setting out to make a living can no longer be known, but this dispute, which secular power could not end, was settled through the divine hand; the water deity they believed in had undoubtedly shown the mighty power of “ordering the world and succoring the people” in a special way. And this kind of survivor-bias self-verification in turn consolidated the local foundation of faith in these grassroots community deities—a most interesting folk phenomenon.

shbl:story-064:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees' in Monuments for Trees, Entry 64 | Wujiang District, Bao'en Temple, Hengshan Town | Ginkgo
shbl:story-064:body-1.text_en:
The towns southwest of Wujiang, such as Hengshan, form the dense core of the lou-and-gang waterway network on the southern shore of Lake Tai, long summed up in the saying 'thirty-six lou and seventy-two gang.' Where there is a harbor there are boats, and where there are boats there are naturally boat people. The predecessor of Bao'en Temple at Tingzi Harbor was called Niangniang Temple (Goddess Temple), and two legends about it circulate locally. One holds that the 'Niangniang' is the Guanyin Bodhisattva invited from Mount Putuo; the other holds that the 'Niangniang' is the Mazu goddess invited by merchants from southern Fujian. Whether Putuo's Guanyin or southern Fujian's Mazu, both are unquestionably water-deity beliefs formed in coastal regions, strongly marked by the religious character of boat people; in some places where different cultures have interpenetrated deeply, the images of Guanyin and Mazu themselves even overlap to a certain degree.
Folk beliefs are often pluralistic in their early stages—vengeful ghosts and floating corpses, heroes and great men, and so on. As people in different regions (though these regions often share certain geographical conditions) gradually infused universal good wishes, deities of quite different origins began to be assigned similar functions, and in the end either became a school of their own through outstanding influence and won official recognition, or merged with other mainstream deities. Their own distinctive images gradually blurred over generations of oral transmission, leaving only a vague, distant title such as 'Lord,' 'General,' or 'Niangniang.' Seen this way, it is hardly surprising that Bao'en Temple should possess two origin stories that are far apart yet exceptionally vague.

shbl:story-065:body-1.context_header_en: "Steles for Trees" Tree Stories, Entry 65 | Wujiang District, Bodhisattva Temple, Daxian Port, Hengshan Town | Ginkgo
shbl:story-065:body-1.text_en:
We were not fortunate enough to enter this Bodhisattva Temple during our survey. According to local people, the temple is also called Xilin Nunnery and enshrines the Three Officials—Yao, Shun and Yu—as the Three Great Emperors. Legend has it that the three officials of Heaven, Earth and Water took the forms of Yao, Shun and Yu to govern the world; yet the Three Officials faith is Daoist, while a Bodhisattva Temple is quite obviously Buddhist. Village community temples have never been strict about such distinctions, so whether there was some succession or replacement here is hard to guess. I suspect "Bodhisattva Temple" is a local colloquial name, and "Xilin" is also a common name for community temples, probably meaning "the western Chan grove."
Judging by size alone, this tree is no inferior to the thousand-year ginkgo of Taiping Old Street; unfortunately its branch form is a bit messy, and its growing environment is not ideal. Yet messiness has its own charm: it can interact with the wild stairs and revetments around it, striking sparks full of the flavor of daily life—life is truly magnificent.

shbl:story-066:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees Told by Steles,' Story 66 | Yongle Temple, Zhenze Town, Wujiang District | Ginkgo
shbl:story-066:body-1.text_en:
Yongle Temple was somewhat luckier than Chongwu Jiaosi: it preserves ancient trees, an old bridge, an old Guanyin Hall, and several huge bluestone lotus-shaped column bases. Besides sharing with Chongwu Jiaosi the legend that trees were planted at the dying wish of Princess Baihua, Yongle Temple also gained a story from its name: folk tradition has it that the Yongle Emperor Zhu Di met with disaster in Wujiang, hid in the temple to tide over the crisis, and after ascending the throne bestowed on the temple the name "Yongle Chan Temple" and personally planted a ginkgo in commemoration.
The biggest flaw in this legend is that the tree's age does not match the Yongle reign. The Hongzhi edition of the Wujiang Gazetteer says: "Yongle Chan Temple is in the Eleventh Du. In the seventh year of Chunyou of the Song, the monk Shiji founded the mountain [established the temple], and it was granted the name Chongfu Yongle." The Qianlong edition of the Zhenze County Gazetteer is more detailed: "Yongle Chan Temple is in Shuangyang Village, the Eleventh Du, covering nine mu. In the seventh year of Chunyou of the Song, the local man Zhou Legang donated the land, and the monk Shiji built it; the imperial kinsman and military commissioner Xie Zhi, petitioned the court on its behalf, and it was granted the name Chongfu Yongle." Moreover, constrained by the early Ming court's cool attitude toward Buddhism, Yongle Temple was not rebuilt until the Xuande era, which shows clearly that its name has nothing to do with Zhu Di.
Mr. Gu Jiegang held that layered history "can show that the later the era, the more the central figure in the legend is magnified." This case is an endless magnification of the coincidence of the name "Yongle," so that a connection with no trace in the old gazetteers miraculously appears in later oral history. I personally think this legend very likely borrowed the template of the relatively recent folk tales of the Qing emperors' southern tours, with Yongle taking Qianlong's place.
Yongle Village, where Yongle Temple is located, originally belonged to Shuangyang Village; Shuangyang Village was originally called Shuangyang (双杨, "Double Poplar") Village. Legend has it that the village had a Liutang Bridge, with a tall poplar on each side, north and south of the bridge, hence the name. In a special period it was changed to Xiangyang Village, and when it was changed back a mistake crept in; I think it very likely that by then the double poplars were gone, and although people changed the name back out of habit, they no longer remembered which "yáng" it was.
Today the ancient ginkgo stands in the fields, especially conspicuous, taking over the baton from the double poplars to become the new landmark, and Yongle Village has gradually separated from Shuangyang Village to become a separate new administrative division. Willow, poplar, ginkgo—the names and their origins may not be accurate, but the bond established between this village and its ancient trees is genuine.

shbl:story-067:body-1.context_header_en: 'Trees with Steles and Biographies' Tree Stories, No. 67 | Wujiang District, Wang Xichan Memorial Hall, Zhenze Ancient Town | Chinese Zelkova
shbl:story-067:body-1.text_en: Before the Wang Xichan Memorial Hall in Zhenze Ancient Town, Wujiang, a 330-year-old Chinese zelkova sways in a blaze of red in autumn. In Jiangnan in former times, tree planting followed the tradition of 'zelkova in front, hackberry behind'; 'zelkova' (榉, jǔ) is homophonous with 'to raise up' (举, jǔ), carrying the wish that one may study well and become an official. But the owner of this ancient zelkova lived his whole life in poverty and never entered officialdom. Wang Xichan was born at the end of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE); at the age of 17 he met the great upheaval of the Ming–Qing transition, and after attempts to drown himself and to fast to death both failed, he gave up the imperial examinations, devoted his heart to scholarship, and dedicated himself to studying the calendrical systems of ancient and modern times, China and abroad, writing several works on astronomy and calendrical calculation. His contemporary Gu Yanwu commented, 'His learning fathoms Heaven and man, and he stands firm indeed—I am not the equal of Wang Yinxu.' While Lin Zexu served as governor of Jiangsu, he raised funds to build a tomb for Wang Xichan and set up before the tomb a stele inscribed 'Tomb of the Lofty Scholar Mr. Wang Xiao'an.' The zelkova before the tomb sends its roots down and grows upward, and 300 years later it still stands firm between Heaven and Earth.

shbl:story-068:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees Told by Steles' Entry 68 | Wujiang District, Yinxing Village, Jinjiaba, Lili Town | Ginkgo
shbl:story-068:body-1.text_en:
In Yinxing Village, Jinjiaba, there is a towering ginkgo. Though tall, it is not dense; only when the main trunk reaches one-third of its height does it suddenly burst out lateral branches in three directions. From a photograph alone its bulk cannot be felt; only standing beneath the tree does one marvel at its thickness.
Villagers say there was once a Jiqing Temple here, and in the narrow courtyard in front of the hall there were once two ancient ginkgos; one was unfortunately cut down because it affected the safety of the buildings. I could not find the Jiqing Temple described by the villagers in the old gazetteers. Although the Guangxu 'Continued Gazetteer of Wujiang County' (Qing dynasty, 1644–1912 CE) does mention a Jiqing Temple located at Nandouwei in Bache, it is clearly a considerable geographical distance from this one.
But I believe there must once have been a hall of no small size here, and there must once have been the narrow courtyard in front of the hall that the villagers describe. From the branching pattern of the ginkgo it is not hard to imagine that it could scarcely stretch its body in the narrow space, and only began to spread its forks once it rose above the surrounding houses; but beside it there was another ancient ginkgo, so it could only grow in the other three directions.
The incense offerings here may have ceased; the villagers I asked could not even clearly remember which deity was enshrined in the temple. Yet every one of the villagers treasures this ancient tree as if it were a jewel: an elderly man spent his own money seeking experts to re-measure the tree's age (villagers currently claim the tree is 1,500 years old and no longer hang the ancient-tree plaque marked 700 years, but the new age has not received official recognition from the Wujiang Housing and Urban-Rural Development authorities); when the ancient tree fell ill, they raised funds among the village to find a doctor for it; and now everyone has renamed Hangtou Village as Yinxing Village, planted new ginkgos beside the ancient tree to keep it company, and built a brand-new Ginkgo Square.
Some information is recorded in writing, and must be carefully sifted; some memories are imprinted in the mind, and will grow blurred; some answers have their solution right in the riddle itself, and only lack someone to understand them.

shbl:story-069:body-1.context_header_en: "Steles for Trees" Tree Stories, Entry 69 | Huqiu District (Suzhou New District), Zhenhu Subdistrict, Xijing Village | Ginkgo
shbl:story-069:body-1.text_en: In late autumn, in the inner courtyard of Zhiping Temple at the eastern foot of Shangfang Mountain, you look up to a blaze of gold and look down to brilliance spread across the ground. There were originally two ginkgos over 300 years old, but one was felled last century, leaving the other. The fate of the ancient tree is also a microcosm of Zhiping Temple's transformations. Like the many Jiangnan temples of the "four hundred and eighty temples of the Southern Dynasties," Zhiping Temple was first built in the Liang dynasty and was once immensely prominent, closely connected with Lengjia Temple, another temple on Shangfang Mountain. It once gathered literati and was remembered by Wen Zhengming: "When shall I return to Lengjia Temple, to keep company with the forest monks and watch the ancient pines?"; it also once received an emperor, leaving behind a Qianlong inscription: "Riding up Shangfang, I come down the mountain, resting briefly at the serene monastery, delighting in Zhiping." During the Taiping Heavenly War, the temple buildings were destroyed, the sound of wind in the pines gradually faded, and by the 1950s there was no longer any incense burning; the surviving temple rooms were borrowed as dormitories and offices for the Shangfang Mountain orchard. The Zhiping Temple we see now was rebuilt on its original site in 2008; a single ginkgo tree that has weathered the ups and downs of the years is enough to make a grove by itself.

shbl:story-070:body-1.context_header_en: 'Tree Stele Biographies' Tree Story No. 70 | Huqiu District (Suzhou New District), Donghe Chan Temple, Zhenhu Subdistrict | Ginkgo
shbl:story-070:body-1.text_en:
The ancient tree at Donghe Chan Temple bears a plaque saying 1,400 years, while the Suzhou Gazetteer of Ancient and Famous Trees records 300 years; the volunteers who write tree steles and biographies joke that this is a fraud-grade overstatement. At Fuji Temple outside Changmen Gate in Gusu there was the custom of 'ga shenxian'—'ga' meaning to join the crowd and squeeze through people; a Wu-dialect proverb, 'ga naomang,' vividly depicts the sea of people at temple fairs. Legend says that on the 14th day of the fourth lunar month, the birthday of Lü Dongbin, he would descend to the mortal world disguised as a beggar, relieve suffering, write out divine prescriptions, and heal people's illnesses; this gradually evolved into a blessing-seeking activity.
Today's Donghe Chan Temple in Zhenhu Community of the Suzhou New District, though different legends circulate, has a similar activity: legend tells that the daughter of the Suzhou prefect fell ill and no doctor could cure her, until a local Zhenhu physician, Li Huaichun, cured her with acupuncture. Later, to commemorate the divine doctor, the villagers built Li Xianren Shrine, and every year on the 24th day of the seventh lunar month the people along the shores of Lake Tai would go to burn incense and pray for blessings—locally called 'ga xianren.'
One wonders whether it was influenced by the legendary Li Huaichun's good deeds; likewise for a daughter, the local prominent Zhang family, when marrying off a daughter, built three tea pavilions on the shores of Lake Tai to 'chongxi'—to dispel ill fortune with joyous celebration—and to convenience the local people. The Tongfu Tea Pavilion in front of Donghe Chan Temple is the only one remaining today. Beside the temple is the ginkgo; beneath the ginkgo is the tea pavilion; beside the tea pavilion is a landing; where does the landing lead? Naturally, to Tongfu ('reaching blessings'). The Zhang family's grand Xiande Hall has not survived, but through this tea pavilion—an unintended legacy—we remember this kind local worthy. We could not find Donghe Chan Temple in the old gazetteers, nor could we find Li Xianren Shrine; the truth of these legends is hard to verify, but the customs that have come down to today are beyond dispute. The ancient ginkgo in the courtyard, through more than three hundred years of passing time, still guards the residents of this native place.

shbl:story-071:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees Told Through Steles' Story 71 | Huqiu District (Suzhou New District), Zhiping Temple on Shangfang Mountain | Ginkgo
shbl:story-071:body-1.text_en: The winds of Lake Tai nurtured the gentle, delicate art of Suzhou embroidery, and also gave rise to a steadfast, solid stone pagoda. In Xijing Village, Zhenhu, a stone pagoda was first built in the Southern Song dynasty (1127–1279 CE) to ward off floods, as a guardian object of Zhenhu. In traditional Chinese architecture, there is often a custom of using a dome to symbolize the vast heavens; entering the flame-shaped light gate on the south side of the stone pagoda, one finds inside a dome formed of rows upon rows of small seated Buddha figures, as numerous as the stars, and hence it is named the 'Ten Thousand Buddhas Pagoda.' Standing within it is like being surrounded by a Buddha realm, as if crossing 700 years to enter the Huazang world of the Yuan dynasty (1271–1368 CE). The thousand-year-old ginkgo is even a little older than the ancient pagoda rebuilt in the Yuan dynasty; day and night it shields it from wind and rain, together guarding the peace of the region.

shbl:story-072:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees' No. 72 | Xiangcheng District, Taiping Chan Temple, Taiping Town | Ginkgo
shbl:story-072:body-1.text_en:
The thousand-year ginkgo at Taiping Chan Temple is renowned throughout Suzhou, but the name "Taiping Chan Temple" itself does not have a long history. According to the Xiangcheng District Gazetteer, "Taiping Chan Temple" was originally the ancestral shrine of the Middle Sha branch of the Three Sha Wang family of the Southern Song (1127–1279 CE); at the end of the Yuan dynasty (1271–1368 CE) it was changed into the ancestral hall of Wang Guisan, a superintendent; in the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE) it was used again as the Wang family nunnery Yongli Nunnery; and in the second year of the Yongzheng reign of the Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE; Yongzheng reigned 1723–1735), the front hall of the nunnery was rebuilt as a Mengjiang Hall, known locally in older times as the "Shang Tianwang Liu Chengzhong Temple"; only in recent years was it expanded into today's Taiping Chan Temple.

Although Liu Mengjiang is a "water people" (shuishang ren) belief widely spread along the shores of Lake Tai, it survives only sparsely in the northern part of Suzhou prefectural city, and such beliefs often share similar causes. Professor Zhao Shiyu holds that "water people" families of Dongting East Mountain often took advantage of wartime opportunities when the state redefined land rights to come ashore through means such as uxorilocal marriage, and after gaining a firm foothold they "manufactured" ancestral origins by compiling genealogies to gloss over the family's standing—for example, claiming that "our ancestor was a recluse who came south with the Song imperial house." Seen in this light, the claim by the Taiping Wang family to be "descendants of the Taiyuan Wang who moved south" seems to share something in common with this, and the conversion of the family nunnery into a Mengjiang Hall likewise shows the close connection between the Taiping Wang family and "water people" beliefs. Taiping Town is adjacent to the Yangcheng Lake basin, and the Mengjiang belief there, similar to that of the Lake Tai basin, may hint at the possible true identity of the Taiping Wang family's ancestors.

By coincidence, every year on the 28th day of the third lunar month, Taiping's Mengjiang Hall holds the "Shang Tianwang Liu Mengjiang Procession." This procession date is entirely different from those along the shores of Lake Tai, but it happens to fall on the birthday of the Eastern Peak (Dongyue); recently some scholars have proposed that Liu Mengjiang may be an auxiliary deity of the Eastern Peak, and the date may serve as mutual corroboration for this view. Although Liu Mengjiang is found everywhere in the Wu region, the belief takes various forms; even though Liu Mengjiang entered the official sacrificial register during the Yongzheng reign, this could only unify it in form, while the content in each township still has its own distinctive character. In-depth study of folk beliefs is an important component of completing the social history of a locality. And today, roughly updating the Mengjiang belief, which has been transmitted in an orderly sequence, into a universal faith represented by "Taiping Chan Temple" may still require further discussion.

shbl:story-073:body-1.context_header_en: “Stories of Trees” in Shubei Lizhuan, Entry 73 | Xiangcheng District, Huangdai Town, Bai Guo Yuan | Ginkgo
shbl:story-073:body-1.text_en:
The market towns of northern Suzhou were heavily affected by warfare in modern times. Although Xiangcheng District has few ancient trees, the living conditions of those that survive are mostly rather comfortable. For example, this ancient ginkgo at the Huangdai City God Temple site is enormous, occupying an entire small square by itself; its branch shape somewhat resembles the bed-head look of someone who has stayed up all night and just woken up. The tangled electric wires and airing quilts beside it deepen its languid air, and its conspicuously protruding branch tips seem to be stretching.
Huangdai, Huangdai—it is easy to think of Lord Chunshen, Huang Xie. According to the town's elders, the City God Temple in Huangdai naturally enshrines Huang Xie, and so this ancient ginkgo is also tied to him. Huangdai, Huangtiandang, the Huangpu River… People may long have forgotten that Lake Tai was not always a land of fish and rice, and that the Xu River was far more than a golden waterway, yet the Wudi people's words of praise for Lord Chunshen, Huang Xie, are clearly conveyed to us through these place names spanning a thousand years.

shbl:story-074:body-1.context_header_en: 'Steles for Trees' Story No. 74 | Suzhou Industrial Park, Loufeng Subdistrict, north of Chuangyuan Road east of Xinghua Street; Qingyuan Huayan Water, Jinyan Road | Ginkgo
shbl:story-074:body-1.text_en:
Suzhou Industrial Park has only four ancient and notable trees, three of which are ginkgos; one of those ginkgos has died and been deregistered, so only the two ancient ginkgos described in this text remain. The villages where these two ancient trees stand were long ago demolished, yet at the gate of the water company—and even inside the construction site of the industrial park—traces of incense offerings can still be glimpsed. This shows that both trees were community trees (she shu) of village temples; even though the surroundings have been transformed beyond recognition, the believers of the original villages have not forgotten the coordinates of their old home.
Although they are registered under the park, the villages where they stand—Chaoqian Village and Wangbang Village—belonged to Wuzhong District until 2004, so in the Gazetteer of Ancient and Notable Trees of Suzhou the prefixes of these two trees' numbers read directly '吴中' (Wuzhong) rather than '园区' (Industrial Park). In its early years the park's redevelopment was carried out on a remarkably bold scale; perhaps being transferred to park management relatively late was one of the reasons they unexpectedly survived.
If we spread out a map, we find ancient ginkgos scattered like stars across the junction of today's Suzhou Industrial Park, Wuzhong District and Wujiang District. Although describing this location today is inevitably long-winded, twenty years earlier we could simply have called it the 'Chefang area.' The ginkgos of Chaoqian and Wangbang villages also originally belonged to Chefang Town. Although experience tells us they were once village-temple trees, the events of 2004 have already grown dim, and it is hard to learn whom the incense that has continued to this day is offered to—and in another generation, perhaps even this folk custom, which looks somewhat out of place amid steel and concrete, will be hard to sustain.
The memory of Chefang Town is already distant, but through ancient trees one after another and old bridges one after another, it seems we can still piece together her outline here in 2024.

shbl:story-075:body-1.context_header_en: "Stories of Trees" (Shu Bei Li Zhuan), Story 75 | Tinglin Garden, Yushan Town, Kunshan City | Qionghua Viburnum
shbl:story-075:body-1.text_en:
Yufeng Mountain in Tinglin Garden is to Kunshan what Tiger Hill is to Suzhou. The old Yufeng Mountain and Tiger Hill shared many similarities: the garden-like feel of a real mountain that seems artificial, concentrated clusters of shrines and tombs and of temples and monasteries, rich resources of ancient and notable trees, cliff inscriptions and traces of famous visitors... But the most similar thing was the immortal-hero air of a mountain hidden within a temple and ancient pagodas rising into the clouds.
The paired confrontation of the Lingxiao Pagoda of Huazang Temple and the Miaofeng Pagoda was once an iconic scenic site of Kunshan during the Republican period; regrettably, after the founding of the People's Republic, a radar station was built on Yufeng Mountain, and the two pagodas had to be demolished one after another. Yet according to the Suzhou Gazetteer of Ancient and Notable Trees, the thousand-year-old ginkgo below Huazang Temple is classified as a relic of Huiju Temple—so where does this Huiju Temple here come from? According to the Gazetteer of Kunshan's Tinglin Garden, Huiju Temple was founded earlier, and Huazang Temple was once a subsidiary courtyard of Huiju Temple; in the Yuan dynasty Huiju Temple fell into disuse, and in the Ming dynasty Huazang Temple occupied the pagoda courtyard of Huiju Temple on Yufeng Mountain and was rebuilt there, while the site of Huiju Temple at the foot of Yufeng Mountain was used for the City God Temple. Today the site of Huazang Temple at the summit is still a radar station, and Huazang Temple has had to be rebuilt at the foot of the mountain. When the thousand-year-old ginkgo was planted, the foot of the mountain was still the mountain gate of Huiju Temple, and Huazang Temple had not yet risen to prominence; hence it is classified as a relic of Huiju Temple. Although Tinglin Garden today has lost the iconic landscape of the two pagodas facing each other, thanks to ancient sites such as the old ginkgo it remains a high ground of Kunshan's humanistic history.
In addition, at the entrance of Tinglin Garden's east gate, east of the Chonggong Shrine dedicated to Gu Wenkang Gong, is a gathering place of nearly half of Kunshan's ancient and notable trees; the most famous of these should be a 310-year-old ancient qionghua viburnum, and the qionghua is precisely one of the Three Treasures of Kunshan famed throughout Jiangnan. Gu Wenkang Gong is Gu Dingchen; although the ancient city of Kunshan has a long history, it was not until the Yuan dynasty that rammed-earth walls were built, and during the Jiajing era of the Ming dynasty Gu Dingchen began building brick-and-stone walls at Kunshan to guard against Japanese pirates—one could say that the present outline of the ancient city of Kunshan took shape in Gu Dingchen's time, and building a shrine in such a conspicuous place and maintaining it down to the present naturally reflects his important place in the history of Kunshan's urban construction.
Most of the ancient trees in Tinglin Garden are around 110 years old; this is because during his tenure Mr. Fang Huan, the first civil affairs chief of Kunshan County in the Republican period, vigorously promoted the modernization of Kunshan County and built a large amount of public infrastructure, and the modern park-style layout of Tinglin Garden today was gradually established during this period; Mr. Fang Huan's tomb is hidden among these ancient trees. From the founder of the old-era city of Kunshan to the opener of Kunshan's modernization in the new era, Tinglin Garden and Kunshan remember the city's worthies.

shbl:story-076:body-1.context_header_en: Tree Stories, Entry 76 | Xiaqiao Neighborhood Center, Lujia Town, Kunshan City | Ginkgo
shbl:story-076:body-1.text_en:
Suzhou's Lujia Lane (菉葭巷) was originally called Lujia Lane (陆家巷), named because a wealthy Lu family lived in the lane. Lujia Town in Kunshan, by contrast, was originally called Lujia Town (菉葭镇) and was changed to its present name in 1966. Whether in daily life or in refined elegance, and whether it is a simple designation fixed by custom or a beautiful misunderstanding born of the soft Wu dialect—whether one sets the record straight or lets the error stand—this story does not really matter to us today.
As for the origins of Xiaqiao Village, one cannot avoid mentioning the Xiajia River. Legend has it that during the Yongle era (1403–1424 CE), Xia Yuanji, Minister of Revenue, personally led men to dredge the thoroughfare from the Wusong River to the Lou River. Minister Xia, rich in flood-control experience, was like an immortal who had tamed the Dragon King of the Jing River; under his command the two rivers were linked with practiced ease, settling a flood that stretched for a thousand li and irrigating a hundred mu of fine farmland. From then on this nameless wild creek was named the "Xiajia River." A river alone was not enough: the "Qingyun Bridge" rose up and spanned both banks. Later the areas on both sides of the bridge grew into a town called Xiajiaqiao Town, one of Kunshan's important commodity distribution centers at the time. In old Jiangnan, waterways were like today's railways in China, so the people naturally held Minister Xia in deep affection—how could "Qingyun Bridge" ever roll off the tongue as smoothly as "Xiajia Bridge"?
Today these two ancient ginkgos of Xiaqiao Village tower in front of the Neighborhood Center. Five hundred and fifty years ago was precisely the early-to-mid Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE); it is not impossible that people of that time planted them in memory of Xia Yuanji. Beside the ancient trees is a small rebuilt temple, its door locked; I still could not learn whom the little temple enshrines, but by now I already have an answer in my heart. This place was formerly the village committee compound, and before that a primary school. These two trees may not have witnessed Xia Yuanji's wondrous feat of flood control, but they have witnessed the profound changes of Xiaqiao Village's gradual modernization over half a century. "Qingyun Bridge" is gone, yet Xiaqiao Village today is more prosperous than in any era before. When the Neighborhood Center was nearing completion, the two trees' tenacious roots reached into the construction site; the builders were at a loss, and the villagers grew anxious. In the end, after coordination among many parties, the Neighborhood Center was recessed with a notch to let these two sacred trees live out their years in peace. The villagers cherish them just as they cherished Xia Yuanji in those days.
History remembers those who deserve to be remembered. However wealthy the Lu family may have been in their day, they left no name behind; Xia Yuanji fattened the common people and starved himself, and his name will be fragrant through the ages and passed down for ten thousand generations.

shbl:story-077:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees Told by Steles' Story 77 | Qiyu Village, Dianshanhu Town, Kunshan City | Ginkgo
shbl:story-077:body-1.text_en:
Beside Qiyu Pond there is Qiyu Village, and in Qiyu Village there is Qiyu Temple. Where the name 'Qiyu' comes from, no documentary record remains; recently, perhaps to promote a simplified place name, a spelling 'Ze'o' has also appeared. For the ruined temples and monasteries of other towns in Kunshan, source material is rarely found; Qiyu Temple is different, and we can roughly sort out two versions.
Version one: Sun Quan's mother and Sun Shangxiang, on their way back to Suzhou, heard that worship at Qiyu Temple was efficacious; an eminent monk had foreseen this and had them plant a ginkgo tree, to pray for the fulfillment of Eastern Wu's great enterprise.
Version two: Sun Quan, Emperor of Eastern Wu, himself planted a ginkgo tree and personally ordered the building of Qiyu Temple, to seek the eternal endurance of Eastern Wu's realm and a lifespan longer than the ginkgo's.
Let us look at what the old gazetteers say. According to the Revised Joint Gazetteer of Kun and Xin Counties (Kun Xin Liang Xian Xu Xiu He Zhi), Qiyu Temple was originally named Fuyan Chan Temple, 'built by the monk Youshan in the first year of the Zhiyuan era of the Yuan'—and so the various wondrous tales that circulate collapse of themselves. I suspect these are a collection of stories passed down generation after generation in Qiyu Village, compiled and recorded when oral history was being done. As for exaggerated claims cited by officials, such as 'the First Ancient Monastery of Jiangnan' and 'one of only two and a half temples under heaven,' one can only laugh them off. This 1,700-year-old ginkgo is also often marketed as the 'King of Trees of Jiangsu,' when in fact Dongshan alone has a 2,000-year-old ginkgo; it is hard to understand where these bizarre claims came from. Though the stories are somewhat exaggerated, they do show the scale of Qiyu Temple in its day. According to the Dianshanhu Gazetteer: 'Qiyu Temple, billed as the First Temple under Heaven, drew pilgrims from near and far, and was especially thriving at each temple fair. On that day the temple grounds were filled with all kinds of food stalls, general merchandise stalls, and toy stalls, with goods of every description dazzling the eye. Pilgrims, fairgoers, and traders flocked to the temple grounds from all directions, a sea of people packed so tightly that not a drop could squeeze through.'
Today, in front of the ancient Qiyu ginkgo stands a tobacco-and-liquor supermarket; in winter old people often gather beside the tree to bask in the sun. Not far away, Qiyu Temple's Great Incense-Flower Bridge, 'Chongfu Bridge,' still spans the pond; though now hidden among the reed marshes and ignored by all, it can still be crossed, while the 'Small Incense-Flower Bridge' has been demolished and rebuilt as a modern highway bridge. In a sense, though Qiyu Temple no longer exists, the various benefits it brought to Qiyu Village continue to this day.

shbl:story-078:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees' Entry 78 | Kunshan City, north of Penglai Road, east of Pengqian Road, Penglang Town | Ginkgo
shbl:story-078:body-1.text_en:
The name "Penglang" comes from "Penglai Langyuan" (the fairy gardens of Penglai), which shows how outstanding the people and spirit of this land have been. According to the Penglang Town Gazetteer, ancient ginkgos were very common in Penglang Town at that time, mostly distributed in front of temples and shrines. Yet today these two thousand-year-old ginkgos at the junction of Penglai Road and Pengqian Road are hard to identify; we tried asking local elders and, combining online materials with our own understanding alone, offer a simple reconstruction of their history.

In the Penglang town area there used to be one temple each in the south and the north, commonly called the South Temple and the North Temple. The South Temple was the City God Temple; who occupied the main seat is no longer known. It stood beside today's Penglai Road in the south of the town. In the late Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE) the City God Temple newly established the "Pengxi Second-Class Primary School," commonly called the "foreign-style school"; during the Republic it was reorganized as the "Penglang Town National Central Primary School"; after Liberation it became "Kunshan County Penglang Middle School"; later the middle school moved out and the site was used for government offices. Now that the town area has been demolished, only these two thousand-year-old ginkgos remain, in an unowned, overgrown yard, but incense still burns outside the wall. Originally the City God Temple and the school coexisted, and through successive reconstructions the temple gradually withdrew from the stage of history. It is said that the teacher and student Hu Shiyu and Ye Shengtao once taught and learned from each other here, and these two thousand-year-old ginkgos may also have witnessed the growth of these Republican-era masters. The North Temple was the Jinli Nunnery, dedicated to the Three Officials (Sanguan) faith, located beside Taiping Bridge, also called Huanlong Bridge, in the north of the town; the "Jinsu Evening Bell" was once one of the "Eight Scenes of Pengxi." In the late Qing a "Pengxi Public Primary School" was founded on the nunnery's original site, and thus Penglang Town acquired the curious distinction of calling its two primary schools the South Temple and the North Temple respectively. Today the original site has been rebuilt as the Sanguan Hall. There are now two towering ginkgos in the temple, but they are not ancient trees; according to Hu Shiyu's "Record of the Ancient Plum," the Jinli Nunnery once had two ancient plum trees. Today the ancient plums are gone, and Taiping Bridge has been repaired into disfigurement, so the old traces are hard to find.

shbl:story-079:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees' No. 79 | Wenxing Pavilion, Jinxi Town, Kunshan City | Buddhist Pine
shbl:story-079:body-1.text_en:
The Lotus Pond Zen Temple occupies the site of the former Chenmu Middle School. Beside Wenxing Pavilion there were originally one cypress and one pine; now only the Buddhist pine remains. Perhaps the beautiful wish for 'evergreen pines and cypresses' had its effect: although Wenxing Pavilion and the Jinxi cultural lineage it represents have weathered many hardships, they have survived to this day. Wenxing Pavilion was originally a landmark of the ancient town, also known as Pianyun Pavilion. Legend has it that, climbing the pavilion and gazing into the distance, one saw water and sky merge into a single hue, sails dotting the view, and white gulls flocking in flight. Today, with the Yuantong Hall on its left and the Jinxi Covered Bridge on its right, this giant that has stood for a century instead seems hunched and constrained.
Wenxing Pavilion no longer rises towering and precipitous, the Ten-Eye Bridge no longer lies like a long rainbow across the waves, and Jinxi is no longer called Chenmu. The outcome seems tinged with melancholy, yet they are still here, and perhaps that is already the best outcome. Today's Ten-Eye Bridge seems to connect two times and spaces: every winter, the sunlight of old follows the Tropic of Cancer and, together with the evening bell of the ancient temple, passes through the bridge's arches, and the Lotus Pond's bright mirror is just as it was a hundred years ago.

shbl:story-080:body-1.context_header_en: "Steles for Trees" Tree Stories, Entry 80 | Kunshan City, Zhangpu Town, Tang Village | Ginkgo
shbl:story-080:body-1.text_en:
According to the Zhangpu Town Gazetteer · Nangang Volume, this ginkgo in Tang Village is a relic of the village's "Yingzhen Daoist Abbey." The abbey was built in the mid-Chenghua era and was ultimately destroyed in the 1950s; its specific form is difficult to verify. Adding the "about 1476" mentioned in the town gazetteer to the tree age of "about 540 years" gives exactly 2016, while the plaque for the ancient and notable tree is dated 2017. From this it appears the ancient tree was dated through documentary sources.

This ancient ginkgo in Tang Village stands right beside a small stream that runs through the village, close to a reinforced-concrete bridge. Beneath the tree is a small riverside landing, covered by the ginkgo. Perhaps we can divide "ancientness" into two kinds. The first is the "ancient" inherent in an ancient object itself—for example, construction methods peculiar to a certain period, traces of weathering and moss, marks of blows and damage, and so on. Defined this way, perhaps only this tree in Tang Village deserves to be called "ancient." The second is "ancient" in the fabric of the place: the temperament of Tang Village, where every household seems to pillow its head on the river, and the orderliness of houses arranged along the water, carrying a Jiangnan-specific "complexity"—perhaps this too can be called a "sense of life," a "sense of plainness." From this point of view, Tang Village is brimming with ancient charm. Unfortunately, after talking with the village elders, we learned that the old people of the village are growing old and the young are surging toward the new town; in the future the village will inevitably become quieter and emptier. Now seems to be the last window of opportunity for a visit. We seem to stand at just such a crossroads: even today, gathering oral accounts about the ancient tree is difficult—so how, in the future, can these seldom-visited corners continue to pass on their stories? And the riot of autumn leaves is precisely a tragic, heroic last radiance, burning up life to achieve the final glory before all things wither and flourish in turn. Gazing at the gradually slanting sunset in the distance, one sighs: is this not also a microcosm of the "Tang Villages" of the world?

shbl:story-081:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees' No. 81 | Kunshan City, Yanfu Chan Temple, Qiandeng Town | Ginkgo
shbl:story-081:body-1.text_en:
Qinfeng Pagoda was built in the first year of the Dazhong Xiangfu era of the Northern Song dynasty (960–1127 CE), in 1008 CE. It was originally named for being close beside Qinzhu Hill, but most hills in Jiangnan were never as grand as their names suggest. By the eleventh year of the Qianlong era of the Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE), villagers took earth to repair the Tongyu Community Granary and simply dug this little earthen mound away entirely. From then on, Qinfeng Pagoda itself became Qiandeng's Qinzhu.
The thousand-year ginkgo on the northwest side of the pagoda has a listed tree age of 1,010 years. The tree leans to the north, like a devout old man at worship; a friend, imitating Zijin Temple's phrasing, called it 'the ginkgo worshipping the Buddha.' Although from the ground the tree looks unremarkable, seen from the air its form is extraordinarily lively, like a rising golden auspicious cloud, as if a Dunhuang flying apsara had been expressed as a tree, or like a hairpin thrust into the bun of the petite, lovely town of Qiandeng. 'Viewed broadside, a ridge; from the side, a peak'—yes, Qin 'Peak.' People today have the benefit of drones; the ancients would presumably have climbed Qinfeng Pagoda to admire the ginkgo. This tree has a temper of its own, refusing every angle from the pavilions and terraces near and far; only Qinfeng Pagoda alone can take in her beauty, and she and Qinfeng Pagoda seem to be one body. If we subtract the listed age of 1,010 years from the listing year of 2020, the result is exactly 1,010—almost the same lifespan as Qinfeng Pagoda. One pagoda and one tree nestled together for a thousand years: truly a fine tale.

shbl:story-082:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees' Entry 82 | Kunshan City, Yushan Town, Kunshan City Federation of Trade Unions | Ginkgo
shbl:story-082:body-1.text_en:
In the southwest of Kunshan county town there is a series of incongruous place names: Xiyuan Street, Xisi Lane, Shichuang Lane. Needless to say, there must once have been a temple of no small scale here. According to the map in the Continued Revised Combined Gazetteer of Kunshan and Xin, this place was once marked 'West Temple'—that is, the renowned Jingde Teaching Temple of Kunshan's history. Though the Jingde Teaching Temple no longer exists, it has passed down the precious Song dynasty (960–1279 CE) manuscript edition of the Buddhist canon, the Kunshan County Jingde Temple Great Canon, now held in the Tianjin Museum.
According to modern historical sources, the Republican-era Kunshan County government built a public library on the old foundation of the Jingde Teaching Temple—today's 'Red Building,' the Hou Beiren Art Museum. And now, not far from the Red Building, in the car park of the Federation of Trade Unions, two century-old ginkgos are hidden; I think they too must have stood within the Jingde Teaching Temple's bounds in their day.
The origin of the Jingde Teaching Temple is not hard to explain; old gazetteers describe it in much the same way: in the second year of the Xianhe era of the Eastern Jin (327 CE), the local official Wang Min donated his residence to found Baoma Temple, and in the third year of the Jingde era of the Song it was changed to its present name. Friends familiar with Suzhou place names may already feel a sense of déjà vu—does 'Jingde Road' near Guanqian seem to have a similar origin?
According to the Daoguang-era Suzhou Prefectural Gazetteer, the Shrine of Duke Wenke Wang (today's provincially protected Wang Ao Shrine) stands on the foundation of the old Jingde Temple, showing that there was indeed a Jingde Temple on Jingde Road at that time. The Republican-era Investigations of Song Pingjiang City Walls and Lanes gives a literature review of materials on Suzhou's Jingde Temple; though it cites several old gazetteers, there are no obvious contradictions, only differences in detail, from which we can obtain two important pieces of information: 1. The Jingde Temple was east of Huangniufang Bridge in the northwest of the county—Huangniufang Bridge being the name on the Southern Song (1127–1279 CE) Pingjiang Map, now called Huanglifang Bridge, which matches the present location of the Wang Ao Shrine. 2. The origin of the Jingde Temple is connected with the former residence of Wang Xun or his younger brother Wang Min; the Record of Wu Lands says 'in the second year of Xianhe of the Jin, Duke Xianmu Wang Xun's younger brother Min donated his residence to build it,' which is exactly the same as the record of Kunshan's Jingde Teaching Temple.
Content about the Jingde Temple first appears in the Tang dynasty (618–907 CE) Record of Wu Lands; in that old gazetteer both Suzhou's Jingde Temple and Kunshan's Jingde Teaching Temple were built in the second year of Xianhe of the Jin, and Suzhou's Jingde Temple was assigned the story of Wang Min donating his residence as a temple. However, much of the Record of Wu Lands has been lost, and Kunshan's Jingde Teaching Temple is already called Jingde Temple rather than Baoma Temple in the book, showing that this is content added after the third year of the Jingde era of the Song. And in Kunshan's earliest gazetteer, the Chunyou-era Yufeng Gazetteer of the Song (960–1279 CE), Kunshan's Jingde Teaching Temple is also recorded as founded in the second year of Xianhe of the Jin by Wang Min donating his residence, with the addition: 'Today the eastern side-hall of the temple has a Shrine of Prefect Wang. The prefect is Min.'
To sum up: Suzhou's Jingde Temple was the first to claim the story of Wang Min, while Kunshan's Jingde Teaching Temple has more supplementary detail, making it hard to judge which Jingde Temple it was whose residence was donated to become a temple.
At this point we are surely full of curiosity about Wang Min—could this old gentleman have gone around the world donating his residence to found temples, in the same year, with the temples happening to share the same name? Wang Min happens to be included in volume 65 of the Book of Jin; though his life is not covered in much detail, we can learn that he died in the thirteenth year of Taiyuan of the Jin (388 CE) at the age of 38, from which we can calculate that he was born in 351 CE. But the 'second year of Xianhe of the Jin' mentioned in several old gazetteers is 327 CE—how could he have donated his residence to found a temple before he was born? The Kunshan Daily article 'Wang Min and Jingde Temple,' published on 23 February 2011, also pointed out this problem, and found that among Kunshan's successive old gazetteers only the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE) author omitted the year, perhaps having noticed the contradiction between Wang Min's life and the Jingde Teaching Temple's history, while the other old gazetteers basically continued the Yufeng Gazetteer's account.
But now both temples are destroyed, and this documentary farce seems to have sunk into the sea of history, its truth hard to find.

shbl:story-083:body-1.context_header_en: "Stories of Trees" No. 83 | Xinyang Street, Yushan Town, Kunshan City | Chinese Scholar Tree
shbl:story-083:body-1.text_en: Gu Yanwu is a spiritual totem of Kunshan, and the Gu clan behind him also left a vivid mark on Kunshan. For example, at the center of today's Xinyang Street stands a century-old Chinese scholar tree; legend says this tree was part of the Gu family's grand residence in former days. Xinyang Street takes its name from the Xinyang County Office on the street. After the second year of the Yongzheng reign (Qing dynasty, 1644–1912 CE), the Kunshan county seat was governed separately by Kunshan County and Xinyang County. Although in the late Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE), when Gu Yanwu was active, the Xinyang County Office building did not yet exist, the fact that Gu descendants could occupy a core location beside a government office shows the strong social standing of the Gu clan at the time. In addition, Chaiwang Lane once had a Ming dynasty hall called Yiqing Hall, said to have been built by Gu Yanwu's grandfather Gu Shaofang, which shows that Chaiwang Lane was also a gathering place of prominent families in former days. Although it is hard for us to imagine Gu Yanwu socializing at the Gu residence, Yiqing Hall, on Chaiwang Lane in those days, the Former Residence of Gu Yanwu in Qiandeng has thoughtfully relocated a Ming dynasty hall from Dongshan, and perhaps through this we can better appreciate Gu Yanwu's living conditions at the time.

shbl:story-084:body-1.context_header_en: "Stories of Trees Told by Steles" Story 84 | Kunshan Second People's Hospital, Yushan Town, Kunshan City | Camphor Tree
shbl:story-084:body-1.text_en:
The original famous Jiangnan garden Banjian Garden, formerly named "Chunyu Pu" (Spring Jade Garden), was destroyed during the War of Resistance Against Japan. In modern times the site successively became Yuege School, Kunshan Public Hospital, Kunshan First People's Hospital and Kunshan Second People's Hospital; a city road continues to use the name "Yuege," and a pharmaceutical company continues to use the name "Banjian Garden." The present garden retains a residual earthen mound showing no trace of landscaping, one 500-year-old ancient camphor tree, several broken lake stones, eight column bases and one broken bluestone. The "Lotus Pond" mentioned as extant in the 1996 edition of the Yushan Town Gazetteer has been filled in, and the "Hancui Stone" mentioned as still extant in that book's Banjian Garden entry had, according to some sources, already been scattered and lost by the 1950s; experts including Tong Jun and Chen Congzhou all mention this famous peak in their garden monographs.
The edges of the earthen mound have been re-piled with stones, suspected to be remains of the original Lotus Pond revetment; no trace of the original climbing steps remains. The Yishan Pavilion has been rebuilt on the mound, but its renewal is so extensive that it cannot be determined whether it still stands on its original site. The ancient camphor tree beside the pavilion has two different tag numbers: one is 昆027, 460 years, and the other is 昆229, 500 years; the Suzhou Gazetteer of Ancient and Notable Trees accepts the latter. Around the rockery are two multi-stemmed wintersweet trees of considerable size, suspected to be old specimens. On the garden ruins remain four large column bases and four small column bases, possibly relics of "Xiaoyou Tang" (Little Existence Hall) in old photographs; the hospital authorities, on the basis of that name, rebuilt a steel-structure "Xiaoyou Pavilion," and on the other side stands a steel building of the same structure, the "Qingfeng Pavilion."
Though it has weathered every calamity, this important former cultural landmark of Kunshan has fortunately survived to this day with astonishing vitality.

shbl:story-085:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees, Inscribed for Eternity' Story 85 | Changshu City, Changshu Confucian Temple | Ginkgo
shbl:story-085:body-1.text_en: For more than a thousand years, the hundred-li Yuanhe Tang has linked the two ancient cities of Suzhou and Changshu. After the Yuanhe Tang enters Changshu city, it is renamed the Changshu Tang; today it is also called the Zhu Family River. Reaching Changshu Confucian Temple, the river's source runs far back, like the Changshu literary tradition opened by Yanzi more than two thousand years ago; the river flows long, like the ancient city of Qinchuan, silently civilizing a whole region. Taking the river as its Pan pond, south of the Zhu Family River there was once the temple wall, described figuratively as towering ten thousand ren high; today eight ancient ginkgos stand tall, their yellow leaves fluttering as if the palace wall has reappeared. North of the Zhu Family River stands the towering School Palace, where the Supreme Teacher and Sage is enshrined, accompanied by the county school on the west route and the auxiliary shrine to Yanzi on the east route. Unlike the ginkgos that flourish and stand on one side of the Pan pond in Confucian temples elsewhere, the nearly five-hundred-year-old ginkgo west of the Dacheng Gate at Changshu Confucian Temple is the most elegant of all the temple's trees. It appears prominently in the 'Plan of the School Palace' in the Guangxu Changzhao Combined Gazetteer. Now, having lived through nearly half a millennium, its trunk and branches cross the divide between the main path and the west route of the building complex, scattering a golden yellow over the human world. On the west route, ancient steles stand in clusters, piled with Changshu's long ages; a robe of golden yellow falls over the bluestone, and so trees and steles hand down biographies, and civilization is present here.

shbl:story-086:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees Told by Steles' Entry 86 | Changshu City, Fangta Garden | Ginkgo
shbl:story-086:body-1.text_en:
The ancient ginkgo in Fangta Garden is almost the same age as the Chongjiao Xingfu Temple Pagoda. Today the temple has vanished into history, and only the pagoda and the ginkgo remain. Looking at the square pagoda from Ta Nong, it is very much like a yellowed old photograph: the narrow strip of sky is full of tangled electric wires, and the pagoda labors to thrust itself out through the gaps, then stands tall. Considerately, it has kept watch over the heights of the surrounding garden buildings, not rising too far above them, and together with the ginkgo it forms a harmonious and elegant golden ratio—just like the Jiangnan of a painting.
Unlike the slender forms of other square pagodas in Jiangnan, the Guangfu Temple Pagoda is a brick-and-timber pagoda that combines the grace of the Song dynasty (960–1279 CE) with the stately beauty of the High Tang. Sitting on Yushan and with Shang Lake at its back, its unique geographical setting lets its flying eaves kiss the blue of water and sky as one, and share with the flocks of homing birds the clearest stretch of sky in Yucheng. The square pagoda seems to have become a symbol of Changshu: from the old cigarette packs that our fathers kept close at hand to the labels on the caps of yellow-rice-wine bottles on the dinner table, it is as if even the smoke rings breathed out by old Changshu people trace the outline of the square pagoda. It is like a pillar that anchors the sea: never mind how the great households beneath the pagoda come and go, so long as Shang Lake does not run dry and Yushan does not fall, and so long as the pagoda, screened by the ancient ginkgo, still lifts its eaves as it did when first built in the Song, Changshu will remain that ancient and beautiful Haiyu Qinchuan.

shbl:story-087:body-1.context_header_en: Tree Stories, Entry 87 | Yanyuan Garden, Changshu City | Chinese Trumpet Vine
shbl:story-087:body-1.text_en:
The Chinese trumpet vine fits the graduation season remarkably well: enterprising, always spreading upward; clean and crisp, with a simple flower shape that forever faces the sky; optimistic and passionate, with a highly saturated, soothing warm palette that is never cloying, seeming to carry a touch of youthful spirit. Different from all this, this first-grade ancient Chinese trumpet vine in Yanyuan Garden, Changshu, is currently the oldest Chinese trumpet vine in the Suzhou area. It did not bloom with the main wave of trumpet vines in June; now, as the height of summer draws to a close, it blooms brilliantly instead. It seems that whether people or plants, the old possess some unusual wisdom. The full bloom of the Chinese trumpet vine is a rare highlight of the year in Yanyuan Garden's North Garden, combining the elegance of a classical garden with the refinements of modern horticulture.
Drawing on some online sources, one may perhaps guess that it came from the demolished No. 1-1 Zhoushenmiao Lane. Volunteers for the Tree Monuments project visited Yanyuan Garden several times, and the garden's staff all said it was not an original of Yanyuan Garden. First, very few ancient Chinese trumpet vines survive; at present this is the only first-grade ancient tree of its kind in the Suzhou area. Second, in old photographs this ancient tree likewise leaned against a lake rock, so conditions for transplanting existed. Today, however, this lake rock may have been placed the wrong way round; the face displayed outward is not very attractive.
Considering that Chinese trumpet vines are very hard to keep alive when transplanted, it is understandable that this vine is now pruned in a not particularly attractive way; one might even call it lucky enough. Ji Xianlin's "The Tragedy of a Quiet Path" was once included in the Jiangsu Education Press junior-high Chinese textbook; it recounts the special experiences of a vine plant in Beijing's Yanyuan Garden in a special era, and is worth reading.

shbl:story-088:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees' No. 88 | Changshu City, Yushan Subdistrict, Changshu First People's Hospital | Yulan Magnolia
shbl:story-088:body-1.text_en:
The Suzhou Ancient and Famous Trees Gazetteer records a total of three ancient white yulan magnolias from Changshu. The white yulan magnolia at Xingfu Temple has already died; the remaining two white yulan magnolias are hidden in the Zhi Garden at Changshu First People's Hospital. However, the two magnolias labeled on site probably do not have such a long history, and the species is very likely Yulan magnolia × lily magnolia hybrids, not the white yulan magnolias described in the book.
There are many garden remains southwest of Changshu's old county town, but most of them grew out of the remains of Qian Dai's Xiaowangchuan. The Zhi Garden was expanded using the 'Nine-Bend Yellow River' waterway among them, and the character 'zhi' (之) itself carries something of that zigzagging, winding form. Regrettably, even the more recent Zhi Garden now has few architectural remains, yet quite a few old trees have been left in the garden. The saucer magnolia blossoms covering the trees are like one slightly tipsy red wine glass after another; when a gentle breeze passes, they push cups and exchange toasts, and amid clinking glasses they overflow with striking fragrance, fervently singing the brilliant chapter of spring. Perhaps through them we can still glimpse the grand scene of the time when the Qian family's garden occupied half the city. Yes—gardens, garden 'groves': without trees there is no garden. This is perhaps the meaning of seeking out trees.

shbl:story-089:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees' Entry 89 | Dongbang Town People's Government, Changshu City | Chinese Wolfberry
shbl:story-089:body-1.text_en:
The 'King of Jiangnan Wolfberries' was originally located at West Guanyin Hall in Renyang, Changshu. Legend has it that it twined around a hollow Buddhist pine in the temple; later the river beside the temple changed course, and after several transplants it is now overburdened, and its condition is not considered very good.
The Chinese wolfberry is a classic native plant. Though a deciduous shrub, it has slender, supple branches and is often used in gardens as a climbing ornamental. Because its fruit has health-preserving and medicinal value, it is sometimes associated with immortals and Daoist transcendents—for example, one of its alternate names is 'Staff of the Queen Mother of the West.' Wolfberries are also commonly seen in gardens; for instance, at the three peaks of the Lingering Garden—Guanyun Peak, Ruiyun Peak, and Xiuyun Peak—which I suspect originally carried the meaning of the three immortal mountains of the sea, the Lingering Garden once planted wolfberries beside Xiuyun Peak, evoking the imagery of immortal fruit and elixir pills. At Baosheng Temple in Luzhi, there are also three lake-stone rockeries in front of the Heavenly King Hall, and all of them are climbed by wolfberries; one of these wolfberries is already over a century old. In front of the rockery is a dry bridge, seemingly 'a water scene made in a dry garden,' and very likely also drawing on the imagery of the immortal mountains of the sea. Beyond this, temple gardens often feature mid-lake pavilions simulating immortal isles, such as the mid-lake pavilion at Xiyuan Temple in Suzhou and the mid-lake pavilion at the City God Temple in Shanghai. In the Lingering Garden, the island in the pond is called 'Little Penglai.' Considering the Jiangnan region's former enthusiasm for immortal and Daoist elements, perhaps this form—wolfberries climbing immortal mountains—was also a paradigm once popular in gardens of the past?

shbl:story-090:body-1.context_header_en: 'Steles for Trees' Tree Stories, Entry 90 | Hongdou Villa, Guli Town, Changshu City | Chinese Red-bean Tree
shbl:story-090:body-1.text_en:
Chen Yinke's 'A Separate Biography of Liu Rushi' opens with an ode to the red bean: "In former years, while sojourning in Kunming, I happened to purchase a single red bean from the Qian family's old garden at Baimao Port in Changshu, and so I had the idea of annotating and explaining the poems on the bond between Qian and Liu." The residence of Qian Qianyi and Liu Rushi at Baimao had a century-old red-bean tree planted during the Jiajing reign of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE), and people of the time called it "Hongdou Villa" (Red-bean Villa).
The red-bean tree's flowering and fruiting is a rare event, occurring perhaps once in several decades. In former times it drew literary men to write poems about it; today it attracts media attention, and almost every occasion leaves a written record. In the eighteenth year of the Shunzhi reign of the Qing dynasty (1661 CE), when Qian Qianyi was celebrating his eightieth birthday, "the red-bean tree flowered again after twenty years, and by the ninth day, at the time of my humble birthday, it had set just one seed," delighting the couple immensely; Qian Qianyi wrote eighteen red-bean poems in one burst. In the fourth year of the Daoguang reign of the Qing dynasty (1824 CE), the red-bean tree bloomed in full; Qu Shaoji and his son Qu Yong, owners of the Iron Qin and Bronze Sword Library (Tieqin Tongjian Lou), made a special trip to view it, and after returning asked friends to make a painting and inscribe poems, which were bound together as the 'Red-bean Flower Painting and Poetry Album'—entrusting their longing to ancients of a hundred years before, and leaving it for us a hundred years later.

shbl:story-091:body-1.context_header_en: 'Steles for Trees' Tree Stories, Entry 91 | Changshu City, Meili Town, Jusha Garden | Ginkgo
shbl:story-091:body-1.text_en:
This ancient ginkgo stands in Jusha Garden in Meili. It is said that a Fayun Chan Temple once stood below the Jusha Pagoda, and that there were two ancient ginkgos there that were "taller than the pagoda"; later the temple collapsed, and only this one ginkgo survived. Standing beneath the tree, with gold above and gold below, any question about time seems pale and powerless within its long life—could the holy radiance that the local grandmothers say appeared here be the light filtered down through these golden leaves?
In modern times the Jusha Pagoda has become riddled with holes, with only a ring of hollow pagoda wall still standing; it nestles close to the ancient ginkgo like two old people supporting each other. Fortunately, Jiangnan favored pagodas with brick bodies and wooden eaves, which added a layer of insurance for the survival of history: fire can burn only the outer wooden eaves, and as long as the brick body does not fall and the ginkgo does not wither, Jiangnan can always flourish once again.

shbl:story-092:body-1.context_header_en: 'Steles for Trees' Tree Stories, Entry 92 | Yao Family Tree Peony Hall, Xinzhuang Town, Changshu City | Tree Peony
shbl:story-092:body-1.text_en:
Changshu is the home of tree peonies in Jiangnan. Since 1992, the Shanghu Scenic Area has held a tree peony festival every year, and the origin of that festival must begin with 1990, when the scenic area introduced branches from the old tree peony at Yaojiaqiao in Xinzhuang Town for cultivation.
According to the 1990 edition of the Changshu City Gazetteer, the Yao family was a prominent clan that settled in Changshu after the Song dynasty court moved south. On the last page of their genealogy is precisely a seven-character regulated verse praising this peony, which can corroborate the old peony; many plain and homely peony legends still circulate locally today, which is enough to show how much the Yao clan cherished and valued the old peony.
The peony is a flower of wealth and honor; in former times it could even reflect a family's rise and decline, but today's Yao descendants are not stingy about opening their courtyard gates every flowering season for visitors to admire it. At Yaojiaqiao, besides this old peony, there are four other peonies no smaller than it, because in the 1980s their owner shared cuttings of the ancestral peony with four other branches of the Yao family in the village; today those four peonies have also grown into mature plants, sharing this feast of national beauty and heavenly fragrance with visitors from all directions. At the same time, the peony festival at the Shanghu Scenic Area has also grown livelier; the scenic area cultivates large numbers of offspring plants of the Yao family peony, striving to let more visitors appreciate the splendor of the old peony.
Perhaps the best way to protect a culture is to internalize it in the heart and externalize it in action, elevating it from the possession of a private resource to something shared with the public. From being hidden deep behind high walls to sending out branches and scattering leaves, the Yao family peony has thus become an immortal legend in spirit.

shbl:story-093:body-1.context_header_en: Tree Stories, Entry 93 | Wangyue Lou, Yushan Town, Changshu City | Chinese Chestnut
shbl:story-093:body-1.text_en:
In the noodle shop at the foot of Yushan, beside Xingfu Temple, square tables are set out and canopies pitched; it is busy all year round. Here people drink a cup of tea, eat a bowl of noodles, and begin a day of slow living. Dense stands of towering old trees weave a canopy of green shade, quietly guarding the warm hum of everyday life.
Suzhou's oldest Chinese chestnut tree stands right in front of the old Wangyue Lou noodle shop. Suzhou has abounded in chestnuts since ancient times. The Qing-dynasty (1644–1912 CE) writer Jin Youli records in A Study of Taihu: "Chestnuts come from the Eastern and Western Hills; those from Xiwu on the Eastern Hill are especially fine." Besides the Eastern and Western Hills, there is Yushan in Changshu. Fan Chengda of the Southern Song dynasty (1127–1279 CE) wrote in the Wujun Gazetteer: "Dingshan chestnuts come from Dingshan in Changshu; this chestnut is smaller than the common chestnut. Its fragrance and flavor are superb, and it is also called the 'musk sachet' because it is fragrant and soft; dried in a gentle breeze it is even better." Dingshan is the northern peak of Yushan. Wang Boguang, a Southern Song native of Changshu, wrote the poem 'Dingshan Chestnuts': "Within the yellow hedge the fruit is held; the purple husk puts forth its outer colors. ... Who would have thought the musk sachet could rank foremost in all the world?" In the Yuan dynasty (1271–1368 CE), Zhang Yu sent fresh chestnuts to Ni Zan with a teasing note: "First I offer Yunlin three hundred of them; better than sending sour oranges with a letter in return." Today the people of Changshu call the Yushan chestnuts 'benshan li', meaning locally grown. Because they carry the fragrance of osmanthus, they are also called 'guihua li' (osmanthus chestnuts). Osmanthus fragrance and golden chestnuts are the most enchanting cross-section of Jiangnan in golden October.

shbl:story-094:body-1.context_header_en: Tree Stories, No. 94 | Yushan Subdistrict, Changshu City — Sanfeng Qingliang Zen Temple | Qiu Catalpa
shbl:story-094:body-1.text_en:
These two qiu catalpas stand outside the mountain gate of Sanfeng Temple and have almost become the emblem of Sanfeng Temple; they are one of only three places in greater Suzhou where ancient qiu catalpa blossoms can be enjoyed. The qiu catalpa may be counted a native tree planted everywhere in the north, but on coming to Jiangnan it has become a rare tree whose value lies in its scarcity.
Yet the Chinese name of the tree, qiu (楸), contains the character for autumn (秋), though it is by no means an autumn flower—how is this to be explained? If we exercise a little imagination and cut spring into three parts—early spring, mid-spring, and late spring—then add the Jiangnan early summer, whose profusion of blossoms rivals spring itself, we get four equal parts. The qiu catalpa blooms in late spring, which happens to be the very end of the three springs, precisely the "autumn" of the four equal parts. The two qiu catalpas at Sanfeng Temple are even more special: their flowering season seems to come a week later than that of other qiu catalpas. Seen from a certain angle, they are exceedingly considerate: they do not trouble us when the hundred flowers vie in beauty, and when the blossoms are fading they silently bring a tree full of fragrance before us as consolation. Perhaps few mention them, but they are always here, blooming on time in the season when the fragrance is spent.

shbl:story-095:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees' No. 95 | Longdian Villa, Yushan Subdistrict, Changshu City | Ginkgo
shbl:story-095:body-1.text_en:
This ancient ginkgo stands at the Longdian site of the former Sanfeng Temple at the northern foot of Yushan. Its bark is rough, cracked, and straight and vertical, and at the middle of the trunk it twists spirally upward again; the tree's form resembles a dragon. The ancient ginkgo has put forth nine suckering trunks—children and grandchildren—with luxuriant branches and leaves, and so it is called 'Nine Sons Embracing the Dragon.' A legend about a 'Dragon Mother' also circulates locally, and it is a cultural landscape known to every household in Changshu. The famous modern painter Qian Yankang also left a painting made here.
The surroundings of Longdian are steeped in antiquity: stepping down the stairs, one finds green curtains of pearl-like verdure, gnarled branches blocking the way, an immortal breeze swirling around, and a spring pool facing a wall where flecks of light leap like gold. Moss traces climb the steps, ancient trees reach the sky, gathering the light of heaven and the shadows of clouds into the clear, cool pool water; fish swim in the dragon pool, egrets wander the blue sky, and people are intoxicated amid it all. The ancient ginkgo leans askew, just like a doddering old grandmother letting the children play and romp at her knees—just as she has done through more than a thousand springs and autumns past.
