shbl:story-096:body-1.context_header_en: “Stories of Trees” No. 96 | Yushan Subdistrict, Changshu City, Xiaoyunqi Temple | Chinese Wisteria
shbl:story-096:body-1.text_en:
This wisteria seems to be a relic of the Ming-dynasty (1368–1644 CE) Tengxi Thatched Cottage, and later came into the possession of Xiaoyunqi Temple. Today the temple has been rebuilt; Tengxi, Tengxi—a stream formed by wisteria petals flowing down—is spectacular and romantic. It is a pity that in recent years the wisteria's flowers have been sparse, which is slightly regrettable.
Beside the wisteria, “ten thousand bushels of bright pearls” seep out from a steep, rugged rock face, spilling from the yellow-stone mass as a spring: this is the Pearl Dew Spring in the Small Stone Cave, archaic and secluded. It is said that the tea and plain noodles the temple provides are all prepared with mountain spring water.
The great majority of wisterias in the Suzhou area have been artificially trained to cling to trellises—gentle and well-behaved, dutifully playing the game of filling in color on the trellis lattice, like literati gentlemen of upright character who never overstep the rules. Not so this three-hundred-and-fifty-year-old ancient wisteria at Xiaoyunqi Temple: though its age is not an advantage, its trunk and branches should be relatively thick and sturdy among the surviving ancient wisterias in Suzhou. Using the yellow stone as a natural trellis, it coils upward ruggedly all the way to the vault of heaven, dragon-whisker tendrils hanging down and purple scales revealing their sacredness, bursting forth with astonishing vitality. It has the literary spirit of the wisteria, and also bears some resemblance to those loyal and martial officials at the end of dynasties who laid aside literati reserve to remonstrate bluntly unto death and strive to turn back the tide—Fan Zhongyan, Gu Yanwu… And this seems, by coincidence, to accord with Suzhou's city character.
shbl:story-096:body-1.hook_zh: 三百五十年古紫藤以黄石为天然爬架，粗犷盘旋直至穹宇，龙须垂枝、紫鳞显圣。

shbl:story-097:body-1.context_header_en: "Stories of Trees" No. 97 | Baoyan Scenic Area, Yushan Subdistrict, Changshu City | Chinese Bayberry
shbl:story-097:body-1.text_en:
Baoyan bayberries are renowned throughout Jiangnan. According to the Kangxi-era "Changshu County Gazetteer," "in the fourth month, Baoyan bayberries are at their most abundant, and visitors go in groups to view them, an activity called 'looking at bayberries.'" Yet the listed ancient bayberry trees at Baoyan are not growing especially well. The oldest, 常543, died about eight years ago; its original site was the center of a circular island in the uphill footpath, and its root base has now been filled in. At the original site of 常540, one can find 常543's early blue tag; at that time Changshu's ancient and notable tree numbering had not yet been reorganized, so the number on the tag then was 常0044. The original sites of 常538, 常539, and 常540 were all on either side of the uphill trail. Not long after 常543 died, these three trees underwent the reorganization of ancient and notable tree numbering; in that assessment, their ages were all adjusted from the original 120 years to the present 315 years. According to the recollection of a man who runs a tea room in the scenic area, after the previous round of renovations at Baoyan Scenic Area, the scenic area seems to have transplanted 常540 to the plaza on the south side of the scenic-area entrance, while at 常540's original site they placed 常543's early blue tag as a marker.
In fact, within the tea rooms and bayberry orchards contracted by farming households inside Baoyan Scenic Area, there are many unlisted old trees whose size and growth are far better than those of these few listed ancient trees; the farmers say orally that these trees are all over a hundred years old. Because fruit trees are economic crops, privately contracted ancient trees often receive more meticulous care than ordinary ancient and notable trees.

shbl:story-098:body-1.context_header_en: "Stories of Trees" No. 98 | Jijia Bridge, Mocheng, Mocheng Subdistrict, Changshu City | Ginkgo
shbl:story-098:body-1.text_en:
Beside Jijia Bridge stands an ancient ginkgo, and beside the ancient ginkgo there was once an old temple. According to the villagers, it was originally the Sanyuan Shrine; in recent years some scholars have also suggested it may have been a shrine to Zhou the God (Zhou the Filial Son). Zhou Rong (Zhou the God / Zhou the Filial Son) is a local deity of Changshu who was elevated to divine status; in life he practiced the filial piety taught by Yan Yan, the "Confucius of the South": for his mother, who suffered from an eye ailment, he "licked [her eyes] until her sight returned," and for his gravely ill father he "scraped flesh from his thigh to make a broth and offered it to him." The people of Changshu admired him and built a temple in his memory after his death; the old gazetteers also record many instances of him displaying miracles and saving people from fire and flood. Temples dedicated to him are therefore widespread in the Changshu area, and around most of these temples there are also ancient ginkgos—perhaps somewhat in the manner of the Mengjiang Hall at Dongshan.

Local villagers say that every year many villagers who have moved away return to visit this ancient ginkgo. Many are folk who lived in the village as children and later settled in the city; some even come back specially from Shanghai. Though ordinarily scattered far and wide, each late autumn they seem, touched by the spirit of "Zhou the Filial Son," to gather in their old home without prior arrangement.

Standing beneath the tree, it seems even the sunlight takes on its warm yellow hue; a flood of gold pours down with the light, laying a dignified and splendid golden dress over the aged stone-slab bridge, and paving a golden road home for those who feel timid about nearing their native place—such is the charm of a village tree. However long we have been away, however far from home, we are forever certain that it will be waiting for us beside that bridge we have crossed countless times.

shbl:story-099:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees' in Shubei Lizhuan, Entry 99 | Changshu City, Xieqiao Grain Management Office, Changfu Subdistrict | Ginkgo
shbl:story-099:body-1.text_en:
In the large courtyard of the Grain Management Office on Xieqiao Old Street, a thousand-year-old ginkgo is hidden from view. The Grain Management Office was once Shuangzhong Temple, commemorating two generals who died heroically while besieged at Suiyang during the An Lushan Rebellion: Zhang Xun and Xu Yuan. These two ginkgos were extraordinarily magnificent; even Weng Tonghe, the emperor's tutor, personally came to Xieqiao and made the painting 'Twin Ginkgos of the Shuangzhong Shrine' for the two ancient ginkgos in front of the temple, inscribing two poems. Unfortunately, the temple is now desolate, and one of the ginkgos was struck by lightning and died; of the once-glorious Shuangzhong Temple, only a single ginkgo remains today.
In Jiangnan, many ancient bridges face a small temple directly; sometimes when the temple is destroyed, people burn incense at the bridgehead, and one can often see soot-blackened stones and leftover candle wax by the bridges—this is what is commonly called the temple-bridge culture of Jiangnan market towns. Similar to ancient bridges, when a temple is destroyed, people sometimes also offer incense beneath ancient ginkgos; today many old trees still have small niches and small censers set beneath them, and there is no need to be alarmed on seeing them. These 'incongruous' incense and candles are very interesting: folk belief in Jiangnan seems indestructible. Most of it does not worship universal deities but rather 'Lord So-and-so's Temple,' 'Granny So-and-so's Nunnery,' or 'Fierce General So-and-so's Hall'—figures who may once have benefited a locality, left behind fine poems, and were then deified locally. With stories passed down from generation to generation, steady offerings naturally follow; no wonder temples and shrines of every kind remain scattered across Jiangnan today.

shbl:story-099:body-1.hook_en: The Xieqiao Grain Management Office yard was once Shuangzhong Temple; of its two ancient ginkgos, one died after a lightning strike, leaving one.

shbl:story-100:body-1.context_header_en: 'Trees with Stele Biographies' Tree Stories, Entry 100 | Taicang City, Former No. 1 Middle School, Chengxiang Town | Chinese Wisteria
shbl:story-100:body-1.text_en:
Taicang has a little-known garden called Dongting Fenxiu Garden, whose recent history has been fairly complicated. It was originally a small pleasure garden within Taicang No. 1 Middle School, and successively became the archaeological excavation site of the Fancun Jing site and then the construction site of the Dongting Fenxiu Yayuan residential development. Because its location has always made it hard for outsiders to see, it is somewhat awkward despite its outstanding cultural and historical status. The No. 1 Middle School campus was once the site of the Taicang Prefectural Examination Hall in the Qing dynasty (1644–1912 CE); originally, north of the wisteria trellis stood an examination hall stele inscribed by Lu Zengxiang, of considerable historiographical value, which has now been moved to the school's new campus. In modern times many Confucian temples and examination halls have been converted into schools, which perhaps counts as a kind of continuity in architectural function.
Many campuses in Suzhou have wisteria corridors, among them century-old trees at Suzhou No. 1 Middle School and Taicang No. 1 Middle School; the 'wisteria ensemble' even has a star member in the Wen Wisteria at Prince Zhong Mansion. It could be called Suzhou's most bookish plant, often used as a metaphor for the literary lineage, carrying the fond memories of generation after generation of students. Today Dongting Fenxiu Garden has almost no architectural remains, only more than twenty ancient and notable trees in less than good condition, while the construction site is desolate and overgrown with weeds. Yet some valuable details can still be discerned: the red-brick classroom building on the site was once a landmark structure built uniformly for provincial key middle schools at the time, and the new iron trellis erected in front of the concrete wisteria climbing frame stands every which way yet is extraordinarily sturdy, perhaps made by teachers and students themselves in earlier years. Although the No. 1 Middle School moved away more than ten years ago, standing beneath the dilapidated wisteria trellis one can almost still hear the students' laughter and play and the sound of their reading aloud.

shbl:story-100:body-1.hook_en: More than a decade after Taicang No. 1 Middle School moved away, its wisteria trellis on the derelict site seems to still echo with students' reading.

shbl:story-101:body-1.context_header_en: 'Stories of Trees' in Shubei Lizhuan, Entry 101 | Nanyuan, Chengxiang Town, Taicang City | Chinese Plum
shbl:story-101:body-1.text_en: The noble purity and elegance of the crane and the plum are where traditional literati placed their ideals of transcendence, and also the label by which the many grandees tossed about in the currents of officialdom displayed their detachment from the world. Nanyuan, built in the late Ming dynasty (1368–1644 CE) by Grand Tutor Wang Xijue, Senior Grand Secretary during the Wanli reign, was where he planted his immortal plums; by the time his grandson Wang Shimin, foremost of the Four Wangs, managed it, such features as the Xiuxue Hall, Xiangtao Pavilion and Crane-Plum Immortal Hall set off the garden's ancient plums all the more, and the most celebrated of them was the ancient plum trained by binding into the likeness of a crane, 'A Slender Crane Dancing'—only under artificially imposed suffering did a plum tree come to possess a crane's numinous spirit. Yet splendor ultimately cannot withstand the shifting of times; as the rolling iron hooves came south, the Southern Ming, drugged with dreams of peace in its temporary refuge, could not withstand the piercing cold from beyond the passes, and Taicang city quietly changed hands without bloodshed. Behind this, however, a most romantic story circulated: it was said that the one who led Taicang's gentry out to surrender to the Qing army was none other than Lord Yanke, Wang Shimin, and that the court officials who spoke so loftily of great righteousness completed their change of identity with exceedingly supple postures; yet the immortal crane that Lord Yanke kept at Nanyuan broke free of its enclosure and flew toward the Qing camp outside the city, until it died of exhaustion. Then came another season when plum shadows braved the frost; by then Lord Yanke had already combed his hair into the money-mouse tail braid at the back of his head, and in Nanyuan the Recalling-the-Crane Hall and the Crane Tomb had quietly been built, and above the Crane Tomb stood the ancient plum called 'A Slender Crane Dancing.' The temporary prosperity bought with surrender could not withstand the length of the years; even the Wang family, with four generations holding first-rank office, had nearly declined by the late Qing (1644–1912 CE), and over more than two hundred years Nanyuan changed owners several times, while 'A Slender Crane Dancing' silently watched one party after another take the stage within this patch of heaven and earth. Wind and rain and the years are ultimately heartless; then came another spring day when 'A Slender Crane Dancing' bloomed no more, and the garden's owner at the time, Qian Baochen, Hunan Provincial Governor, wrote 'Record of the Crane-Plum Immortal Shadow' to mourn the ancient plum and invited Qian Pu to make a painting; that year was precisely 1841, the year from which the humiliating history of the vast ancient nation began. Through a century of vicissitudes, Nanyuan was reduced to broken walls and ruined foundations, and the trunk and branches of 'A Slender Crane Dancing' were likewise turned to ashes there. By the reconstruction of Nanyuan at the end of the 20th century, several Ming- and Qing-dynasty old residences in the city were relocated here; the Ming-dynasty Chen residence's ironwood hall on Beimen Street became the new generation's Crane-Plum Immortal Hall, and many century-old plums from the city were also transplanted around it, continuing the story that belongs to 'A Slender Crane Dancing' and distilling the long years and vicissitudes of the city of Taicang.

shbl:story-102:body-1.context_header_en: "Stories of Trees" Story 102 | Taicang City, Liuhe Town, Mingde Junior High School | Crape Myrtle
shbl:story-102:body-1.text_en:
In 1912, Wu Jianxiong was born in Liuhe Town, Taicang. Her father, Wu Zhongyi, planted a crape myrtle at the Mingde Women's Vocational School that he had founded with his own hands, and gave her a gentle childhood name, "Weiwei." Later, she went far away to study in the United States and, for her outstanding achievements in physics, was hailed as the "Oriental Marie Curie."
In 1973, Wu Jianxiong returned with her husband, Dr. Yuan Jialiu, to the Mingde campus from which she had long been parted; the little sapling of those years had already grown into a grand, gracefully spreading tree. Wu Jianxiong donated funds several times to build a classroom building and staff housing, and beside the crape myrtle she had a two-story building in the style of Jiangnan water towns built, named "Ziwei Pavilion." After her death in 1998, her grave was sited beside Ziwei Pavilion. This Jiangnan woman, always in a qipao, intellectual and elegant, was just like the crape myrtle: not contending for beauty in spring, seemingly made of tiny fragments, yet with an extremely long flowering season—stubborn, persistent, displaying vigorous vitality.

shbl:story-103:body-1.context_header_en: "Stories of Trees" No. 103 | Taicang City, Shuangfeng Toll Station on the Shanghai–Yixing Expressway, Shuangfeng Town | Ginkgo
shbl:story-103:body-1.text_en: In the Ming (1368–1644 CE) and Qing (1644–1912 CE) dynasties, Taicang's literary culture flourished, producing a large number of prominent families that endured for over a century. Solemnly commemorating ancestors and fostering closeness and harmony among kin were the most basic requirements that traditional society placed on family organization. Yet times and circumstances have shifted, and today the cemeteries of Taicang's illustrious families are extremely rare; only the Wang family cemetery at Liuhe and the Qian Huan family cemetery at Shuangfeng survive. Behind the one Ming-dynasty ginkgo and eight Qing-dynasty ginkgos encircling Qian Huan's lofty tomb lies the secret of why this cemetery still exists. As the saying goes, "One sees no tombs of the heroes of the Five Mausoleums"; in traditional society, the rise and fall of a family often determined whether its ancestral sacrifices would continue. The disappearance of a family cemetery's sacrifices, until it was buried in the vast fields, was the embodiment of a family's end. In the mid-Ming period, Qian Huan successively served as regional inspector and grand coordinator in Jinan (the region south of the capital), Sichuan, Henan, and Nangan. His governance of a region could bring that region peace and order. At that time, Sichuan and Nangan were both places where Han and non-Han peoples lived together. Qian Huan began with the economy: by reorganizing Sichuan's well salt and by pacifying the Zangke peoples through suppression and appeasement, he realized for the people his political ideal, expressed in the words "If only the Yellow Dragon would go drinking, why trouble the White Horse to cross the river?", and generated tens of thousands of taels of silver in revenue for the court, while he himself always lived frugally. Qian Huan's descendants did not continue their ancestor's achievements in the civil examinations; both of his sons served only as county magistrates after passing as tribute students, and thereafter there were no more high officials. Yet Qian Huan's fine family tradition of "living in the village with integrity and restraint, and disciplining his sons and clansmen" meant that right up to the late Qing and early Republic, the elders of his hometown still "praise his great virtue to this day." Today the Qian Huan family cemetery has been successfully restored, thanks also to years of effort by his fourteenth-generation descendant Qian Li and to government support. And the nine ancient Ming- and Qing-dynasty ginkgos encircling the Qian Huan family cemetery are precisely the best embodiment of Qian Huan's clean and peaceful governance and of his descendants' harmony.

shbl:story-104:body-1.context_header_en: Tree Stories, Entry 104 | Sanjia Market, Fuqiao Town, Taicang City | Ginkgo
shbl:story-104:body-1.text_en:
The Sanjia Market ginkgo was once a relic of Li Wang Temple. The Li Wang faith is fairly common in the three northern counties of Suzhou and usually refers to Li Lu, a Southern Song (1127–1279 CE) general who once earned merit by protecting Emperor Gaozong of Song. According to the Taicang City Gazetteer, the ginkgo was planted by hand by Chancellor Chen Yizhong and the young Song emperor. Though the legend may not be entirely credible, it undoubtedly reflects the patriotic thinking of the local people.
Unlike the West, China has since ancient times had a tradition of sacrificing to ancestors and heroic figures. From the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors of Chinese origins to Lord Guan, who became the Sangharama Bodhisattva, from the model teacher of all ages to each household's ancestral hall, these formed an earthly heaven distinct from gods, Buddhas, ghosts, and spirits, and became a shared memory in the Chinese collective subconscious. Our ancestors seem always to have treated religion with a kind of plain pragmatism, often joking wryly that "a clay Bodhisattva cannot cross the river" or that "a flood has washed away the Dragon King's temple." In Ming (1368–1644 CE) and Qing (1644–1912 CE) storytelling, the black-humor scene of "if it's not efficacious, smash this shabby temple" also often appears. Yet toward those great figures who once benefited a region, the people have always passed down the flame without daring to neglect them.

shbl:story-105:body-1.context_header_en: "Stories of Trees" No. 105 | Shuangxing Temple, Daxin Town, Zhangjiagang City | Ginkgo
shbl:story-105:body-1.text_en:
For many people, the first question upon entering Shuangxing Temple is: why does "Shuangxing" (Double Ginkgo) Temple have three ancient ginkgos? According to the Zhangjiagang Archives, Shuangxing Temple was originally a River God Temple; when it was expanded, the monks planted two ginkgos by hand, and only then was it renamed Shuangxing Temple. Several decades later a third tree was added, creating today's arrangement of three ginkgos. In sharp contrast to the strictly disciplined Shuangxing Temple, the street beside it is the busiest commercial quarter of the old Nianfeng town area. "Humans and gods rejoicing together" seems a more fitting description: in the villages of Jiangnan in former times, temples and shrines often became subtle public spaces, with something of the feel of a council chamber or a great hall. Places with temples are often the liveliest; commerce thrives on foot traffic, and temples need supplies—the two hit it off at once, and the pairing of temple and market quickly became an established and solid social consensus.
The people setting up stalls on old Nianfeng Street are all local grandpas and grandmas; you could say they are doing business, but really they just want to find old friends to chat about family matters and pass the time. In the clear green canal, flecks of white light glimmer; on the bank, an old man in a rattan chair gently waves a palm-leaf fan, and on the ground within reach of his fingertips an old radio sings opera as if no one else were around. My eyes wandered, and I stumbled by mistake into an old barbershop with yellowing wallpaper; the scissors in hand went "snip, snip, snip" like a dancing butterfly, flying together with the ginkgo leaves filling the sky toward a long, distant old time. As for whether the incense at Shuangxing Temple is truly efficacious, people look at these three ancient ginkgos that have weathered every calamity and still stand tall, and in their hearts they have long since made up their minds.
